liyeque.name: Que of Li Ye
liyeque.sub: Zitong · Eastern Han single stone que
liyeque.lede: At the foot of Mount Changqing, a tapering stone que shaft carries the memory of Li Ye. Only one que survives; the capstone seen today is a later replacement.
facts: Generally dated to the early Eastern Han and traditionally to the 12th year of Jianwu (36); it is entered here with an approximate year, and the later capstone is not counted as original Han fabric.
A single stone que survives, its shaft about 2.45 m tall. The south face originally carried an inscription and the Qing-dynasty Record of Moving the Que; the other three faces are plain.
In the 25th year of Daoguang in the Qing (1845), county magistrate Zhou Shutang found the damaged shaft and moved it to the Shrine of Li Jieshi for protection. The plate depicts its present form.
captions: Que of Li Ye · South face of the surviving que

taishique.name: Taishi Que of Dengfeng
taishique.sub: West que · Spirit-way que of Zhongyue Temple
taishique.lede: China's oldest surviving ritual structures are not halls but a pair of stone que gate-towers. In 118 CE (Yuanchu 5 of the Eastern Han), Lü Chang, magistrate of Yangcheng, raised these spirit-way towers before the temple of Mount Taishi, copying the timber gate-towers of his day into stone: a lower 'child' tower leans against each 'mother' tower, and the roofs are carved with ridges, tile rows and rafters. The plate shows the west tower, slightly taller than the east one at 3.96 m, with the seal-script title 'Zhongyue Taishi Yangcheng' still on its south face.
facts: Form: The two towers face each other 6.75 m apart; each joins a mother tower to a lower child tower on its outer side, built up from base, shaft and roof. The west tower stands 3.96 m, its shaft laid in eight courses of stone, its roof imitating a hip roof with main ridge, hip ridges, tile rows and rafters.

Dating: A clerical-script inscription under the eave of the west tower's child tower, on the north face—27 lines of 7 characters—records why Lü Chang and others built the que in 118 CE; the six-character seal-script title 'Zhongyue Taishi Yangcheng' is cut in relief on the south face. In 1971 the east tower's roof was restored from scattered fragments.

Significance: With the Shaoshi and Qimu que (118–123) it forms the 'Three Han Que of Zhongyue', the only Han temple que surviving in China. The shafts carry low-relief scenes of carriage processions, horse acrobatics, cockfights, jugglers, pavilions and the Azure Dragon and White Tiger; in 2010 the site was inscribed as part of the UNESCO World Heritage 'Centre of Heaven and Earth' monuments of Dengfeng.
captions: Taishi Que · South face of the west que
5th year of Yuanchu, Eastern Han

shaoshique.name: Shaoshi Que of Dengfeng
shaoshique.sub: West que · Spirit-way que of Mount Shaoshi
shaoshique.era: Reign of Emperor An of Han
shaoshique.lede: The most densely carved of the three que. The Shaoshi Que was the spirit-way gate of the temple of Mount Shaoshi, a double mother-and-child tower like the Taishi Que, but its four faces are packed with more than seventy scenes: horse races, kickball (cuju), elephant training, cockfights, dogs chasing hares, the dark bird of the Shang legend—the whole bustle of a Han mountain-god festival cut into stone. The inscriptions carry no exact date; because the names match those on the Taishi and Qimu que, it is placed between 118 and 123, while the Zhengzhou Cultural Heritage Bureau gives 123 (Yanguang 2). The plate shows the west tower.
facts: Form: The east and west towers stand 7.60 m apart, both double mother-and-child que built of grey-blue stone blocks in three parts—base, shaft and roof. The west tower is 3.75 m high, the east 3.37 m; the roofs are badly damaged. The towers were restored to their original state in 1972.

Dating: Most of the inscriptions have weathered away; only the six-character seal-script title 'Shaoshi shendao zhi que' on the north face of the west tower and a few clerical-script phrases under the child tower's eave remain legible. Since the names match those on the Taishi and Qimu que, construction is placed in 118–123; the Zhengzhou bureau gives 123.

Imagery: The four faces preserve more than seventy scenes—carriage processions, banquets, winged immortals, the Four Spirits, animal combats, swordplay, hunting, elephant training, cockfights, kickball, the moon palace—of which the horse-acrobatics and hunting scenes are the finest. It holds the richest imagery of the three que, which together are China's only surviving Han temple gate-towers.
captions: Shaoshi Que · South face of the west que
Eastern Han main-and-subsidiary que

qimuque.name: Qimu Que of Dengfeng
qimuque.sub: West que · Spirit-way que of Qimu Temple
qimuque.lede: The legend of Yu the Great's wife turning to stone and giving birth to Qi was given a temple in Han times; the temple is long gone, but the spirit-way gate-towers before it still stand. The Qimu Que was built in 123 CE (Yanguang 2) by Zhu Chong, governor of Yingchuan. Its shafts show Yu transformed into a bear, Guo Ju burying his son, elephant training, conjuring and a scene of women playing kickball, and the surviving tile rows and tile-ends of the roof are a direct sample of a Han roof. The plate shows the south face of the west tower; the two inscriptions on its back, about flood control and prayers for rain, are not in the picture.
facts: Form: The two towers stand 6.8 m apart, the west 3.17 m and the east 3.18 m high. The west tower rests on a two-layer stone base; its shaft is seven courses of stone stacked vertically, 2.75 m in all, topped by a bucket-shaped block and the roof. The roof is badly damaged; what survives shows a hip roof with tile rows, hip ridges, persimmon-calyx tile-ends and flat tiles, the main ridge lost.

Dating: Two inscriptions survive on the north face of the west tower. The seal-script 'Qimu Que Inscription' records that Zhu Chong, governor of Yingchuan, built the que in 123 CE and praises Yu's taming of the floods; below it the clerical-script 'Prayer for Rain', composed by Tangxi Dian, had 18 lines of 5 characters, of which 11 remain. In Han times the name was changed to Kaimu to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Jing (Liu Qi).

Imagery: The shafts carry horse acrobatics, mounted processions, jugglers, conjurers, elephant training, Guo Ju burying his son, Yu turning into a bear, pony riding, hunting, a tiger chasing a deer, twin dragons and the moon palace; the scene of women playing kickball is often cited as physical evidence of the game's popularity in the Han. About 190 m north stands the 'Qimu Stone', said to be the petrified wife of Yu.
captions: Qimu Que · South face of the west que

gaoyique.name: Que of Gao Yi
gaoyique.lede: Beside Hanbei Road in Ya'an, the stone que in front of the tomb of Gao Yi hold the forms of Han timber architecture in red sandstone. The west que preserves the stepped outline of a main que joined to its side que.
facts: Built in the 14th year of Jian'an in the Eastern Han (209) as a ceremonial structure in front of the tomb of Gao Yi, Grand Administrator of Yizhou.

There were originally paired east and west que, and the western main-and-subsidiary que is the better preserved. The plate draws the west que from photographs and does not reconstruct the damaged east que.
The que imitates timber construction with bracket sets, an upper story and eaves; its carvings include historical stories, mythical beasts and processions.

jl_jiangjunfen.name: General's Tomb, Ji'an
jl_jiangjunfen.yearNote: 450 is an ordering placement for the remains of a stone-chamber tomb of about the 5th century, not a precise construction year; the traditional identification of the tomb's occupant is not treated as established fact.
jl_jiangjunfen.place: Jilin · Ji'an · Southern foot of Longshan
jl_jiangjunfen.lede: Huge stones are stacked into seven square tiers, with buttress stones leaning against the steps at the base and the entrance to the burial chamber opening in the upper part. The General's Tomb belongs to the Goguryeo remains and should not be relabeled Northern Wei simply because the dates are close.
facts: The plate is checked against the seven main tiers and does not count each course of masonry as a separate tier.
Identifications of the tomb's occupant differ; this entry does not directly assert that it is the tomb of King Jangsu, and it does not mix in images of the Taiwang Tomb.
The surviving gray-brown stone blocks, joints and pale buttress stones are drawn from a single photograph without digital retouching; this is not an archaeological reconstruction.

sx_yungang.name: Yungang Grottoes
sx_yungang.era: Northern Wei · Period of the Five Caves of Tanyao
sx_yungang.yearNote: Placed by the c. 460–470 construction phase of the Five Caves of Tanyao, to which Cave 20 belongs; 465 is used only for ordering.
sx_yungang.lede: Yungang's most famous face is the product of a collapse: the front wall of Cave 20 fell away long ago, leaving the 13.7-metre seated Shakyamuni in the open air, where it became the emblem of the whole site. It belongs to the five colossal-image caves begun under the monk Tanyao in the early Heping years (c. 460): broad shoulders, deep chest and a robe baring the right shoulder fuse Gandharan exoticism with the physique of the Tuoba Xianbei. The plate shows this main image.
facts: Form: the main image sits cross-legged, about 13.7 m high, with a tall ushnisha, a squarish round face and ears reaching the shoulders; the heavy robe bares the right shoulder, yet a slanting fold covers the shoulder tip, read as a Chinese adaptation of the Western style. The standing Buddha on the east survives; the western Buddha and bodhisattva are mere traces.

Date: the Weishu records that in the early Heping years (460) the monk-superintendent Tanyao petitioned for five caves, today's Caves 16–20; all are colossal-image caves with domed ceilings and horseshoe plans, Cave 20 forming an earlier group with Caves 18 and 19. Excavation in front of the cave in 1992 recovered more than 130 drapery fragments of the lost western Buddha.

Significance: the five colossi stood for five Northern Wei emperors, 'made in the likeness of the emperor', and mark the beginning of imperial cave-building; Yungang preserves 252 caves and niches with some 51,000 images, inscribed as World Heritage in 2001, and the Cave 20 Buddha is its most widely reproduced image.
captions: Yungang Cave 20 · Seated principal figure
Northern Wei · c. 460–470

songyue.name: Songyue Temple Pagoda, Dengfeng
songyue.lede: China's earliest surviving brick pagoda, and its only twelve-sided pagoda with dense eaves. Fifteen tiers of brick eaves draw in tier by tier into a parabola—Liang Sicheng called it 'uncommonly graceful'. The upper shaft opens four arched doors, with a pagoda-shaped niche on each of the other eight faces; the lotus-petal door lintels and flame-jewel capitals carry echoes of Indian and Central Asian forms. The pagoda belongs to the late Northern Wei: tradition gives the Zhengguang era (520–525), while the Zhengzhou Cultural Heritage Bureau records a start in 509 (Yongping 2), and a statue dated Zhengguang 4 came out of the crypt beneath the tower.
facts: Form: A twelve-sided dense-eave pagoda of grey brick laid in clay, about 37–40 m high (37.045 m per the Zhengzhou bureau; 39.8 m in a 1980s survey), with a ground-floor diameter of 10.6 m. The upper shaft has arched doors on four faces and pagoda-shaped niches on eight, with octagonal engaged columns at the corners; above rise fifteen tiers of corbelled eaves, drawing inward to a brick finial.

Dating: Completed in the late Northern Wei—traditionally the Zhengguang era (520–525), while the Zhengzhou bureau records a start in 509 (Yongping 2). In 1986 the crypt yielded a Shakyamuni image with a dedication dated Zhengguang 4 (523). Exposed bricks had been reheated in a fire, so thermoluminescence dating returned Tang values, prompting a 1996 claim of a Tang construction that was later rejected.

Legacy: No earlier dense-eave pagoda is known, so the Songyue Pagoda is regarded as the prototype of the type; two 'heavenly chambers' inside the finial held reliquary jars and a silver stupa. It was listed among the first national key heritage sites in 1961 and inscribed as part of the Dengfeng World Heritage property in 2010.
captions: Songyue Temple Pagoda · Front view
Twelve-sided · Fifteen tiers of eaves

hn_gongyi.name: Gongxian Grottoes
hn_gongyi.yearNote: 520 is only an approximate ordering point for the late Northern Wei sculptural phase and is not taken as an exact inscribed date for any cave or niche.
hn_gongyi.place: Henan · Gongyi · Siwan Village, Heluo Town
hn_gongyi.lede: Besides Longmen, the Northern Wei court cut one more imperial cave temple after moving its capital to Luoyang. Four of the five caves at Gongxian are built around a central pillar that worshippers circled—a cave type Longmen never used. Cave 1 is 6 m high; its square pillar, 2.8 m on a side, opens a niche on each face holding a Buddha, two bodhisattvas and two disciples, with lions crouching beside the throne. The three-tier processions of emperor and empress on the walls inside the door are among the most complete in any Chinese cave temple. The plate shows the main image and attendants on one face of the pillar, without the adjoining wall reliefs.
facts: Cave 1: Square in plan and 6 m high. The central pillar, 2.8 m on a side, carries a niche on each face with one Buddha, two bodhisattvas and two disciples, a lion carved on either side of the throne and strongmen and spirit kings on the pedestal. The east, west and north walls each hold four large niches; below the thousand-Buddha panels flanking the door are three-tier processions—the emperor on the east, the empress on the west.

Dating: A stele of 662 records that Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei founded Xixuan Temple here; a stele of 1494 records cave-cutting under Emperor Xuanwu in the Jingming era (500–503), continued under the Eastern Wei, Northern Qi, Tang and Song. Édouard Chavannes photographed the caves in 1907; several were later looted and the silt was cleared in 1954.

Scale: Five caves, one thousand-Buddha niche, three cliff images, 328 cliff niches and 7,743 Buddha figures survive. The square-pillar caves resemble Dunhuang rather than the stupa-pillars of Yungang and influenced the slightly later Xiangtangshan and Xumishan caves; the imperial processions in Caves 1, 3 and 4 are rare complete examples of the genre.

xinchangdafo.name: Great Buddha Temple, Xinchang
xinchangdafo.yearNote: 516 is the 15th year of Tianjian in the Liang, when the image was completed; 486 is the date of origin linked to Senghu's vow, and another account places the start of carving in the Jianwu era of the Qi. The temple's founding in the Eastern Jin is kept distinct from later restorations.
xinchangdafo.lede: Broad knees support a calm body as the stone Maitreya sits cross-legged in a rock chamber on Mount Shicheng. Carved by successive generations of monks during the Qi and Liang of the Southern Dynasties, it is a valuable surviving example of early large-scale Buddhist sculpture in Jiangnan.
facts: Qi–Liang creation: After Senghu made his vow, Sengshu and Sengyou continued the work, completing it in the 15th year of Tianjian in the Liang (516); it was formerly called the Stone Buddha of Three Generations.
Cliff-cut image: The Maitreya is carved from the rock face of Mount Shicheng, seated in full lotus with both hands resting between the knees; the knees are about 10.6 m apart.

Later care: The image has been redecorated and repaired over many periods and conserved several times in the modern era. The plate shows the historical stone image as it is today and excludes the modern reclining Buddha of the scenic area.
captions: Great Buddha Temple, Xinchang · Stone Maitreya
Southern Dynasties Qi–Liang · 486–516

hn_xiaonanhai.name: Xiaonanhai Grottoes
hn_xiaonanhai.yearNote: The Palace Museum records excavation from the 1st to the 6th year of Tianbao in the Northern Qi; 553 is only an approximate ordering point within this range and does not mark the exact completion year of any one cave.
hn_xiaonanhai.lede: In the cliff face, low and small cave openings still show carved lintel decoration and damaged figures beside the doors. The three Xiaonanhai caves preserve important evidence for Northern Qi Buddhist sculpture and Pure Land imagery.
facts: Date: According to the Palace Museum, the grottoes were excavated from the 1st to the 6th year of Tianbao in the Northern Qi (550–555) and finally completed by the monk Sengchou.
Three caves: The east, middle and west caves are all square with truncated-pyramid ceilings and three niches on three walls; the Buddha groupings include Vairocana, Amitabha and Maitreya.

Plate scope: The line drawing takes the part of the cave-door facade visible in photographs, keeping the cracks in the rock and the damaged carvings beside the door; the sculptures inside the caves are not added.

xiangtang.name: Xiangtangshan Grottoes
xiangtang.lede: A broad, round Buddha face, heavy shoulders and fine drapery folds are enclosed by a flame-shaped mandorla. The Great Buddha Cave of North Xiangtang preserves the serene mass of Northern Qi sculpture in the rock walls of Mount Gu, and its losses also bear the marks of a long history.
facts: Early Northern Qi: The Great Buddha Cave is one of the earlier large caves at North Xiangtang. Research usually places it in the reign of Emperor Wenxuan of the Northern Qi, about the 550s; the exact founding inscription has been lost.

Central-pillar cave: Cave 9 is a stupa-pillar cave with a central square pillar, the Buddhas of the Three Ages carved on three of its faces; the plate shows the principal figure on the front face, about 3.5 m tall.

Present condition: The principal figure's hands and part of its drapery are lost, but the round head halo and flame mandorla remain recognizable; the carvings of the cave group have suffered weathering, looting and later repairs.

hn_dapishan.name: Great Cliff Buddha of Mount Dapi
hn_dapishan.sub: The Great Stone Buddha of Xun County, seated against the cliff
hn_dapishan.yearLabel: Later Zhao, Northern Qi or other views
hn_dapishan.yearNote: Proposed dates include the Later Zhao and the Northern Qi. Here 560 serves only as an ordering point based on the Northern Qi start-of-carving view recorded in 2004 material from Cultural Relics Press and does not indicate a confirmed start date; a 2026 Henan Daily on-site conservation report adopts the Later Zhao view. The disagreement is retained and should not be read as a settled Northern Qi date.
hn_dapishan.lede: The Great Buddha of Mount Dapi is carved from the mountain cliff, its right hand raised and its left resting on the knee. Its date of carving is variously judged as Later Zhao, Northern Qi and other periods, and its present surface carries later repairs and painting.
facts: Differing dates: Older conservation sources record carving begun in the Northern Qi and completed in the early Tang; recent conservation reports adopt the Later Zhao view. This entry keeps the differing judgments.

Colossal cliff figure: The figure sits in a pendant-leg posture, the right hand in the abhaya mudra and the left on the knee; the plate draws only the part visible in the photograph, from the head to the knees.

Conservation: It was repaired in the 10th year of Zhengtong in the Ming; a new round of conservation of the figure began in 2025, and the line drawing is based on photographs taken in 2024 before the work.
captions: Great Cliff Buddha of Mount Dapi · Visible part from head to knees
Date of carving disputed · Drawn from 2024 photographs of its condition

sx_tianlongshan.name: Tianlongshan Grottoes
sx_tianlongshan.yearNote: The front portico of Cave 16 shown here belongs to the Northern Qi (550–577); 560 is an approximate ordering point. Sui and Tang dates of other caves are not applied.
sx_tianlongshan.lede: At Tianlongshan, the builders of the Northern Qi carved the facade of a timber Buddha hall into the living rock. The porch of Cave 16 is three bays wide: two octagonal stone columns stand on lotus bases, the capital blocks carry an architrave, and above it 'one-block-three-arms' brackets alternate with inverted-V struts beneath a bearing block and eave purlin. Not a single Northern Dynasties timber building survives, so this carved porch is one of the few witnesses to the eaves of that age. The plate shows this porch.
facts: Form: a three-bay porch; two octagonal stone columns taper upward and rest on square plinths with inverted-lotus bases. Capital blocks support the architrave, which carries two inverted-V struts with 'one-block-three-arms' brackets between them, topped by a bearing block, an eave purlin and a projecting roof. The east column is well preserved; the surface of the west column has flaked away.

Date: the Tianlongshan caves were begun under the Eastern Wei, and scholars agree that Caves 1, 10 and 16 were cut in the Northern Qi (550–577). A donor stele on the right wall of the porch has weathered so badly that its date can no longer be read, so no exact year is known. The guardians flanking the door and most of the heads inside were looted in the 1920s.

Significance: of the 25 surviving caves at Tianlongshan, researchers consider Cave 16 the most important Northern Qi cave. Its interior, with three niches on three walls each holding a Buddha, two disciples and two bodhisattvas, survives together with the porch, a rare sample of a Northern Dynasties hall-type cave and of timber-style exteriors; digital reconstruction since 2014 has rejoined seven lost sculptures to the cave.

hb_yicihui.name: Yicihui Stone Pillar
hb_yicihui.sub: Northern Qi stone pillar with a three-bay stone hall on top
hb_yicihui.yearNote: Its present location is Shizhu Village, Gaoli Township, Dingxing County; Yi County, given as the location in the old national listing, is an outdated administrative attribution. The Northern Wei wooden predecessor is kept separate from the Northern Qi stone structure.
hb_yicihui.lede: The pillar is not the surprise; the surprise is the little stone hall on top, three bays wide and two deep: rafters, hip rafters, bracket sets, lintels, columns and window frames are all carved in stone, in effect a model of timber architecture left by Northern Qi craftsmen. The Yicihui Stone Pillar (Yicihui Shizhu) stands about 7 m tall; its octagonal shaft carries more than 4,000 characters recounting how, after the failed uprisings of Du Luozhou and Ge Rong at the end of the Northern Wei, local people gathered and buried the dead and raised a pillar to mark their righteousness. An inscription at the top dates it to the 2nd year of Daning of the Great Qi (562).
facts: Form: limestone, about 7 m tall overall. A square base stone carries a lotus-petal plinth and an octagonal shaft 4.5 m high with a slight taper; the capping slab supports a small stone hall, three bays by two, with a single-eave hip roof and a carved Buddha image at the centre of its front and back.

Inscription: the shaft bears the nine large characters 'Biao yi xiang Yicihui shizhu song', a eulogy of more than 3,000 characters and nearly 1,000 characters of names, including the date 'Great Qi, Daning 2, 4th month, 17th day'. Weathering and cracks were repaired in 1990, and the protective pavilion was reinforced and renovated in 2011.

Origin: after the uprisings of Du Luozhou and Ge Rong (Northern Wei, 525-528) were crushed, villagers buried the insurgents' remains and set up a wooden pillar as a marker; the Northern Qi replaced it with this stone pillar and carved the eulogy. The earlier Northern Wei wooden pillar and the surviving Northern Qi stonework should be kept distinct.

hn_lingquan.name: Lingquan Temple Grottoes
hn_lingquan.sub: Armored guardians flanking a Sui cave doorway
hn_lingquan.yearNote: Uses the excavation date of the Dazhusheng Cave, not a single date for all the Lingquan Temple caves.
hn_lingquan.place: Henan · Shanying Town, Long'an District, Anyang
hn_lingquan.lede: The Dazhusheng Cave at Lingquan Temple was excavated in the 9th year of Kaihuang in the Sui. On either side of the doorway, armored divine kings hold weapons, their long beards falling to their chests; in low relief they carry the guardian imagery of the Northern Dynasties on into the Sui.
facts: Dazhusheng Cave: The excavation of this cave was directed by Lingyu and is dated to the 9th year of Kaihuang in the Sui (589); the surrounding cliff niches and images vary in date.
Paired guardians: The divine kings Kapila and Narayana are carved on either side outside the door. The two differ in posture and in what they hold, and each is drawn from its own photograph.

Partial plate: The plate selects the two low-relief figures beside the door, keeping their damaged outlines and the cracks in the rock; it does not add the doorway between them or the Buddhas inside the cave.

hb_anjibridge.name: Zhaozhou Bridge (Anji Bridge)
hb_anjibridge.sub: Side elevation of an open-spandrel stone arch bridge
hb_anjibridge.yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau's description gives 605–616, and another account gives 595–605; 610 is only an approximate ordering point within the Sui and does not indicate an exact completion year.
hb_anjibridge.lede: Two small arches open in each shoulder of the great arch, an 'open-spandrel' device that Europe did not arrive at until the late nineteenth century; Zhaozhou Bridge (Anji Bridge) had it in the Sui dynasty. A single, shallow segmental arch with a clear span of 37.02 m and a rise of only 7.23 m makes the deck as gentle as a slope. Zhang Jiazhen's Tang-dynasty inscription calls it 'the work of the Sui craftsman Li Chun'. A major repair in the 1950s replaced most of the stone, leaving the bright, new-looking surface seen today, which Liang Sicheng regretted for years.
facts: Form: a single-span open-spandrel segmental stone arch bridge, 50.82 m long and about 9 m wide; the main arch consists of 28 parallel rings of voussoirs with a clear span of 37.02 m and a rise of 7.23 m, and each shoulder carries two small arches to pass floodwater and reduce weight, the earliest known example of the open-spandrel arch.

Date: Zhang Jiazhen's 'Inscription for Zhaozhou Bridge' (Kaiyuan era, Tang) calls it 'the work of the Sui craftsman Li Chun'; Liang Sicheng surveyed it in 1933 and published 'The Great Stone Bridge of Zhaoxian, i.e. Anji Bridge'. Sources disagree on the exact year of completion within the Sui, so this entry is placed only approximately in that dynasty.

Repairs: in 1952-1956 the bridge was dismantled and rebuilt with cement grout, with about 87 percent of the stone newly bought; in 1963 Liang Sicheng wrote regretting that it had been made 'brand new'. In 1991 the American Society of Civil Engineers designated it an International Historic Civil Engineering Landmark.

sd_simen.name: Four Gates Pagoda of Shentong Temple, Jinan
sd_simen.sub: Sui single-story stone pagoda · Arched doors on four sides
sd_simen.yearNote: Takes the inscription inside the stone pagoda, “made in the 7th year of Daye,” corresponding to 611; the Eastern Wei inscription of 544 on a Buddha image inside is not equated with the date of the pagoda itself.
sd_simen.lede: There are no stacked stories, only arched doors on four sides and a pyramidal roof of masonry stone. With its plain, massive chamber, the Four Gates Pagoda preserves the outline of Sui stone architecture to this day.
facts: Dating evidence: An inscription reading “made in the 7th year of Daye” was found inside the top of the pagoda, corresponding to 611; the Eastern Wei images inside predate the structure and are not treated as the same date.
Form: A single-story pavilion-type stone pagoda, square in plan with a door on each side; Buddha images are set around the central pillar, facing the four directions.
Plate scope: Shows the exterior of the whole stone pagoda; the Buddha images inside are not enlarged as a separate subject.

kaiyuan.name: Kaiyuan Temple, Zhengding
kaiyuan.era: Founded in the 10th year of Zhenguan
kaiyuan.lede: Pagoda and bell tower face each other in front of the main hall, with the hall behind them, the transitional layout of a Tang monastery moving from a pagoda-centred to a hall-centred plan, and the only surviving example in China. On the west, the Xumi Pagoda (Xumi Ta), begun in 636, is a plain, unornamented square pagoda of nine close-set eaves, a decade or so older than the Great Wild Goose Pagoda; on the east, the lower storey of the bell tower is still Tang work, making it the only surviving Tang bell tower in China. Liang Sicheng recognised it here in 1933.
facts: Form: the Xumi Pagoda is a square brick pagoda of nine dense eaves, plain-faced, 42.5 m tall; the bell tower has two storeys on a square plan three bays by three, with a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, 14 m high, brick-walled below and timber-framed above, and still hangs a Tang bronze bell.

History: the monastery was founded in 540 (Eastern Wei) and took its present name in 738; a stele of 777 preserved in the temple records a three-bay gate tower, a 'wild goose' pagoda and the Fachuan main hall at that time, and the bell tower was added in the late Tang.

Dating: after his 1933 survey Liang Sicheng judged the lower storey of the bell tower to be Tang, noting in his History of Chinese Architecture that its outer eaves 'seem Jin-Yuan below and Qing repair above'; most other halls have perished, leaving only the site of the Fachuan Hall.

sn_xingjiao.name: Xuanzang Pagoda of Xingjiao Temple
sn_xingjiao.sub: Square five-story brick pagoda · Relic pagoda of Xuanzang
sn_xingjiao.yearNote: 669 is the construction year of the Xuanzang Pagoda; the two disciples' pagodas at Xingjiao Temple each have their own histories, and the plate does not treat the three pagodas as a single subject of one date.
sn_xingjiao.lede: The square brick pagoda narrows story by story, with brickwork under the eaves imitating timber columns and architraves. Xuanzang's relics are enshrined here; of the three pagodas at Xingjiao Temple, the plate takes only the central Xuanzang Pagoda.
facts: Main subject: The relic pagoda of Xuanzang, built in the 2nd year of Zongzhang in the Tang (669); the three pagodas were not all built in the same year.
Form: A square five-story pavilion-style brick pagoda with corbeled eaves; brick columns and architraves imitate timber architecture.
Plate scope: Only the tall central pagoda is drawn; the disciples' pagodas to its left and right are not included.

longmenshiku.name: Longmen Grottoes
longmenshiku.era: Fengxian Temple completed in the 2nd year of Shangyuan
longmenshiku.lede: Carving began after the Northern Wei moved its capital to Luoyang in the 17th year of Taihe (493) and continued into the Tang. The great niche of Fengxian Temple was begun in the 3rd year of Xianheng (672) and completed in the 2nd year of Shangyuan (675), with Wu Zetian donating twenty thousand strings of cash from her cosmetics allowance. The 17-meter Vairocana sits at the center, and the nine figures, with disciples, bodhisattvas, heavenly kings and guardians, stand in a single row — of all the niches in the grottoes, the one most like a hall.
facts: The Vairocana is 17.14 m tall overall, with a head 4 m high and ears 1.9 m long; it sits in full lotus on a lotus throne, and its round head halo is carved with lotus-petal and flame patterns.

The niche is about 36 m wide, with nine figures arranged symmetrically: Kasyapa and Ananda stand in attendance, Manjushri and Samantabhadra are 13.25 m tall, the heavenly kings trample demons, and the guardians are 9.75 m tall.

The two hills of Longmen hold more than 2,300 surviving caves and niches and over 100,000 statues. The Northern Wei Guyang Cave (493) and Central Binyang Cave came first, and the Tang Ten-Thousand-Buddha Cave (680) later; the site was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2000.

xiuding.name: Xiuding Temple Pagoda
xiuding.era: Founded in the Northern Qi · Rebuilt in the Tang
xiuding.lede: A single-story square brick pagoda is covered entirely with 3,775 molded decorative bricks, rhombuses, rectangles and triangles fitted together into a net of relief. Archaeologists have called it “the true first flower pagoda of China.”
facts: First built in the 1st year of Tianbao in the Northern Qi (550) and rebuilt in the Tang; the decorative bricks of the surviving body were all fired in the Tang, so it is called a Tang pagoda.
It is 20 m tall overall, with a body 9.3 m high and 8.3 m wide, close to a cube; it is capped by corbeled eaves and a four-sloped pyramidal roof, with an inverted-bowl finial on top.
The decorative bricks show guardians, apsaras, the Azure Dragon, the White Tiger, monks and scrolling vines in more than seventy designs, fitted together with tight joints.

sn_qianling.name: Wordless Stele of Qianling
sn_qianling.sub: Stele with chi-dragon head · Later inscriptions
sn_qianling.yearLabel: Tang · Exact year of erection undetermined
sn_qianling.yearNote: The date of and motive for erecting the stele are interpreted differently; 700 is only an approximate Tang ordering point, not an established year of erection. The stele is not entirely blank today: inscriptions have been added since the Song and Jin.
sn_qianling.lede: When first erected, the tall stele bore no main text, and its chi-dragon head and single block of stone give it a solemn outline. Visitors' inscriptions from the Song and Jin onward gradually accumulated on its face, so the name “wordless” does not mean it is still blank today.
facts: Material: Carved from a single block of limestone, with eight chi dragons carved on the head and a rectangular stone base.
Inscriptions: It originally had no main text, and inscriptions were added one after another from the Song and Jin onward; the name is not a literal description of the present stele face.
Date: A Tang survival whose exact year of erection is undetermined; the plate does not treat the approximate ordering year as historical fact.

xian.name: Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, Xi'an
xian.sub: Da Ci'en Temple · Seven-story pavilion-style brick pagoda
xian.era: Founded in the 3rd year of Yonghui · Rebuilt in the Chang'an era of the Wu Zhou
xian.yearNote: First built in 652; dated by the seven-story form of the rebuilding in the Chang'an era of the Wu Zhou, with later brick casing and repairs described separately.
xian.lede: The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda stands in Da Ci'en Temple, a brick pagoda built by Xuanzang to house the Buddhist scriptures he brought back from India. First built in the 3rd year of Yonghui (652), it was rebuilt with seven stories in the Chang'an era of the Wu Zhou (701–704). Its pavilion-style body tapers story by story, and its present appearance also reflects later brick casing and repairs.
facts: A square seven-story pavilion-style brick pagoda about 64.5 m tall overall; the brick walls render the form of a timber pavilion with columns and architraves in low relief.
Each story has arched openings on its main faces; the tapering body and corbeled brick eaves give a clear outline, and the finial survives at the top.
The subject drawn is the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda itself, excluding the temple's other buildings; it is catalogued separately from the Small Wild Goose Pagoda of Jianfu Temple.

sn_xiangji.name: Shandao Pagoda of Xiangji Temple
sn_xiangji.sub: Tang square pagoda · Present form with damaged top
sn_xiangji.era: Built in the early Tang, repaired over the centuries
sn_xiangji.yearNote: Sources give differing interpretations: construction in 681 with repairs in 706, or construction in 706. The year 706 follows Table 1 of the Palace Museum Journal as an ordering reference, without asserting that the whole present pagoda is original fabric of that one year. The damaged top is kept, and the original thirteen stories are not reconstructed.
sn_xiangji.lede: Layered brick eaves gradually draw the square pagoda inward, and its damaged top still bears the marks of time. The Shandao Pagoda has shared the history of Xiangji Temple, and its present form is not reconstructed to a full thirteen stories.
facts: Date: Sources give two interpretations, 681 and 706, for the building and repair of the pagoda; the timeline uses an approximate Tang placement.
Form: A square brick pagoda, now with eleven stories and layered projecting eaves; the top is damaged.
Present form: Remains repaired over the centuries; the two upper stories that have vanished are not added.

xian_small.name: Small Wild Goose Pagoda, Xi'an
xian_small.sub: Jianfu Temple · Thirteen-tier multi-eaved brick pagoda
xian_small.era: Jinglong era of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang
xian_small.yearNote: Founded in the Jinglong era of the Tang; 707 is used as the starting point for ordering, and the drawing shows the thirteen-tier form with the damaged top left after Ming-dynasty earthquakes.
xian_small.lede: The Small Wild Goose Pagoda, originally called the Jianfu Temple Pagoda, was built in the Jinglong era of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang (707–710). The square brick pagoda narrows upward through dense corbeled brick eaves. It originally had fifteen tiers, but Ming-dynasty earthquakes destroyed the top two; thirteen tiers and a damaged top remain today.
facts: A square multi-eaved brick pagoda with thirteen surviving tiers, about 43.4 m tall in its damaged state, with ground-story sides about 11.38 m long; the ground story is tall and the upper eave tiers are closely set.

The pagoda has been through several earthquakes, and its 14th and 15th tiers at the top have been lost. The plate follows the present damaged top and does not restore the vanished tiers or add a finial.

The subject drawn is the Small Wild Goose Pagoda of Jianfu Temple itself, excluding the galleries of the Xi'an Museum and the temple's other buildings; visits are recorded separately from the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda of Da Ci'en Temple.

gs_bingling.name: Bingling Temple Grottoes
gs_bingling.era: Carved in the 19th year of Kaiyuan, Tang
gs_bingling.yearNote: The plate shows the Great Buddha of Niche 171, dated to its carving in the 19th year of Kaiyuan in the Tang (731) as stated by experts of the conservation institute. The upper body is carved stone and the part below the abdomen is clay sculpture, with later repairs; the dates of the early Western Qin caves are not substituted for the date of this figure.
gs_bingling.lede: The Great Buddha sits upright against the rock cliff, its broad kasaya leaving large, quiet planes. The hand resting on the knee on one side is still intact, while the other side keeps its present damage; the caves and plank walkways above are not drawn in.
facts: Main subject: The Great Maitreya Buddha of Niche 171.

Date: The plate shows the Great Buddha of Niche 171, dated to its carving in the 19th year of Kaiyuan in the Tang (731) as stated by experts of the conservation institute. The upper body is carved stone and the part below the abdomen is clay sculpture, with later repairs; the dates of the early Western Qin caves are not substituted for the date of this figure.

Plate scope: The complete seated Maitreya, with curled hair, long ears, broad kasaya and pendant legs. The present state is kept, with one hand intact on the knee and damage on the other side, rather than showing both hands whole; only the shallow rock niche close around the body is retained, and Cave 169 and the walkways are not drawn.

hn_fengxue.name: Fengxue Temple
hn_fengxue.sub: A High Tang pagoda beneath nine tiers of multi-eaves
hn_fengxue.yearNote: Entered by the date of the surviving Tang main structure of the Seventh Patriarch Pagoda, not mixed with the Song Hanging Bell Pavilion or the Jin Middle Buddha Hall.
hn_fengxue.lede: The Seventh Patriarch Pagoda stands at the center of Fengxue Temple, built in memory of Chan Master Zhen. A tall square lower story supports nine tiers of multi-eaves, and the spire rings of the finial still keep a clear outline.
facts: High Tang body: The Seventh Patriarch Pagoda was built in the 26th year of Kaiyuan in the Tang (738) as the relic pagoda of Chan Master Zhen.
Square, nine tiers: The pagoda is 24.17 m tall, a square hollow brick pagoda whose outer eaves recede tier by tier in a slightly curved outline.
Coexisting periods: The temple also has a Song-dynasty Hanging Bell Pavilion and a Jin-dynasty Middle Buddha Hall; this plate draws only the Tang pagoda.

hb_daodejing.name: Daodejing Pillar of Longxing Daoist Temple
hb_daodejing.sub: Detail of the shaft and lotus base
hb_daodejing.yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hb_daodejing.lede: In 733 Emperor Xuanzong ordered every prefecture to set up a stone-carved Daodejing in a major Daoist abbey; the pillar at Yixian is the only reasonably complete surviving example in China. Its octagonal white-marble shaft, 4.29 m high, carries all eighty-one chapters of the emperor's annotated Daodejing and an imperial edict of some two hundred characters, signed 'erected by imperial order by Tian Renwan, prefect of Yizhou and commander of Gaoyang Army' in the tenth month of 738. The calligrapher is unsigned; since Qian Daxin it has usually been attributed to Su Lingzhi. The plate shows part of the shaft and the lotus base of the Longxing Guan Daodejing Pillar.
facts: Form: 6 m tall overall, in three parts, cap, shaft and base. The octagonal shaft is 4.29 m high and 90 cm across, assembled from two blocks; it rests on an upturned-lotus base 1.10 m in diameter, beneath which the original lotus-patterned Sumeru pedestal was rediscovered during the 2001 restoration.

Inscription: the upper shaft carries the eighteen-character title 'Daodejing of the Supreme Mysterious Primordial Emperor, annotated by the Kaiyuan Divine-Martial Emperor of Great Tang' and a 205-character edict; below is the full annotated text, dated at the end to the tenth month of 738, followed by later colophons including one by Weng Fanggang.

Vicissitudes: blown down in a storm in 1873, the shaft was reassembled facing the wrong way, so that the text began on the north-east face, an error not corrected until 2001. The attribution to Su Lingzhi rests on Qian Daxin's inference in his 'Jinshiwen bawei'; the pillar itself bears no signature.

haichunxuan.name: Haichunxuan Pagoda, Dongtai
haichunxuan.era: Built in the Tang, repaired in the Song · Founding year yet to be determined
haichunxuan.yearNote: 750 is only an approximate mid-Tang placement on the timeline and does not represent an evidenced construction year; construction supervised by Yuchi Jingde is treated only as legendary history.
haichunxuan.lede: Beside the waters of Xixi, seven tiers of brick eaves recede one above another, giving the pagoda a plain, steep outline. The Haichunxuan Pagoda has witnessed changes in the Jianghuai salt works and coastline, and it carries the long accumulation of Tang construction and Song repairs.
facts: Dating: The national protection listing classes it as Tang, and local sources record Song repairs; the specific founding year is not settled on the basis of legend.
Form: A seven-story octagonal brick pagoda about 20.8 m tall; the lower walls are tall, while the upper stories recede closely and have small niches.

Names: Also called the Guangfu Temple Pagoda and the Yuchi Pagoda. The county gazetteer's account of construction supervised by Yuchi Jingde is legendary history; the surviving brick body and exterior outline must be understood together with repairs over the centuries.

nanchan.name: Main Hall of Nanchan Temple
nanchan.lede: The oldest surviving timber building in China. Ink on the underside of the west collar beam reads 'Jianzhong 3rd year of the Great Tang (782) ... hall rebuilt', seventy-five years before the East Hall of Foguang Temple. It is only a three-bay hall paid for by villagers, and its remoteness is what saved it from the Huichang suppression of Buddhism; its roof is the shallowest of any surviving Chinese building, twelve eave columns carry the bracket sets directly, and there is not a single column inside.
facts: Form: three bays wide and three deep, nearly square, about 11.6 by 9.9 m; a single-eave hip-and-gable roof. Twelve eave columns carry the bracket sets directly, the capitals have five-puzuo sets with two projecting arms and no intermediate sets; the interior has no columns and no ceiling, four-rafter beams span front to back, and the walls are partitions, not supports.

Date: the ink inscription under the west collar beam records a rebuilding in 782; it was identified during the heritage survey of the early 1950s. In 1974–75 Qi Yingtao and Chai Zejun directed a restoration that removed later alterations. The three square columns on the west side are more archaic and are thought to survive from the original building.

Significance: only three Tang timber buildings with dated evidence survive, this hall, the main hall of Guangrenwang Temple at Ruicheng and the East Hall of Foguang Temple at Wutai. Of the original seventeen Tang statues inside, three were stolen in 1999 and fourteen remain, the earliest set of hall sculpture in China outside the Mogao Caves.

sx_longshan.name: Longshan Grottoes
sx_longshan.sub: Cave of the Great Master of the Three Heavens · Principal figure
sx_longshan.era: Tang niche figures · Later Yuan extensions
sx_longshan.yearNote: The niche of the Great Master of the Three Heavens is dated to the Tang following on-site signage and Jinyuan culture and tourism materials, and 800 is only an approximate placement; the Yuan-dynasty main body of the grotto group is described separately.
sx_longshan.lede: Longshan near Taiyuan is the largest surviving Daoist cave complex in China, cut mainly under the early-Yuan Quanzhen Daoist Song Defang (Piyunzi); but the two earliest niches on the hill, the Xuanzhen niche and the niche of the Three Heavens Great Masters, are dated to the Tang by the site signage and local heritage materials. The plate shows the central seated figure of the Three Heavens Great Masters niche: hair in a high topknot, a loose robe, a face worn smooth by weathering, with the plain reserve of a Daoist image, nothing like the colossal Buddhas of Buddhist caves.
facts: Form: the figure shown is the main image of the Three Heavens Great Masters niche, seated cross-legged, with a high topknot and a wide robe whose folds are cut as simple parallel lines; the face is weathered, the outline soft. The plate takes only the central figure, from topknot to knees, and does not stand for the whole niche.

Date: the complex has eight caves, the Xuhuang, Sanqing, Woru, Xuanzhen, Three Heavens Great Masters and Qizhen niches plus two 'debate' niches; the main body was cut in the early Yuan under Song Defang, a disciple of Qiu Chuji. The Xuanzhen and Three Heavens Great Masters niches are dated to the Tang by the site signage and Jinyuan district heritage materials, with Yuan enlargement beside them; this entry follows that dating.

Significance: the largest and best-preserved purely Daoist cave site in China, with some sixty-odd stone figures whose plain dress and grave bearing set them apart from Buddhist sculpture; the Yuan carving is tied directly to the spread of Quanzhen Daoism in Shanxi, and the caves include images of Quanzhen patriarchs such as Wang Chongyang.

sd_longhu.name: Dragon and Tiger Pagoda of Shentong Temple, Jinan
sd_longhu.sub: Tang carved body · Later replacement top
sd_longhu.era: Tang body, top repaired in later periods
sd_longhu.yearNote: The base and carved body are attributed to the Tang on the basis of form, and the exact founding year is unknown; 800 serves only as an approximate placement on the Tang timeline. The brick top is a later addition, so the whole pagoda cannot be called original fabric of one date.
sd_longhu.lede: Dragons, tigers and apsaras climb the stone walls of the pagoda, the fine carving set off by a massive Sumeru plinth. The Tang stone body of the Dragon and Tiger Pagoda carries a later replacement top, so repairs of different periods are layered in a single pagoda.
facts: Dating: The base and body are usually attributed to the Tang on the basis of architectural and carving style; the exact founding year is unknown, and 800 is only an approximate placement on the timeline.
Surviving layers: The carved stone body and the later brick top should be considered separately; the whole pagoda cannot be treated as original fabric completed in one year.
Form: A square pagoda chamber with doorways on four sides and stacked Sumeru plinths. Its name is the Dragon and Tiger Pagoda; it is not the twin pagodas of Lotus Pond in Kaohsiung.

guangren.name: Temple of King Guangren, Ruicheng
guangren.lede: Of the three Tang timber buildings left in China, this is the only one that is not a Buddhist hall: it is the main hall of a dragon-king temple where villagers prayed for rain. It stands on a terrace beside the ruined walls of the ancient Wei city; five bays wide yet little more than eleven metres across and four rafters deep, with not a single column inside. The capital brackets project two arms without intermediate sets, and the architrave rests directly on the column tops with no plate above. A stele of 832, the sixth year of Dahe, records that rebuilding.
facts: Form: the hall is five bays wide and four rafters deep, only 11.47 m across and 4.92 m deep, the end bays less than half the width of the second bays; a single-eave hip-and-gable roof on sixteen eave columns, with no interior columns and four-rafter beams spanning front to back. Capital sets are five-puzuo with two projecting arms, no intermediate sets and no transverse arms; the architrave does not project at the corners and there is no plate above it.

Date: two Tang steles were once set into the walls: the Record of Guangrenwang's Dragon Spring of 808 tells how a magistrate channelled the spring to irrigate fields, and the Record of the Dragon Spring of 832 records the rebuilding of the temple; the surviving hall is dated Tang on this evidence and its structure. A 1958 repair shortened the front eave rafters and altered the walls; a full dismantling restoration followed in 2013–14.

Significance: the only Daoist hall among the three surviving Tang timber buildings, and the earliest Daoist temple building in China. In 1108 the Song court ennobled the five dragons as kings, the Azure Dragon as 'Guangren King', hence the temple's name; locals still call it the Five Dragons Temple, after the spring that once issued from the bank below.

longxingchuang.name: Dharani Pillar of Longxing Temple, Hangzhou
longxingchuang.sub: Tang stone pillar · Detail of the shaft
longxingchuang.era: 2nd year of Kaicheng · Upper part repaired in the Qing
longxingchuang.lede: Beside a busy street, an octagonal stone pillar still carries scriptures carved in the Tang. Cracks run across its faces, and characters and repair seams overlap, leaving more than a thousand years of preservation and repair on the same stone.
facts: Tang date: The pillar was erected in the 2nd year of Kaicheng (837) and also bears an inscription of the 5th year of Dazhong (851); there were originally two, and one survives.
Later repairs: The shaft, base and other parts retain Tang components, while the upper part is a Qing repair; the surviving whole cannot simply be regarded as its original form of 837.

Partial plate: The plate selects the octagonal shaft and its supporting stone, showing the visible cracks and damage; the scripture is suggested with sparse strokes and is not a readable transcription.

chongsheng.name: Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple, Dali
chongsheng.sub: Dali · Qianxun Pagoda and the north and south pagodas
chongsheng.lede: At the eastern foot of the Cang Mountains, the Qianxun Pagoda and two smaller pagodas to the north and south stand in a triangle. The central square pagoda rises tall and straight, while the octagonal pagodas on either side are somewhat shorter, preserving the different outlines of Nanzhao and Dali Kingdom pagodas.
facts: The Qianxun Pagoda is generally dated to the reign of Quanfengyou of Nanzhao (823–859); it is a square sixteen-tier brick pagoda 69.13 m tall, and the catalogue orders it by this approximate date.
The north and south pagodas are dated separately to the Dali Kingdom; each is octagonal with ten tiers and 42.19 m tall, and they are not recorded as built in the same year as the Qianxun Pagoda.

The plate groups the three pagodas as seen from the east, with the Qianxun Pagoda in the center, the south pagoda on the left and the north pagoda on the right; the finials, bodies and bases of all three are drawn in full.
captions: Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple · Group view from the east
Qianxun Pagoda with sixteen tiers, the smaller north and south pagodas with ten each

foguang.name: East Hall of Foguang Temple
foguang.lede: In June 1937 Liang Sicheng, Lin Huiyin and their party read, on the underside of a beam, the words 'donor of the Buddha hall, the lay woman Ning Gongyu, bearer of offerings from the capital', and matched the name to the sutra pillar of 857 standing before the hall: the first time Chinese scholars had found a Tang timber building with their own hands. The seven-bay hall stands on a terrace more than ten metres high; its bracket sets rise to nearly half the column height beneath deep eaves, and inside more than thirty Tang statues share the hall with Tang murals and inscriptions, the 'four wonders' in Liang's phrase.
foguang.quote: “This is the only Tang timber building we have encountered in all our years of searching… the foremost treasure among China's ancient buildings.” — Liang Sicheng, Notes on the Architecture of Foguang Temple on Mount Wutai
facts: Form: seven bays and 34 m wide, four bays or eight rafters and 17.66 m deep, under a single-eave hip roof; capital sets are seven-puzuo with two projecting arms and two downward cantilevers, intermediate sets five-puzuo with two arms, the brackets about half the column height. The plan is a 'hall-type' frame with inner and outer rings of columns of equal height, and under the ridge purlin only inclined struts are used, with no king post.

Date: the ink inscription under the north exposed beam and the sutra pillar of 857 before the hall both name 'the lay woman Ning Gongyu', the basis for dating; the temple was destroyed in the suppression of 845 and rebuilt after Xuanzong restored Buddhism. In June 1937 Liang Sicheng's team from the Society for Research in Chinese Architecture surveyed it, and Mo Zongjiang recalled that scholars had believed no Tang building survived in China.

Significance: the largest surviving Tang timber building and the earliest example of a hip roof; 33 Tang statues on the altar, a Tang 'Amitabha preaching' mural in the bracket-eye panels and Tang ink inscriptions survive together with the architecture, the 'four wonders' of Liang Sicheng's History of Chinese Architecture. Inscribed as World Heritage with Mount Wutai in 2009.
captions: Line drawing · Seven bays wide
Single-eaved hipped roof

sh_tangchuang.name: Tang Dharani Pillar, Songjiang
sh_tangchuang.sub: Dharani pillar of the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani Sutra
sh_tangchuang.lede: Tier upon tier of stone pedestals raise a slender octagonal shaft, with carved scripture alternating with reliefs of lotus petals, coiled dragons and Buddhas. Erected in the 13th year of Dazhong in the Tang, this pillar still stands on a school campus in the old town of Songjiang.
facts: Built in the 13th year of Dazhong in the Tang (859), it is the oldest above-ground cultural relic surviving in Shanghai; it was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 1988.
It is about 9.3 m tall overall, with 21 surviving stone sections; the octagonal shaft is engraved with the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani Sutra and donors' inscriptions.

Pedestals, waisted sections, canopies and waist eaves are stacked in alternation, carved with lotus flowers, coiled dragons and Buddhist figures. The plate simplifies the weathered reliefs and scripture and is not a facsimile of the inscription.
captions: Octagonal stone pillar · Stacked carvings
Tang · 13th year of Dazhong (859)

hlj_shideng.name: Balhae Stone Lantern of Xinglong Temple
hlj_shideng.era: Balhae period · Date of construction unknown
hlj_shideng.yearNote: 800 is only an ordering placement for a Balhae-period stone carving, not an exact date of making; surviving repaired components and the temple's later buildings are not all treated as Balhae originals.
hlj_shideng.place: Heilongjiang · Ning'an · Xinglong Temple, Bohai Town
hlj_shideng.lede: A lotus base, a long stone column, an octagonal lamp chamber and a pavilion-style cap make up a freestanding carved stone lantern for an ever-burning flame. It is catalogued as Balhae period; the later temple behind it does not become ancient original fabric along with the lantern.
facts: The stone lantern is a freestanding carving; the plate draws only this subject and excludes the modern railing and the temple background.
The stone is now gray and weathered; the yellow-green patches on the cap and base are lichen, not glazed tiles or painted timberwork.

The openwork windows visible in the lamp chamber and the low reliefs on the base are treated differently, the latter kept solid. On the map it is grouped under a representative point for Ning'an City, not the exact coordinates of the lantern.
captions: Stone Lantern of Xinglong Temple · Octagonal pavilion-style lamp chamber

gongchen.name: Gongchen Pagoda, Lin'an
gongchen.lede: In the 1st year of Zhenming in the Later Liang (915), Qian Liu, King of Wuyue, built a pagoda on Mount Gongchen, where his rise had begun. Square and five stories high, of brick imitating timber, it is the earliest surviving square pagoda in Zhejiang, and it still looks Tang.
facts: It is 25.3 m tall overall, with a five-story body 22.06 m high; brick engaged columns, architraves and bracket sets imitate a timber pavilion-style structure.
Each story has cusped kunmen openings on all four sides and corbeled eaves; the finial is iron.
Qian Liu was born in Lin'an, and Mount Gongchen takes its name from him; only the site of Gongchen Temple beside the pagoda remains.
captions: Line drawing · Square, five stories
Brick imitating timber · Five Dynasties

longmen.name: West Side Hall of Longmen Temple
longmen.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Yuantou Village
longmen.lede: Only six or seven Five Dynasties timber buildings survive in all China, and three of them crowd into the Zhuozhang valley; the west side hall of Longmen Temple is the earliest. A sutra pillar of 950 says the monastery 'began building in the yiyou year', that is 925, the third year of Tongguang of the Later Tang. A three-bay hall under a gable roof, with no columns inside: the four-rafter beams run straight out over the column tops to form the simplest brackets, the architrave does not project at the corners, and there is no plate above it. Tang practice survived in the side hall of a village temple.
facts: Form: three bays wide and four rafters deep under a single-eave gable roof; no interior columns, the four-rafter beams span front to back, meeting the capital blocks and projecting as bracket arms, so the sets are 'dougong tiao' with no intermediate sets; the column tops are gently rounded, there is no plate and the architrave does not project. On the collar beam a camel-hump block carries a short post topped by another block, the earliest known instance.

Date: a statue stele of 930 in the temple already uses the name 'Longmen Cloister', and the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani pillar of 950 records that building began in the yiyou year (925), the basis for dating the west hall; an inscription records that stone columns were replaced in 1543.

Significance: timber buildings of six dynasties stand in one temple: the main hall of 1098 (Northern Song), a Jin gate hall, a Yuan Dipankara hall and an east side hall rebuilt in the Hongzhi years of the Ming, earning it the name 'museum of ancient architecture'; with Tiantai Hermitage and Dayun Monastery it is one of the valley's Five Dynasties survivals.
captions: Line drawing of the West Side Hall · Three bays wide
Single-eaved overhanging gable · Five Dynasties

protection.scope: West Side Hall of Longmen Temple

hb_zdwenmiao.name: Dacheng Hall of the Zhengding County Confucian Temple
hb_zdwenmiao.yearNote: The subject drawn is dated to the late Tang–Five Dynasties; the numerical year is only an approximate ordering point.
hb_zdwenmiao.lede: The main hall of a county-town Confucian temple, yet the oldest surviving Dacheng Hall of any Confucian temple in China. When Liang Sicheng saw it in 1933 he compared its exterior with the buildings in the Dunhuang murals and 'strongly suspected it to be a relic of the late Tang or Five Dynasties'. Five bays by three under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof of low pitch, with massive, plain bracket sets, double-arm column-top sets without intermediate sets, it predates the Dacheng Hall at Qufu by several centuries. The county gazetteer dates the temple to 1374, but that is the founding of the Confucian temple, not of this hall.
facts: Form: five bays wide and three deep, about 650 square metres, with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; the column-top bracket sets have two projecting arms without cross-arms and there are no intermediate sets, the brackets sitting directly on the column heads in the early manner.

Dating: the gazetteer records the temple's founding in 1374 (Hongwu 7), but in 1933 Liang Sicheng judged the hall on its form to be late Tang or Five Dynasties; after a 1991 visit Luo Zhewen called it the earliest extant Dacheng Hall in China, and the national register lists it under the Five Dynasties.

Repairs: listed as a Hebei provincial protected site in 1956; in 1997 the government spent over 700,000 yuan on emergency reinforcement, and in 2015 the National Cultural Heritage Administration funded repairs to the platform, roof tiles and timber members. This is the county temple, distinct from the Zhengding prefectural Confucian temple.
captions: Dacheng Hall, Zhengding County Confucian Temple · Front of the Dacheng Hall
Five Dynasties · Late Tang–Five Dynasties

tiantai.name: Tiantai Hermitage
tiantai.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Wangqu Village
tiantai.lede: A little three-bay hall, counted for decades among the 'four Tang timber buildings', until the dismantling repair of 2014 turned up ink on the ridge purlin and flying rafters: 'founded in the fourth year of Tiancheng of the Great Tang' and 'ninth month, second day, fourth year of Changxing ...'. Tiancheng 4 (929) and Changxing 4 (933) are both Later Tang reign years; the Later Tang, who styled themselves 'Great Tang', still built the way Tang carpenters had. It is the smallest, and the most Tang-like, of the three Five Dynasties timber halls in the Zhuozhang valley.
facts: Form: three bays wide and four rafters deep, about 7.15 m east-west by 7.12 m north-south, nearly square; a single-eave hip-and-gable roof on twelve eave columns. Each capital block sends out one bracket arm that carries the eave purlin through a bearing block, with no intermediate sets, the simplest 'dougong tiao'; a short post on the four-rafter beam carries the collar beam. The glazed ridge ornaments were replaced in the Jin.

Date: during the dismantling repair in November 2014 Shuai Yinchuan found the inscription 'ninth month, second day, Changxing 4 (933)' between ridge purlin and bearing block, and on a flying rafter the ink text 'founded in Tiancheng 4 (929) of the Great Tang, repaired in the renwu year of the Great Jin ... repaired in Kangxi 9 of the Great Qing'; He Dalong dates the hall to the Later Tang on this basis, while Wang Chunbo holds that a Tang foundation repaired in the Five Dynasties cannot be excluded.

Significance: the Tang stele before the hall is illegible, but micro-trace imaging in 2024 recovered more than eight hundred characters, not yet published; a pair of small stone lions at the corners was stolen in recent years. Together with the west hall of Longmen Temple and the Amitabha Hall of Dayun Monastery it is one of the valley's Five Dynasties survivals, and in form the closest to Nanchan Temple and Guangrenwang Temple.
captions: Line drawing · Three bays wide
Single-eaved hip-and-gable · Five Dynasties

protection.scope: Tiantai Hermitage · Wangqu Village

dayun.name: Amitabha Hall of Dayun Monastery
dayun.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Shihui Village
dayun.lede: The Amitabha Hall of 940, the fifth year of Tianfu of the Later Jin, still keeps Five Dynasties murals on its east wall and screen wall: among all surviving temple murals in China, these are the only ones of that era, with the debate between Vimalakirti and Manjusri spread over nearly thirty square metres. The hall is only three bays wide, yet it is the earliest surviving timber building to set a plate on top of the architrave, and one intermediate bracket set per bay adds a layer of order unknown in Tang halls.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; eighteen eave columns with rounded tops and a slight inward lean, capital and intermediate sets alike five-puzuo with two projecting arms, one intermediate set per bay; a plate beneath the capital blocks, the earliest instance in surviving timber architecture. Columns are omitted inside, leaving only two.

Date: the monastery was founded in 938 by Fengjing, a monk from Youzhou, as Xianyan Cloister; the Buddha hall and abbot's quarters were begun in 940, the Seven-Treasure Pagoda built in 954 under the Later Zhou, and the name changed to Dayun Chan Cloister in 983. In 2015 state funds repaired water damage to roof and floor.

Significance: the Vimalakirti sutra scene on the east wall and the painting behind the screen wall cover about 28.8 square metres, with another 11 square metres on the bracket-eye panels and beams, the only Five Dynasties temple murals in China; Japanese troops failed in an attempt to strip the west and north walls during the war, villagers plastered over the east wall to hide it, and the paintings were rediscovered in a survey of 1962.
captions: Line drawing of the Amitabha Hall · Three bays wide
Single-eaved hip-and-gable · Five Dynasties

fuzhouwuta.name: Black Pagoda, Fuzhou
fuzhouwuta.place: Fujian · Fuzhou · Gulou District · Eastern foot of Mount Wu
fuzhouwuta.lede: Planned with nine storeys, it stopped at seven. In 941, the third year of Yonglong of the Min kingdom, Wang Yanxi proclaimed himself emperor and began a pagoda on the site of a Tang-era Wugou Jingguang Pagoda at the eastern foot of Wushan; three years later he was killed in a coup and work halted at the seventh storey. The whole body is granite, with corbelled eaves and a narrow walkable gallery on each level; the weathered stone has turned dark, so Fuzhou people call it the Black Pagoda (Wuta). The name tablet set into the east wall of the fourth storey still opens with Wang Xi's title.
facts: Form: an octagonal seven-storey pavilion-style granite pagoda, 34.74 m in total height, with the base buried nearly 2 m below ground, leaving 32.86 m above it; each storey has corbelled eaves and a balustraded gallery, a guardian Buddha sits at the end of each of the eight ridges (56 in all), and the top carries an iron gourd finial.

Inscriptions: a black-shale name tablet reading 'Chongmiao Baosheng Jianlao Pagoda' is set into the east wall of the fourth storey, with 42 characters naming the donor Wang Xi and 80 naming the supervising officials; a pagoda record is set in the south wall of the fifth storey and a prayer tablet naming Min royalty and officials in the seventh. Southeast of the pagoda stands the stele of the Tang Jingguang Pagoda, dated 799.

History: a major repair in 1621 added eight guardian figures at the corners of the ground storey; a 1696 repair recast the finial; in 1958 the tilting body was banded storey by storey with steel. It is one of China's few surviving Five Dynasties stone pagodas, and its images and inscriptions are first-hand material for the history of the Min kingdom.
captions: Black Pagoda, Fuzhou · Chongmiao Baosheng Jianlao Pagoda

wenfeng.name: Wenfeng Pagoda
wenfeng.lede: In the fifty-three years of the Five Dynasties, few timber buildings survived in the Central Plains, and this brick pagoda is a rare relic of that turbulent age. Wider at the top than at the bottom and shaped like a parasol canopy, it has almost no parallel among China's ancient pagodas.
facts: Five stories and octagonal, it widens story by story, each story projecting outward on corbeled brick eaves; the top story is the widest.
The top is not an ordinary finial but a Tibetan-style lama stupa about ten meters tall.
The eight faces of the body carry brick carvings of the life of the Buddha; a stair inside leads to the top for a distant view.
In the Qianlong era of the Qing, Huang Bangning, prefect of Zhangde, inscribed the words “Wenfeng songxiu” (the literary peak rises in elegance), and the pagoda was renamed after them.
captions: Line drawing · Five stories, octagonal

hb_cangzhoulion.name: Iron Lion of Cangzhou
hb_cangzhoulion.sub: Original iron lion surviving at the old city (damage retained)
hb_cangzhoulion.yearNote: The enlarged replica made in 2011 for Lion City Park is not used; the real damage, the lotus basin on its back and the necessary supports follow photographs.
hb_cangzhoulion.lede: Cast in 953 under the Later Zhou, 6.26 m long, 5.47 m tall and 32 tonnes, the Cangzhou Iron Lion (Cangzhou Tie Shizi) is the largest surviving ancient cast-iron object. Its body is inscribed 'made by Li Yun of Shandong', it carries a lotus basin on its back and seems to bear the Diamond Sutra inside its belly, which makes it look more like the mount of Manjusri in a temple than the legendary 'Sea-Quelling Roar'. Over a thousand years it has been blown over, hacked, filled with sulphur and had its legs packed; today its four feet bear no load and a steel frame holds it up. The plate follows the original, breaks and props included.
facts: Form: 6.264 m long, 2.981 m wide and 5.47 m tall, hollow-bellied, weighing 32 tonnes against an estimated original of over 40; cast in sections with stacked clay moulds, about 500 in all. Head raised and mouth open, with straps across chest and haunches and a huge iron lotus basin on its back.

Inscriptions: 'cast in the 3rd year of Guangshun of the Great Zhou' on the right of the neck and along the teeth, 'made by Li Yun of Shandong' on the left flank, 'Lion King' on the head and under the neck, and what appears to be the Diamond Sutra inside the belly. Three explanations of its purpose, town guardian, sea-quelling image or the mount of Manjusri in a temple, remain unsettled.

Repairs: blown over by a gale in 1803 and righted in 1893; moved 8 m north in 1983, then damaged further by a sulphur compound poured in 1987 and by leg fillings in 1994-1995, so that the legs no longer bear weight and the lion stands only on external steel supports.
captions: Original iron lion of Cangzhou
Damage and protective supports retained as in 2020 photographs

zhakoubaita.name: Zhakou White Pagoda
zhakoubaita.era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Wuyue
zhakoubaita.lede: The Zhakou White Pagoda carves the columns, tie beams, bracket sets and tiered eaves of a timber pavilion-style pagoda in miniature in white stone. Its nine-story body tapers up from a Sumeru plinth, and weathered stone eaves and an iron finial together outline this Wuyue structure on the bank of the Qiantang River.
facts: Conservation sources date the pagoda to the late Wuyue of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; no specific year of construction is firmly assigned.
It is an eight-sided, nine-story stone pagoda imitating a timber pavilion, each story made up of a balcony platform, a body and eaves.

The base is carved with the Nine Mountains and Eight Seas and with Buddhist sutras, and the body with reliefs of Buddhas, bodhisattvas and other figures; the plate keeps the present damage and does not complete it as a new pagoda.

huqiuta.name: Yunyan Temple Pagoda, Tiger Hill
huqiuta.era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Wuyue
huqiuta.lede: On the summit of Tiger Hill, the brick eaves of the Yunyan Temple Pagoda recede tier by tier, and its seven-story body keeps traces of timber-style columns, tie beams and bracket sets. The pagoda's lean and the successive changes to its brick and timber structure together make up the present form of this old Suzhou pagoda.
facts: The present pagoda was begun in 959 and completed in 961; the national listing dates it to the Five Dynasties, and historically it belongs to Wuyue.
It is a seven-story, eight-sided brick pagoda imitating a timber pavilion; its timber eaves have been lost, while the brick eaves and balcony platforms remain.
The body has long leaned to one side; repairs over the centuries and modern reinforcement are recorded separately from the date the original pagoda was built.

qixia.name: Relic Pagoda of Qixia Temple
qixia.era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Southern Tang
qixia.lede: The Relic Pagoda of Qixia Temple raises its sculpted body on upturned lotus petals; five stone eaves recede upward, and a carved finial stands at the top. Buddha niches, guardians and narrative reliefs on the base give this Southern Tang stone pagoda both an architectural and a sculptural scale.
facts: The surviving stone pagoda is a Southern Tang rebuilding, dated to the Five Dynasties in the national listing; its Sui-dynasty timber predecessor is recorded separately from today's stone pagoda.
It is an octagonal five-story multi-eaved stone pagoda resting on a Sumeru plinth and upturned lotus, with five stone eaves stacked above the body.
The body is carved with doors and with figures such as heavenly kings and guardians, and the base with Buddhist stories; the plate renders the reliefs as simplified line drawing.

lingyin.name: Stone Pagodas and Dharani Pillars of Lingyin Temple, Hangzhou
lingyin.lede: The stone pagodas freeze tiers of timber eaves in stone, while the dharani pillars stack scripture and Buddha images on tall columns. This group of Wuyue survivals at Lingyin Temple dates from across the founding of the Northern Song, yet still belongs to Jiangnan under the rule of the Qian family.
facts: The stone pagodas were built in 960; two survive, octagonal and nine stories high, rendering in stone the columns, tie beams, bracket sets and projecting eaves of a pavilion.

The dharani pillars were built in 969, and two also survive; their shafts are carved with scripture, and the pedestals and upper parts are stacked in tiers. They belong to a different construction date from the stone pagodas.

The plate selects one stone pagoda and one dharani pillar and sets them side by side for comparison from historical photographs; the timber halls of the present temple have their own history of later rebuilding.

sx_zhenguo.name: Zhenguo Temple, Pingyao
sx_zhenguo.yearNote: Dated to the 7th year of Tianhui of the Northern Han. Although 963 already falls within the Northern Song reckoning, this part of Shanxi still belonged to the Northern Han, so the hall is not reassigned as a Song structure.
sx_zhenguo.lede: The Northern Han lasted only twenty-eight years, and this hall is the one building it left above ground. The Wanfo Hall of 963, the seventh year of Tianhui, is three bays square; its eave columns are only 3.4 m tall, yet the bracket sets on them rise 1.7 m, seven-puzuo clusters with two arms and two cantilevers that push the eaves out nearly two metres. The brackets take up almost sixty per cent of the column height, the last enlargement of the Tang manner of big brackets on a small hall. Eleven Five Dynasties statues inside are as old as the building.
facts: Form: three bays wide and three deep, nearly square at 11.58 by 10.78 m and 8.8 m high, under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; twelve eave columns 3.42 m tall, no plate, the architrave not projecting at the corners. Capital sets are seven-puzuo with two projecting arms and two downward cantilevers, intermediate sets five-puzuo with two arms; the brackets are 1.74 m high and the eaves project 1.94 m.

Date: an inscription under the ridge purlin records construction in 963, the seventh year of Tianhui of the Northern Han, a date confirmed by a stele of 1819; the temple, originally Jingcheng Temple, was renamed Zhenguo Temple in 1540, and steles record repairs in the Jin, Ming and Qing.

Significance: the only surviving building of the Northern Han and one of the earliest Five Dynasties to early Song timber structures; the eleven figures on the altar, a Buddha, two disciples, two bodhisattvas, two attendants, two heavenly kings and two offering boys, are original Five Dynasties work, the only hall sculpture of that era outside the Mogao Caves. Inscribed as World Heritage with the Ancient City of Pingyao and Shuanglin Temple in 1997.
captions: Ten-Thousand-Buddha Hall, Zhenguo Temple · Front view
7th year of Tianhui, Northern Han · 963

hualin.name: Hualin Temple, Fuzhou
hualin.era: 2nd year of Qiande, Northern Song · Built under Wuyue
hualin.place: Fujian · Fuzhou · Gulou District · Southern foot of Mount Ping
hualin.lede: The oldest surviving timber building south of the Yangtze, and a small hall built with 'first-grade timber': only three bays wide, yet its brackets use the largest module that the Yingzao Fashi reserves for halls of nine to eleven bays; the cap-blocks are huge, and the roof is carried almost entirely by the bracket sets over the columns. In 964 Fuzhou still belonged to Wuyue, and the prefect Bao Xiurang built this Yueshan Jixiang Chan Cloister from the dismantled timbers of the Min kingdom's palaces, so the hall is at once early Northern Song and late Five Dynasties. During the 1980s dismantling repair the whole hall was also moved more than ten metres east.
facts: Form: three bays (15.84 m) wide and four bays (14.70 m) deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; an eight-rafter frame with front and rear rufu beams on four columns. Only 18 columns in all (14 eave columns, 4 interior), column-top bracket sets of seven tiers with two huagong and three downward ang, very large timber module, and an open ceiling.

Dating: the Chunxi Sanshan Zhi records the founding in 964; samples taken during the 1980s repair were carbon-dated to generally over a thousand years old. Enlarged to seven bays with double eaves in the Jiaqing-Daoguang era, the hall was dismantled and rebuilt in 1984-1989 to its early three-bay single-eave form, on a site 14.6 m east of the original.

Comparison: by date it follows the Tang and Five Dynasties timber halls of Shanxi such as Nanchan and Foguang temples, making it the oldest timber building south of the Yangtze, about half a century earlier than the main hall of Baoguo Temple in Ningbo; Chinese and Japanese scholars widely see its entasis columns and oversized brackets as a source for Kamakura-period architecture in Japan.
captions: Line drawing of the Main Hall of Hualin Temple · Three bays wide
Single-eaved hip-and-gable · 2nd year of Qiande, Northern Song
