chongming.name: Chongming Temple, Gaoping
chongming.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Hexi Town · Guojiazhuang Village
chongming.lede: The Middle Buddha Hall at the eastern foot of Shengfo Mountain was finished in 971, the fourth year of Kaibao of the Northern Song, a hundred and thirty years before the Yingzao fashi was issued, yet it is still built the Tang way: seven-puzuo capital sets with two arms and two cantilevers match those of the East Hall of Foguang Temple almost exactly, the brackets stand nearly as tall as the columns, and there is no plate, the architrave not projecting at the corners. Not one interior column stands inside; look up and the main load-bearing beam turns out to be two short timbers butted end to end, held under the joint by a longitudinal tie, the so-called 'broken beam', a unique case of making big use of small timber.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with a shallow pitch and deep eaves; capital sets are seven-puzuo with two arms and two downward cantilevers, the bracket height close to the column height in a ratio near 1:1, column tops gently rounded, no plate, architrave not projecting. There are no interior columns, the roof load passes through the bracket layer to the eave columns, and the beams are comparatively slender.

Date: a stele of 991, the Record of the Founding of the Imperially Named Chongming Temple on Shengfo Mountain, says the temple was founded in the Kaibao years; in the Taiping Xingguo years the founding monk Xingyong went to the capital and Emperor Taizong bestowed the name. The Middle Hall is dated to 971; major repairs followed in 1591 and 1826. The temple was originally called Langgu Temple.

Significance: the main load-bearing beam of the double-beam system is made of two short timbers of equal diameter and length butted together, carried under the joint by a longitudinal tie and resting at both ends on the tails of the front and rear eave brackets, the 'broken beam', unique among surviving ancient buildings; its bracket sets are one of nine surviving examples of this type predating the Yingzao fashi, hence the phrase 'Song structure in Tang manner'.

longxing.name: Longxing Temple
longxing.sub: Moni Hall · Hall of Great Compassion · Revolving Sutra Cabinet
longxing.lede: In 971 Emperor Taizu of Song ordered the Longzang Monastery enlarged and a bronze Guanyin seven zhang three chi tall cast; from this Longxing Temple (Longxing Si) became the most complete surviving ensemble of Northern Song official architecture. The Moni Hall of 1052 has a cruciform plan with a gabled porch on each of its four sides, gable ends facing outward, which Liang Sicheng called 'common in Song painting but never before found in a surviving building'. The 21.3 m Thousand-armed Guanyin in the Dabei Pavilion and the seven-metre revolving sutra repository in its own hall are, respectively, the largest surviving ancient bronze Guanyin and the earliest surviving revolving repository.
facts: Moni Hall: seven bays by seven on a near-square body, with a hip-and-gable porch projecting from the centre of each side, gable forward, forming a cross-shaped plan; a double-eave hip-and-gable roof over thick walls, with doors and windows only in the porch fronts, a form close to the buildings seen in surviving Song paintings.

Dates: founded in 586 as Longzang Monastery, with the Longzang Temple stele of that year still on site; enlarged by imperial order in 971, when the Guanyin was cast; the Moni Hall was built in 1052, and the name Longxing Si was conferred in 1710 under Kangxi.

Song superlatives: the bronze Thousand-armed Guanyin in the Dabei Pavilion is 21.3 m tall with forty-two arms, the largest surviving ancient bronze Guanyin; the revolving sutra repository is about 7 m across, carried on eight-tier bracket sets with five projecting arms, and is the earliest surviving example. The present Dabei Pavilion was rebuilt around 1940.
captions: Line drawing of the Moni Hall · Seven bays wide

hn_jidu.name: Jidu Temple
hn_jidu.sub: A Song-dynasty Sleeping Hall at the source of the Ji River
hn_jidu.yearNote: Based on the date of the timber Sleeping Hall; the Sui founding history of Jidu Temple is not applied to the Song hall.
hn_jidu.lede: Jidu Temple honors the god of the Ji River, and its Sleeping Hall preserves timber construction of the 6th year of Kaibao in the Northern Song. Under the low, gentle roof, massive bracket sets and a simple column grid support a five-bay facade.
facts: Northern Song Sleeping Hall: The Sleeping Hall was built in 973 and is the main timber structure in the temple with a clear Song date.
Five bays, hip-and-gable: The hall is five bays wide and four rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the front eaves retain large bracket sets.
Conservation: Professional conservation and repair were carried out in modern times, and the plate is drawn from photographs of its present state after repair.

hn_fanta.name: Fan Pagoda, Kaifeng
hn_fanta.sub: Surviving three-story main body and small pagoda
hn_fanta.yearNote: 974 is the year the Song main body was built; the small pagoda on top and the repaired details are not dated by this year.
hn_fanta.lede: Only three stories of the broad hexagonal body remain, yet they still carry layered brick carvings and Buddha niches. The incomplete outline of the Fan Pagoda records the demolition and repairs that followed the building of this Song pagoda.
facts: The Fan Pagoda was built in the 7th year of Kaibao in the Northern Song (974), and its tall lower three stories survive.
The hexagonal body is covered with Buddha-image bricks and timber-style details, and on top is a small pagoda rebuilt in a later period.
The plate draws the three-story main body and the small pagoda surviving on top as they are now, without restoring the original nine stories as a complete pagoda.

sh_longhuata.name: Longhua Pagoda
sh_longhuata.sub: Eight-sided, seven stories · Brick-and-timber pavilion-style pagoda
sh_longhuata.era: 2nd year of Taiping Xingguo · Rebuilt by Qian Chu of Wuyue
sh_longhuata.yearNote: The main body of the surviving pagoda is placed by its rebuilding by Qian Chu of Wuyue in the 2nd year of Taiping Xingguo (977); the national listing dates it to the Song. The timber eaves, railings and other parts have been repaired over the centuries, and the legend of a founding in the Three Kingdoms period is not taken as the date of the surviving pagoda.
sh_longhuata.lede: Seven tiers of flying eaves unfold story by story around the pagoda core, with timber railings and yellow walls alternating around it. The Longhua Pagoda carries on the ancient body rebuilt under Wuyue while keeping, through repairs over the centuries, the layered outline of a brick-and-timber pavilion-style pagoda.
facts: Traditionally said to have been first built in the Three Kingdoms period, the main body of the surviving pagoda was rebuilt by Qian Chu, King of Wuyue, in the 2nd year of Taiping Xingguo in the Northern Song (977); the legendary date and the surviving main body are recorded separately.
A pavilion-style brick-and-timber pagoda, eight-sided and seven stories high, about 40.4 m tall overall; the body tapers story by story, with timber eaves and balcony railings on the outside.

After many repairs, the exterior timberwork is not all the same age as the ancient brick body. The plate depicts the present appearance from daytime photographs and includes only the old pagoda, not the temple's later halls.
captions: Eight-sided, seven stories · Brick-and-timber pavilion style
Rebuilt under Wuyue · Northern Song date (977)

luohanshuangta.name: Twin Pagodas and Main Hall Ruins of Luohan Monastery, Suzhou
luohanshuangta.sub: Seven-tiered, eight-sided twin pagodas · Song stone columns
luohanshuangta.era: Begun in the 7th year of Taiping Xingguo
luohanshuangta.lede: Two slender brick pagodas stand side by side, their long iron finials reaching into the sky. The main hall beside them has vanished, but its stone columns and column bases still mark the scale of the hall on the original site.
facts: The twin pagodas were begun in the 7th year of Taiping Xingguo in the Northern Song (982) and completed in the Yongxi era; both are seven-tiered, eight-sided pavilion-style pagodas.
The brick bodies imitating timber taper story by story, rendering the pavilion form with columns, tie beams, bracket sets and brick eaves, and the long finials give a striking outline.
Main hall ruins: The hall has been destroyed, but stone columns and carved column bases remain; the plate selects a few of these remains and presents them alongside the twin pagodas.
captions: Twin Pagodas of Luohan Monastery · Remains of stone columns
Northern Song · Begun in the 7th year of Taiping Xingguo

sx_youxian.name: Youxian Temple, Gaoping
sx_youxian.era: Chunhua era, Northern Song · Vairocana Hall
sx_youxian.yearNote: Local culture and tourism accounts give 990, but no inscription recording a founding at that time has been found for the front hall; the period 990–994 is used as an approximate placement, without claiming a precise completion year.
sx_youxian.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Mount Niu, Zaili Village, Hexi Town
sx_youxian.lede: On Niushan hill, a stele records that the temple was founded in 990, the first year of Chunhua of the Northern Song, and the Vairocana Hall is dated to the Chunhua years. Three bays wide, six rafters deep and nearly square, its thick walls wrap the eave columns inside, and the deep eaves press down on the wall mass; the capital sets are five-puzuo with one arm and one cantilever, the cantilever and the head both cut in the sharp 'split-bamboo' profile, and neither plate nor architrave projects at the corners. The frame inside is left open to view, and the hip rafter beam is simply a naturally bent log sawn to shape, the offhand ingenuity of local craftsmen.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafters deep, nearly square in plan, under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof of flat and cylinder tiles with carved-brick ridge ornaments; capital sets are five-puzuo with one arm and one cantilever, open-heart construction, one five-puzuo intermediate set with two arms in each bay, the heads shaped as split-bamboo cantilevers; plate and architrave both stop at the corners. The frame uses a four-rafter beam against a rear two-rafter beam on three columns, exposed without a ceiling.

Date: according to steles in the temple it was founded in 990, originally named Cijiao Cloister, and repaired in the Jin, Yuan, Ming and Qing. The Vairocana Hall is identified as original Northern Song work, placed approximately in the Chunhua years (990–994) since no inscription of its own has been found; the Three Buddhas Hall is a Jin structure and the rest Ming and Qing.

Significance: the hip rafter beam is sawn from a naturally curved timber, preserving the local Song-period practice of southeastern Shanxi; the Song Sumeru-style altar inside, carved with waist panels, cusped openings and flowers, is one of the few surviving original Song altars. The temple is noted locally for its many steles and for the scene of 'the dawn bell of Youxian'.
captions: Youxian Temple · Vairocana Hall
Chunhua era, Northern Song · c. 990–994

songyangyanqing.name: Yanqing Temple Pagoda, Songyang
songyangyanqing.lede: The hexagonal body of the Yanqing Temple Pagoda tapers tier by tier, with balcony galleries running around it and two broad eaves spreading at the base. A slender iron finial stands atop the seven-tier brick-and-timber structure, showing the form of early pavilion-style pagodas in southwestern Zhejiang.
facts: Work on the pagoda began in the 2nd year of Xianping in the Northern Song (999) and was completed in 1002; this entry is recorded by its Song brick core.
The pagoda is a six-sided, seven-tier pavilion-style brick-and-timber structure; the ground story has a double-eaved peristyle (fujie), so eight eave lines can be counted on the complete exterior.
Major repairs began in 1983 and were completed in 1991; the repair history of today's timber eaves and galleries must be distinguished from the Northern Song body.
captions: Songyang · Yanqing Temple Pagoda
Six sides, seven tiers · Double-eaved peristyle at the base

yuanqi.name: Yuanqi Temple, Lucheng
yuanqi.era: Founded in the 6th year of Tianbao, Tang · Surviving Song structures
yuanqi.place: Shanxi · Lucheng · Bank of the Zhuozhang River · Xin'an Village
yuanqi.lede: The temple sits on the summit of Fenghuang Hill on the west bank of the Zhuozhang River, barely twenty-two metres north to south and thirty-three east to west, and was founded in 747, the sixth year of Tianbao of the Tang. Its surviving main hall and Azure Dragon Pagoda are both Song: a three-bay, four-rafter hall under a hip-and-gable roof with plain brackets, and west of it an octagonal seven-storey brick pagoda about seventeen metres high, carved-brick brackets under each tier of eaves and a vase-shaped finial tied by eight iron chains to eight iron figures at the corners. Hall and pagoda stand side by side on the cliff top; from the valley the pagoda catches the eye first.
facts: Form: the main hall is three bays wide and four rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, plain in form with simple brackets; the Azure Dragon Pagoda west of the hall is an octagonal seven-storey brick pagoda about 17 m high, with eaves on every storey, carved-brick imitation brackets beneath them and a vase-shaped finial, each of the eight corners anchored by an iron figure holding an iron chain.

Date: the temple was founded in 747; the main hall and pagoda are Song buildings, the pagoda by one account of 1087, the second year of Yuanyou of the Northern Song; the offering pavilion and side halls are Ming and Qing. The heritage authorities date the complex as a whole to the Song.

Significance: the site measures only 22.3 m north-south by 32.7 m east-west, 729 square metres, yet hall and pagoda side by side on the lone peak make a complete composition, the pagoda set west of the hall rather than on the axis; with Dayun Monastery and Tiantai Hermitage a little downstream it forms the Song link in the sequence of early buildings along the Zhuozhang valley.
captions: Line drawing · Hall and pagoda side by side

gd_meian.name: Mahavira Hall of Mei'an, Zhaoqing
gd_meian.sub: Song timber frame · Present flush gable roof
gd_meian.yearNote: Mei'an was founded in 996; 1000 is only an approximate ordering point for the Song structure, without asserting that every component of the surviving hall was completed in the same year. The Mahavira Hall retains features of Song timber construction; its roof was changed to a flush gable roof in later repairs, and the plate follows the present state.
gd_meian.lede: The timber frame of the five-bay hall retains features of Song architecture, while its roof bears the changes of later repairs. The small hermitage does not impress by its size; what is worth seeing is precisely its timber structure and its accumulated layers of history.
facts: Main subject: The complete Mahavira Hall of Mei'an.

Date: Mei'an was founded in 996; 1000 is only an approximate ordering point for the Song structure, without asserting that every component of the surviving hall was completed in the same year. The Mahavira Hall retains features of Song timber construction; its roof was changed to a flush gable roof in later repairs, and the plate follows the present state.

Plate scope: The present flush gable roof and the five-bay Song timber body of the hall, three bays deep; it is not changed back to the hip-and-gable roof of the original construction, and the incense burner and trees are not drawn.

ruiguang.name: Ruiguang Pagoda, Suzhou
ruiguang.era: Built from the 1st year of Jingde to the 8th year of Tiansheng
ruiguang.lede: Beside Panmen Gate, seven tiers of eaves recede one above another, and the body and its exterior timberwork together form the outline of a Jiangnan pavilion-style pagoda. It has undergone Song alterations and modern restoration, so its date must be read from the early brick body.
facts: Northern Song construction: The foundation was laid in the 1st year of Jingde (1004) and the pagoda was completed in the 8th year of Tiansheng (1030); it was later altered and repaired.
The seven-tier, eight-sided brick body bears the load, while the exterior timber eaves and galleries display the pavilion form; the present state includes parts restored in modern times.
Pagoda treasures: Objects found inside the pagoda, such as the Pearl Relic Pillar, are now in the Suzhou Museum and can be read alongside the pagoda's building history.

Northern Song body · Later timber eaves

baoguo.name: Baoguo Temple, Ningbo
baoguo.lede: The Main Hall of the 6th year of Dazhong Xiangfu in the Northern Song (1013) is the earliest surviving timber building south of the Yangtze. It was originally a three-bay hall with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; in the Qing a peristyle was added all around, producing the five-bay, double-eaved hall seen today — the central three bays are still Song construction from a thousand years ago.
facts: The plan is deeper than it is wide, and three caisson ceilings in the front bay of the interior hide the beam frame, which is why it is popularly called the “Beamless Hall.”

The melon-ribbed columns are each assembled from four smaller pieces into one large column, the earliest surviving example of composite columns in China; the bracket sets are seven-puzuo, with two projecting arms and two descending cantilevers.
“Birds do not roost, insects do not bore, spiders spin no webs and no dust settles on the beams” — legend credits the timber, but in fact it is the cross-draft through the hall.
No Buddha images are enshrined in the temple; it is now a museum of ancient architecture.
captions: Line drawing of the Main Hall · Five bays wide
Double-eaved hip-and-gable · Peristyle added in the Qing

sx_chongqing.name: Chongqing Temple, Zhangzi
sx_chongqing.era: 9th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Northern Song · Thousand-Buddha Hall
sx_chongqing.place: Shanxi · Zhangzi · Mount Ziyun, Ju Village, Setou Town
sx_chongqing.lede: The Thousand-Buddha Hall of Chongqing Temple sits on the slope of Mount Ziyun, its wide eaves covering three plain bays of thick walls. The Northern Song timber structure stands next to the temple's Song painted clay arhats, so the different dates of architecture and sculpture can be read side by side in one small temple.
facts: Song structure of 1016: The Thousand-Buddha Hall dates from the 9th year of Dazhong Xiangfu in the Northern Song; it is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, and the surviving main structure is recorded as Song.

Wide eaves, thick walls: The walls lie close to the plane of the eave columns; the central timber door and the vertical-bar windows on either side are tucked under the great eaves, and the bracket sets beneath the eaves are sturdy and clear.
Song sculpture next door: The temple's Dashi Hall and its eighteen arhats bear a date of 1079, and the walls and other halls have later repairs; this drawing depicts only the Thousand-Buddha Hall.

hb_xiude.name: Xiude Temple Pagoda
hb_xiude.sub: Surviving brick pagoda combining pavilion and flower-pagoda forms
hb_xiude.yearNote: The county gazetteer says the pagoda was completed in 1020; the provincial cultural heritage bureau dates it only to the Song and records six tiers with no surviving finial. Later photographs were checked against the surviving tiers, and the common seven-story account is not used to reconstruct it.
hb_xiude.lede: Below, a plain storeyed body; in the middle it suddenly swells into a 'flower pagoda' tier studded with miniature stupa niches; above, it returns to storeyed form. Two pagoda types joined in one, the 32 m brick Xiude Temple Pagoda (Xiudesi Ta) at Quyang is a rare variant of the flower pagoda. A tablet set in the body records that 'on the 8th day of the 4th month of Tianxi 3 of the Great Song (1019) the villagers of Shuidouyan and other villages together repaired one tier of the relic pagoda'; the county gazetteer says the pagoda was finished the following year (1020), while the stone casket in the crypt dates the original relic pagoda to 601. In 1953 a large hoard of white-marble Buddhist statues from the Northern Dynasties to the Tang was unearthed beneath the base, now divided between the Palace Museum and the Hebei Provincial Museum.
facts: Form: an octagonal brick pagoda 32 m high. The second storey is exceptionally tall and ringed with 110 small stupa niches in the flower-pagoda manner; the tiers below and above are storeyed in form. Usually counted as seven storeys, though the provincial heritage bureau records six; the finial is lost.

Dates: a tablet in the body reads 'Tianxi 3 (1019), 4th month, 8th day ... together repaired one tier of the relic pagoda', and the gazetteer records completion in 1020; the crypt casket inscription puts the first relic pagoda in 601 (Sui). Xiude Temple, founded north of the pagoda in the Yuanyou era (1086-1093), no longer exists.

Finds: in 1953 white-marble statues from the Northern Wei to the Tang were excavated under the base, including 48 of the Sui Daye era and 33 of the Northern Qi Tianbao era, now in the Palace Museum and the Hebei Provincial Museum; the crypt itself was found in 1994.

jiwang.name: Jiwang Temple, Wanrong
jiwang.place: Shanxi · Wanrong · Nanzhang Township · Taizhao Village
jiwang.lede: A low, spreading hipped roof covers a five-bay facade, and a deep gallery encloses the ritual space within. The temple is dedicated to Houji, the ancestor of agriculture, and its main hall, framed without full-length great beams, preserves a distinctive Northern Song structural solution.
facts: Northern Song structure: Official sources date the main hall to the Northern Song and record that the temple was founded no later than the 1st year of Tiansheng (1023).
Five-bay hipped hall: The main hall is five bays wide with a single-eaved hipped roof, and bracket sets on the column heads and between the columns carry the deep eaves.

“Beamless Hall”: The popular name comes from the absence of full-length great beams inside; it still has a timber beam frame and is not a masonry beamless hall. It was listed in the 5th batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level in 2001.
captions: Jiwang Temple, Wanrong · Main Hall

haiqing.name: Ashoka Pagoda of Haiqing Temple
haiqing.place: Jiangsu · Lianyungang · Foot of Huaguo Mountain
haiqing.lede: The Ashoka Pagoda of Haiqing Temple tapers upward through nine tiers of corbeled brick eaves, its tall ground-story chamber and tiers of arched doors setting a clear rhythm. This brick pagoda at the foot of Huaguo Mountain preserves its Northern Song outline, plain and upright in appearance.
facts: The pagoda had a Tang predecessor; the present pagoda is recorded by its rebuilding in the 1st year of Tiansheng in the Northern Song (1023), and the Tang history is not taken as the date of the main structure.
The body is eight-sided with nine tiers; its brick eaves are corbeled tier upon tier, and the arched doors and low top form its present outline.
Repairs in the 1970s found a stone casket, a silver coffin, porcelain vases, relics and other objects in the pagoda core; they are now kept by the Lianyungang Museum.

hb_tuoluoni.name: Zhaozhou Dharani Pillar
hb_tuoluoni.yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hb_tuoluoni.lede: At 16.44 m the tallest surviving sutra pillar, the Zhaozhou Dharani Pillar (Zhaozhou Tuoluoni Jingchuang) stands where two main streets of Zhaoxian meet, like a stone pagoda built up from scripture and carving. It was erected in 1038 under prefect Wang Decheng; each of the seven tiers of the shaft is cut from a single block, and between them canopies, upturned lotus, an octagonal walled city and straining strongmen appear in turn. The third-tier eave carries the Prince Siddhartha leaving the city by its four gates; on the fifth tier eight strongmen hold up the tier above with hands or heads. The original Kaiyuan Temple is long gone, but the pillar still stands in place; lightning wrecked tiers three to five in 1983 and they were restored in 1990.
facts: Form: 16.44 m tall overall, facing south. A square podium 1.9 m high and 7.35 m on a side carries a two-tier octagonal Sumeru pedestal; the shaft has seven tiers, each carved from one stone and stepping inward, topped by a peach-shaped bronze flaming jewel.

Inscriptions: the south face of the first tier bears in seal script 'Reverently made for all living beings on land and water of the great earth, the Usnisa-vijaya Dharani Pillar'; the tiers carry dharani texts and donor names, and the sixth tier records a repair in the ninth month of Longqing 5 (1571).

Carving: the third-tier eave is an octagonal walled city whose four cardinal faces form 'Prince Siddhartha at the Four Gates'; each of the eight faces of the fifth tier has a strongman supporting the eave; the podium has strongmen at the corners and 'women closing doors' reliefs on three sides. Struck by lightning in 1983, restored in 1990 with a protective pool added.
captions: Zhaozhou Dharani Pillar · Seven-tier stone dharani pillar
Song · 1038

lingxiao.name: Lingxiao Pagoda of Tianning Temple
lingxiao.era: Founded in the Tang · Rebuilt in the 5th year of Qingli, Song
lingxiao.lede: The lower four storeys are Song brick, the upper five Jin timber: two dynasties stacked in one pagoda, and no rebuilding ever started from scratch. At the centre of the fourth storey rises a central mast bound from nine round logs and running to the top; Luo Zhewen called this structure unique among surviving buildings. The inscription on the crypt casket records that the Lingxiao Pagoda (Lingxiao Ta) of Tianning Temple was first built in the reign of Tang Daizong; it was rebuilt on the Tang ruins in 1045 (Northern Song) and its upper part rebuilt in 1141 (Jin). The 1966 Xingtai earthquake wrecked everything above the seventh storey, and repairs began in 1981.
facts: Form: octagonal, nine storeys of pavilion type, about 41 m high; storeys one to four are brick, five and above timber. A central mast of nine bundled logs rises from the fourth storey to the top; the central-mast system was the main way of building pagodas before the Tang, and this is the only surviving example.

Dates: a crypt found beneath the base in 1982 held a casket inscribed 'pagoda built in the reign of Daizong', placing the foundation between 756 and 779; rebuilt in 1045 (Qingli 5 of Northern Song) and the upper part rebuilt in 1141 (Huangtong 1 of Jin). Its original name was Huiguang Pagoda.

Repairs: in the Northern Song the monk Huaibing replaced the rotten central mast, and the tale behind the idiom 'steal the beam, change the pillar' has attached itself to the pagoda; the 1966 Xingtai earthquake badly damaged the storeys above the seventh, and Hebei's heritage authorities rebuilt them after a full survey begun in 1981.
captions: Line drawing · Octagonal, nine stories

hn_tieta.name: Iron Pagoda, Kaifeng
hn_tieta.yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hn_tieta.lede: Thirteen tiers of closely set eave lines slowly converge toward the top. The Iron Pagoda of Kaifeng is not cast in iron; its dark brown glazed bricks gave this Song pagoda the name it still bears.
facts: The Youguo Temple Pagoda was built in the 1st year of Huangyou in the Northern Song (1049); it is an octagonal thirteen-story pagoda of glazed brick.
Its surface is assembled from molded glazed bricks forming bracket sets, doors, windows and ornament, and the closely spaced eaves create a steady rhythm.
The plate is based mainly on a photograph of the whole pagoda, supplemented by close-ups of the ground story; it keeps the thirteen stories and does not reconstruct the earlier timber pagoda.

fotou.name: Fotou Temple, Pingshun
fotou.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · South bank of the Zhuozhang River · Chedang Village
fotou.lede: On the slope above Chedang village, on the south bank of the Zhuozhang River, a small temple has been reduced to a single hall of a hundred and thirty-one square metres. Three bays and four rafters under a hip-and-gable roof, five-puzuo sets with two cantilevers at both capitals and intermediate positions, a three-rafter beam meeting a rear single-rafter tie inside, a short post carrying the collar beam: the State Council's list dates it Song. The four walls inside carry murals of the Twenty-four Devas from a different age than the timber frame, two periods' handiwork layered in one hall.
facts: Form: the hall faces south, three bays wide and four rafters deep, with a floor area of 131 square metres, under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with glazed ridge ornaments; capital and intermediate sets are both five-puzuo with two downward cantilevers; the frame sets a three-rafter beam against a rear single-rafter tie on three columns, and a short post carries the collar beam.

Date: the temple takes its name from the hill behind, shaped like a Buddha's head; its founding date is unknown. The surviving hall is dated Song in the list published by the State Council in 2006; the murals are said to be Yuan, while a local newspaper calls the building 'Jin structure, Ming painting', so both dates are disputed. This entry follows the official list and gives Northern Song.

Significance: the Twenty-four Devas painted on the four walls are rare Yuan (or, by one account, Ming) murals in the Zhuozhang valley; with Chunhua Temple and the Jiutian Shengmu Temple it belongs to the small Song and Jin shrines of Pingshun county, and though modest in size its frame and brackets are complete, a Song three-bay hall that can be read at a glance.

baosheng.name: Baosheng Temple
baosheng.yearNote: 1050 is only an approximate Northern Song placement on the timeline, not an exact date of sculpting; the original 1961 national listing gives Northern Song, and the traditional attribution to Yang Huizhi of the Tang is not treated as settled authorship.
baosheng.lede: Arhats sit among undulating rocks and clouds, their lean faces and the folds of their broad robes still full of spirit. The surviving half of the sculpted wall at Baosheng Temple models figures and landscape together into the wall surface.
facts: Northern Song sculpture: The first national listing of 1961 dated the arhat sculptures of Baosheng Temple to the Northern Song; the claim that they were created by Yang Huizhi of the Tang is a traditional attribution.
Nine figures, half the set: Nine seated arhats survive, arranged irregularly across the sculpted wall, each with a different posture and expression; this drawing selects one of them.

Landscape in the wall: Rocks, clouds, caves and other features form the background of the sculpted wall, with the figures set into the landscape; the date of today's protective hall is counted separately.
captions: Baosheng Temple · Arhat sculpture and sculpted rock wall (detail)

hb_puli.name: Puli Temple Pagoda
hb_puli.sub: Square seven-story body and balcony eaves
hb_puli.yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau clearly gives the 3rd year of Huangyou; the surviving seven stories are kept, and other pagodas of the same name are not confused with it.
hb_puli.lede: A Northern Song pagoda on a square plan, the only one preserved in China: after the Tang most brick pagodas went octagonal, but the Puli Temple Pagoda (Pulisi Ta) at Lincheng kept the square. It is 33 m tall, its outer walls studded with thousand-Buddha brick reliefs, a balcony ringing it beneath the second storey, and the eaves above tightly stacked. Storey counts disagree: the provincial heritage bureau says seven, the national register eight, the local gazetteer nine, the difference being whether the balcony eave counts as a storey. The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau dates it to 1051; the temple is long gone and the pagoda stands alone on its high terrace.
facts: Form: a square brick pagoda 33 m high in the timber-imitating dense-eave style. The outer walls carry 974 brick-relief Buddhas and the inner walls 40, hence the alternative name Ten-Thousand-Buddha Pagoda; a tall body below the second storey projects a balcony, and above it the eaves are closely stacked and taper upward.

Date: the Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau records construction in 1051 (Huangyou 3 of Northern Song); the national register of protected sites gives 1052 (Huangyou 4), and the local gazetteer claims supervision by Emperor Huizong. Puli Temple was founded in the Northern Dynasties and only the pagoda remains.

Storeys: counts of seven, eight and nine exist depending on whether the balcony eave is included; this entry follows the provincial bureau's seven. Iron bells once hung at the four corners of every storey and rang in the evening wind, the 'Puli evening bells' of old.
captions: Puli Temple Pagoda, Lincheng

liaodi.name: Kaiyuan Temple Pagoda, Dingzhou
liaodi.era: Begun in the 4th year of Xianping · Completed in the 2nd year of Zhihe
liaodi.lede: At 83.7 m, the tallest surviving brick pagoda in China. Work on the Kaiyuan Temple Pagoda of Dingzhou (Kaiyuansi Ta, the Liaodi Pagoda) began in 1001 under Emperor Zhenzong of Song and was not finished until 1055 under Renzong, fifty-four years in all, leaving the local saying 'they felled every tree on Jiashan to raise the Dingzhou pagoda'. Dingzhou was a military stronghold on the Song-Liao frontier, and from the top one could watch for Khitan movements, hence the name Liaodi, 'gauging the enemy'. Eleven storeys taper upward; inside, a corridor runs between an inner core and the outer shell, a pagoda within a pagoda. In 1884 the north-east face collapsed from top to bottom, and the gash stayed open for over a century until it was closed early this century.
facts: Form: an octagonal brick pagoda of eleven storeys in pavilion style, 83.7 m high and tapering storey by storey; it combines a through-core with a ring corridor in a double inner-and-outer structure, with stairs to climb inside, the only pagoda in north China built on the through-core system. Doors open on four faces, and the top carries a honeysuckle-carved inverted bowl and a bronze finial.

Date: in 1001 the monk Huineng of Kaiyuan Temple returned from India with relics and Emperor Zhenzong ordered the pagoda built; it was completed in 1055 after more than fifty years. During the Song-Liao standoff it served as a lookout for enemy movements, hence its other name, Liaodi Pagoda.

Repairs: in the sixth month of 1884 the north-east face of the body collapsed from top to bottom and remained broken for over a hundred years; large-scale restoration by the national heritage authorities began in 1986 and the pagoda reopened in 2002, ending the 'beauty of imperfection' of the ruined silhouette.
captions: Line drawing · Octagonal, eleven stories
Brick · Corbeled eaves · Balcony platforms

sd_pizhi.name: Pizhi Pagoda of Lingyan Temple, Jinan
sd_pizhi.sub: Octagonal, nine stories · Brick pagoda with twelve eaves
sd_pizhi.era: Rebuilt from the 5th year of Chunhua · Completed in the Jiayou era
sd_pizhi.yearNote: The pagoda inscription records rebuilding in the 5th year of Chunhua (994); image inscriptions of 1057–1058 provide the basis for completion in the Jiayou era, and 1057 is used as an approximate placement on the timeline.
sd_pizhi.lede: The Pizhi Pagoda stands amid the mountain scenery of Lingyan Temple, its octagonal body tapering story by story. The lower three stories each have two brick eaves and the upper six one each, so the nine-story body shows twelve tiers of eaves; an iron finial and fine chains close the outline at the top.
facts: The surviving pagoda is a Northern Song rebuilding. The pagoda inscription records that work began in the 5th year of Chunhua (994), and image inscriptions of the Jiayou era provide the basis for its completion date.
Octagonal with nine stories, double eaves on the lower three and single eaves on the upper six, twelve eaves in all; the brick eaves organize the outline with timber-style details.

The plate is drawn from daytime photographs of the surviving pagoda, keeping the gray-brown brick and stone, the dark eaves and some ochre-red door and window frames; it is not a reconstruction of historical paintwork.

hb_yuquan.name: Iron Pagoda of Yuquan Temple
hb_yuquan.sub: Northern Song iron pagoda · Octagonal, thirteen tiers
hb_yuquan.yearNote: The iron body is dated by its casting in the 6th year of Jiayou in the Northern Song (1061), while the finial on top is a later Qing-dynasty replacement; the drawing distinguishes the components of the two periods and does not date the modern temple buildings to the Song along with it.
hb_yuquan.lede: Thirteen tiers of small eaves recede one by one, and the cast-iron bracket sets also imitate timber construction. The dark brown rust of the body differs from the finial added later at the top.
facts: Main subject: The thirteen-story iron pagoda of Yuquan Temple, Dangyang.

Date: The iron body is dated by its casting in the 6th year of Jiayou in the Northern Song (1061), while the finial on top is a later Qing-dynasty replacement; the drawing distinguishes the components of the two periods and does not date the modern temple buildings to the Song along with it.

Plate scope: The octagonal thirteen-story pavilion-style iron pagoda, with its complete finial and story-by-story taper; only the iron pagoda and its short base are drawn, not the tall retaining wall or the surrounding trees.

hn_xiangshan.name: Guanyin Pagoda of Xiangshan Temple
hn_xiangshan.era: Northern Song · Rebuilt in the 1st year of Xining
hn_xiangshan.yearNote: Takes the rebuilding in the 1st year of Xining in the Song recorded by the municipal culture and tourism bureau; the original founding date of the temple and pagoda is unknown, and repairs continued in later periods.
hn_xiangshan.lede: Two tiers of closely set small niches support an octagonal body that tapers story by story. The Song pagoda of Xiangshan Temple and the stele written by Cai Jing preserve the Guanyin faith of the Central Plains in brick and stone.
facts: Surviving Song pagoda: According to the Pingdingshan Municipal Culture and Tourism Bureau, the pagoda was rebuilt by imperial grant in 1068; it is octagonal with nine tiers and 33 m tall, and has been repaired repeatedly since.
Form: Corbeled brick eaves with balcony platforms above them; small Buddha niches line the lower walls and the upper stories have doorways, tapering tier by tier.
Scope drawn: The plate takes the body visible today from two photographs; the part of the ground story hidden by the neighboring hall is left blank, and the hidden base is not reconstructed.

sx_kaihua.name: Kaihua Temple, Gaoping
sx_kaihua.era: 6th year of Xining, Northern Song · Mahavira Hall
sx_kaihua.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Mount Sheli, Wang Village, Chenqu Town
sx_kaihua.lede: The Mahavira Hall of Kaihua Temple is a hall where three kinds of Song work can be seen at once: the timber frame of 1073, the sixth year of Xining; Song 'full polychrome' painting on beams and brackets; and eighty-eight square metres of Northern Song murals on the east, west and north walls, dated by the painters' own labels to 1096, the third year of Shaosheng, with fishermen, farmers, pavilions and boats woven into the sutra stories, earning the name 'Qingming Scroll of mural painting'. A three-bay, six-rafter hall under a hip-and-gable roof, with square eave columns in the central bay.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafters deep, nearly square in plan, under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with glazed ridge ornaments; the front and rear eave columns of the central bay are square, carrying architrave and plate; capital sets are five-puzuo with one arm and one cantilever, cantilever and head both cut in the sharp split-bamboo profile, with doubled arms in full-heart construction. The frame sets a four-rafter beam against a rear two-rafter beam on three columns, left exposed.

Date: an eave column bears the inscription 'Xining 6 of the Song', and the hall is dated to 1073; the murals are dated by the painters' labels to 1096 and are recorded separately from the timber frame. The temple was first called Qingliang Temple, its steles tracing it to the reign of Emperor Zhaozong in the late Tang, and in 1030 it was renamed Kaihua Chan Cloister.

Significance: the east, west and north walls are covered with Song murals totalling 88.68 square metres, the west wall illustrating the Sutra of the Great Skilful Means of Repaying Kindness and the east wall the Avatamsaka Sutra, the largest Northern Song temple murals in existence; the Song polychromy on beams and brackets is of the highest 'full polychrome' grade, its patterns close to those in the Yingzao fashi, the most complete Song architectural painting surviving.
captions: Kaihua Temple · Mahavira Hall

hb_jingzhouta.name: Relic Pagoda of Kaifu Temple
hb_jingzhouta.yearNote: The provincial bureau gives 1079 alongside the 3rd year of Yuanfeng, a clerical error in the date; it should be the 2nd year of Yuanfeng. 1079 is used, with the source checked against the stele record.
hb_jingzhouta.lede: The Cangzhou lion, Zhaozhou Bridge, the Zhengding bodhisattva and the Jingzhou Pagoda: among Hebei's 'four ancient treasures' the Jingzhou Pagoda (Kaifu Temple Relic Pagoda, Kaifusi Shelita) is the only tall tower. Octagonal, thirteen storeys and 63.85 m high, it is crowned by a finial of five stacked bronze gourds inside an iron cage 3.3 m tall, with iron plaques on four sides, three of them cast 'repaired under Qi and Sui'. The present body dates to a rebuilding in 1079 (Northern Song), on the evidence of a stele inside the first storey; inscriptions found in the finial record further repairs in 1139 (Jin) and 1517 (Ming).
facts: Form: an octagonal thirteen-storey brick-and-stone pagoda of pavilion type, 63.85 m tall, with a base 50.5 m in circumference; the foundation is paved with huge bluestone blocks and the body is brick, with arched doorways on the four cardinal faces of each storey, vaulted galleries from the second storey up, and a brick stair through the core to the top.

Date: a stele in the first storey records rebuilding in 1079 (Yuanfeng 2 of Northern Song); the provincial register's 'Yuanfeng 3' beside 1079 is a slip. Iron plaques on the pagoda read 'repaired under Qi and Sui', and inscriptions in the finial record repairs in 1139 and 1517; the foundation may go back to the Northern Wei.

Finial: five bronze gourds of different sizes stacked 2.05 m high inside an iron cage 3.3 m tall; during repairs in 1973 nine volumes of Ming woodblock sutras and a bronze reclining Buddha were found inside it. Kaifu Temple was built beside the pagoda in 1407, giving it its present official name.
captions: Jingzhou Pagoda · Front view
Thirteen-story octagonal body with iron finial net and bronze gourds

protection.scope: Relic Pagoda of Kaifu Temple · Octagonal thirteen-story pavilion-style pagoda

sh_fangta.name: Pagoda of Xingshengjiao Temple, Songjiang
sh_fangta.sub: Square Pagoda Park · Nine-story square pagoda
sh_fangta.yearNote: Uses the construction range of 1068–1093 recorded in the Songjiang Yearbook 2019; 1080 is used only as an approximate placement on the timeline, not as a confirmed completion year. The temple's founding in 949 is recorded separately from the Northern Song construction of the pagoda.
sh_fangta.lede: On the square body, nine tiers of timber eaves spread like layered wings. Xingshengjiao Temple no longer has its original extent, but this Northern Song brick-and-timber pagoda still stands with slender proportions in the old town of Songjiang, where locals simply call it the “Square Pagoda.”
facts: Xingshengjiao Temple was founded in the 2nd year of Qianyou in the Later Han of the Five Dynasties (949), while the pagoda was built in the Xining and Yuanyou eras of the Northern Song (1068–1093); the two are not conflated as one date.

The pagoda is square in plan and of brick-and-timber construction, a nine-story pavilion-style pagoda about 42.65 m tall overall; the brick walls are divided into three bays by timber-style columns, with a cusped kunmen opening in the middle.

Each story has timber waist eaves, a balcony platform and railings, and an iron finial stands at the top. It has been repaired through the Yuan, Ming, Qing and modern times, and the plate shows its surviving form.
captions: Square, nine stories · Brick-and-timber pagoda
Northern Song · Xining and Yuanyou eras

qinglian.name: Qinglian Temple, Jincheng
qinglian.sub: Sakyamuni Hall of the Upper Temple
qinglian.lede: On the slopes of Mount Xiashi beside the Dan River, Qinglian Temple is divided into upper and lower compounds. Stone inscriptions in the Sakyamuni Hall of the Upper Temple record the 4th year of Yuanyou in the Northern Song; the small three-bay hall stands on a high platform, its stone columns carrying deep eaves. Farther down the mountain, the Lower Temple still preserves Tang painted sculptures.
facts: The Sakyamuni Hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; an inscription on the stone door frame provides the basis for dating it to the 4th year of Yuanyou in the Northern Song (1089).

Square chamfered stone columns carry five-puzuo bracket sets with one projecting arm and one descending cantilever, and there are no intercolumnar sets; the central bay has a door and the two side bays have vertical-bar windows.

The Sakyamuni Hall of the Upper Temple holds four Song sculptures, and the Maitreya Hall of the Lower Temple six Tang sculptures. In one temple, upper and lower, timber structures and painted sculptures each preserve the appearance of different dynasties.
captions: Line drawing of the Sakyamuni Hall, Upper Temple · Three bays wide
Single-eaved hip-and-gable · 4th year of Yuanyou, Northern Song

sx_wubian.name: Wubian Temple, Taigu
sx_wubian.sub: White Pagoda · Ancient City of Taigu
sx_wubian.lede: The tallest thing in the old town of Taigu is a Song pagoda. When the temple was renovated in 1090, the fifth year of Yuanyou, this octagonal White Pagoda went up: seven storeys outside but nine within, with brick purlins, brackets and balconies imitating a timber tower storey by storey, forty-three metres high, gently tapering, with a wooden stair inside. A fire in the Tongzhi years of the Qing burned the temple to the ground and left only this pagoda standing in the smoke; the halls rebuilt in the Guangxu years grew back around it.
facts: Form: an octagonal hollow brick pagoda of the storeyed type, seven storeys outside and nine inside, 43 m high overall; each storey has eaves with carved-brick imitation brackets beneath, giving a doubled-eave effect, the body tapers gently, and a wooden stair inside allows the ascent. The pagoda stands in the second courtyard and is the visual centre of the whole temple.

Date: the Guangxu-era Taigu County Gazetteer records the temple's founding in 272, the eighth year of Taishi of the Western Jin; after a Northern Song rebuilding it was called Puci Temple, and in 1090 it was renovated and the pagoda built. After the Tongzhi fire only the White Pagoda survived; the halls were rebuilt in 1904–06 and the name Wubian Temple restored. The pagoda is dated by the year 1090, not by the legend of the temple's founding.

Significance: the surviving temple covers 3,960 square metres in three courtyards, with gate and rear-facing stage, Siming Pavilion, White Pagoda, Heavenly Kings Hall and Mahavira Hall in sequence on the axis, preserving the early layout with a pagoda at the centre; the State Council's list dates the temple Song to Qing, and the pagoda is its only Song structure. The plate shows the pagoda alone.

hn_chongfa.name: Chongfa Temple Pagoda
hn_chongfa.sub: A Song pagoda raised on tiers of balcony platforms and lotus petals
hn_chongfa.yearNote: Dated by the pagoda's completion in 1098; a foundation's materials give 1093 for the building of the underground crypt and 1095 for the start of the body. Some secondary sources wrongly equate 1093 with the 1st year of Shaosheng; this erroneous conversion is not adopted.
hn_chongfa.lede: The Chongfa Temple Pagoda rises tier upon tier in the old city of Yongcheng. The octagonal nine-story brick pagoda imitates a timber pavilion, tracing the rhythm of a Song pagoda body with closely set eaves and balcony platforms.
facts: Song body: The pagoda was completed in the 5th year of Shaosheng in the Northern Song (1098); the temple's history is earlier than this surviving pagoda.
Octagonal, nine stories: The pagoda is 34.6 m tall, each story with projecting eaves, a balcony platform, doors and windows; eaves and platforms are counted separately, and the body has nine stories.
Brick imitating timber: The pagoda renders columns, bracket sets and railings in brickwork, and inside it preserves glazed Buddha-image bricks and other components; it was repaired in later periods.

anyue.name: Anyue Rock Carvings
anyue.lede: One knee raised, one hand resting lightly on the stone platform: seated at ease in the posture of royal ease, the Water-Moon Guanyin of Pilu Cave leaves the composure of Song stone carving on the rock face.
facts: Principal figure drawn: The Water-Moon Guanyin of Pilu Cave, popularly called the Purple Bamboo Guanyin; this is not a panorama of the Anyue rock carvings.
Royal ease: The right knee is raised with the right hand hanging over it; the left hand rests on the platform and the left foot hangs down onto the lotus pedestal, in a relaxed posture.

Treasures of the two Songs: The Pilu Cave sculptures were carved during the Northern and Southern Song, with work continuing into the Ming and Qing; they were listed in the 5th batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level in 2001.

hn_xiaoshang.name: Xiaoshang Bridge
hn_xiaoshang.era: Song main structure · Repairs over the centuries
hn_xiaoshang.yearNote: 1100 is only an approximate ordering point for the surviving Song main structure. The county gazetteer records the bridge as built in the 4th year of Kaihuang in the Sui; Mao Yisheng considered a founding in the early Sui credible but the form of the surviving bridge still open to study, and Luo Zhewen judged the style and carving of the surviving bridge body to be Song remains.
hn_xiaoshang.lede: A low, gentle main arch has one small spandrel arch opened in each shoulder. The red-stone bridge body and balustrade panels of many periods together record the building and repair of the bridge over the Xiaoshang River.
facts: Distinguishing dates: The founding of the bridge is traditionally traced to the Sui; Luo Zhewen judged the architectural style and surface carving of the surviving main structure to be Song remains.
Structure: The bridge is 21.3 m long and 6.45 m wide, with a segmental main arch flanked by one small spandrel arch on each side, making it an open-spandrel stone arch bridge.
Repairs over time: Repairs in 1994–1995 cleaned and reset many kinds of components; the present balustrade panels and posts include pieces from the Song, Jin, Yuan, Ming and Qing periods.

sn_daqin.name: Daqin Temple Pagoda, Zhouzhi
sn_daqin.era: Surviving pagoda dated to the Song
sn_daqin.yearNote: The 6th batch of the national listing places the surviving Daqin Temple Pagoda in the Song; 1100 is only an approximate Song ordering point. Discussions of the temple's origins or of the Church of the East do not prove that today's pagoda was built in the Tang.
sn_daqin.lede: The seven-story octagonal brick body leans slightly, its corbeled eaves narrowing tier by tier. The present dating of the Daqin Temple Pagoda should be considered separately from the temple's earlier origins; the plate records only the pagoda as it stands today.
facts: Dating: The 6th batch of the national listing of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level places it in the Song; the exact year of construction is undetermined.
Form: An octagonal seven-story pavilion-style brick pagoda; the surviving body leans slightly.
Historical distinction: Discussions of the temple's origins and its links with the Church of the East are not taken directly as a Tang date for the surviving pagoda.

jinci.name: Jinci Temple
jinci.era: Renovated in the 1st year of Chongning, Northern Song
jinci.lede: The Hall of the Holy Mother, built in the Tiansheng years of the Northern Song (1023–32) for Yi Jiang, mother of Tang Shuyu, and rebuilt in 1102, the first year of Chongning, is the oldest building at Jinci. Seven bays wide under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, it is ringed by a gallery, and its front porch is two bays deep, unusually open; on each of the eight front columns coils a carved wooden dragon, the earliest wooden dragons in China. Inside, more than forty Song statues of attendant women stand to either side of the Holy Mother, each with her duty. The plate shows the front of the hall; the Fish Pond Flying Bridge is not included.
facts: Form: seven bays wide and six deep (eight rafters), under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, about 19 m high and nearly square; a 'surrounding secondary eave' gallery runs round all four sides, the front porch two bays deep. Columns are omitted inside, leaving a single row; the eave columns lean inward and rise toward the corners, the upper-eave capitals are six-puzuo with two arms and one cantilever, the lower eave five-puzuo. Each of the eight front columns carries a coiled dragon, carved separately and fitted to the shaft with mortise and tenon.

Date: founded in the Tiansheng years (1023–32) and rebuilt in 1102; the varied dimensions of its members reflect several campaigns of building. The Offering Hall was added in front in 1168, the eighth year of Dading of the Jin, and the hall was dismantled and restored in 1993–96. Of the 43 painted statues inside, 41 are Song and 2 are Ming replacements.

Significance: the Hall of the Holy Mother, the Fish Pond Flying Bridge and the Offering Hall are the 'three treasures of Jinci', the cross-shaped bridge before the hall being the only surviving example of its type; the eight wooden dragons are the earliest extant; the Song attendant statues, the Zhou cypress and the Nanlao Spring are the 'three wonders'. Liang Sicheng recorded his survey in the Preliminary Report on Ancient Architecture of the Jin and Fen Valleys of 1934.
captions: Jinci · Hall of the Holy Mother
Northern Song · Seven bays, double eaves and eight dragon-coiled columns

sx_faxing.name: Faxing Temple, Zhangzi
sx_faxing.era: Northern Song · Song sculpture of the 1st year of Zhenghe
sx_faxing.yearNote: Takes 1111, the year the central Song sculpture of Sakyamuni drawn here was made, not the founding year of the temple or the 1081 enlargement of the Yuanjue Hall. The temple was moved to its present site in 1984–1996, and the painted sculptures have been repaired and redecorated over the centuries; the replica outer eaves of the present hall are not taken as original fabric of 1081.
sx_faxing.place: Shanxi · Zhangzi · Mount Cuiyun, Cilin Town
sx_faxing.lede: At the center of the Yuanjue Hall, the seated Sakyamuni sits cross-legged on a lotus throne, its drapery folds and gestures still keeping the composure of Song sculpture. The plate draws only the principal figure and its pedestal as they are now, recording this group of painted sculptures preserved through the temple's relocation.
facts: Date of the Song sculptures: The Song sculptures in the hall are dated 1111, and records name the sculptor Feng Zongben and the painters Chen Daorong and Lü Rong; this drawing takes only the central Sakyamuni.

Hall and figures dated separately: The Yuanjue Hall was dismantled and enlarged in 1081, before the Song sculptures were made. The hall, the sculptures and later redecoration each have their own dates.

Relocation and protection: The temple was moved to Mount Cuiyun in 1984–1996; the outer eaves of the Yuanjue Hall were reproduced conjecturally from surviving Northern Song structures, so today's entire exterior cannot be regarded as original Song fabric.

hn_chuzu.name: First Patriarch Hermitage of Shaolin Temple
hn_chuzu.sub: Front of the Main Hall of the First Patriarch Hermitage
hn_chuzu.yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hn_chuzu.lede: Stone columns support deep timber eaves, and in just three bays the Main Hall of the First Patriarch Hermitage preserves the layers of Song construction. The carved column shafts and massive bracket sets give this hermitage commemorating Bodhidharma a distinctive appearance.
facts: The Main Hall was built in the 7th year of Xuanhe in the Northern Song (1125) and belongs to the Shaolin Temple building group of the Dengfeng “Center of Heaven and Earth” World Heritage Site.
Three bays with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; carved stone columns support the timber structure, and the column-head bracket sets are prominent in scale.

The plate takes the front elevation as its subject, with the roof checked against a view from another angle; only the First Patriarch Hermitage is included, and the Shaolin Pagoda Forest is not split off and counted separately.

liuhe.name: Liuhe Pagoda, Hangzhou
liuhe.era: Rebuilt in the 26th year of Shaoxing, Southern Song
liuhe.lede: The King of Wuyue built it in the 3rd year of Kaibao in the Northern Song (970) to subdue the tidal bore of the Qiantang River; the surviving brick body was rebuilt in the 26th year of Shaoxing in the Southern Song (1156) and completed in the 1st year of Longxing (1163). The thirteen tiers of timber eaves on the outside were added in the 25th year of Guangxu in the Qing (1899).
facts: Mixed brick and timber, octagonal, 59.89 m tall overall; the brick body has seven stories and the exterior thirteen tiers of eaves — “thirteen outside, seven inside” — with balcony railings around each story.

The brick carvings of flowers, birds and beasts on the Sumeru plinths inside the pagoda match the patterns recorded in the Yingzao Fashi (Treatise on Architectural Methods), making them physical evidence for the study of Song architecture.
In 1934 Liang Sicheng drew up a “slimming” plan for the pagoda, removing the Guangxu-era timber eaves to restore the original appearance of the Song pagoda; it was never carried out.

xuanmiao.name: Sanqing Hall of Xuanmiao Temple
xuanmiao.sub: Suzhou · Nine-bay Southern Song main hall
xuanmiao.lede: The Sanqing Hall of Xuanmiao Temple raises two tiers of hip-and-gable eaves over a broad nine-bay body, and the ridge-end ornaments and the three-halberd (pingsheng sanji) ornament on its long ridge draw the silhouette skyward. This Southern Song hall remains an early timber structure of striking scale in the old city of Suzhou.
facts: The Sanqing Hall was rebuilt in the 6th year of Chunxi in the Southern Song (1179); this date must not be confused with the original founding of Xuanmiao Temple.
The hall is nine bays wide and six bays deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, and stands on a broad platform.
The plate isolates the Sanqing Hall, keeping its double eaves and long-ridge silhouette, and leaves out the temple's front gate and the incense-burner pavilion before the hall.

dazu.name: Dazu Rock Carvings
dazu.era: Southern Song, Chunxi to Chunyou eras
dazu.lede: On the cliff face of Baodingshan, Guanyin's arms spread out in every direction. The principal figure lowers her gaze with palms joined, and the dense array of hand gestures and ritual implements condenses the conception of Southern Song craftsmen into a single niche.
facts: Detail shown: The principal figure of the Thousand-Armed Guanyin in Niche 8 at Dafowan, Baodingshan, with the adjacent arms; not a view of the whole niche.
Southern Song work: The figures were carved between the Chunxi and Chunyou eras and belong to the Baodingshan grottoes, whose construction was directed by Zhao Zhifeng.
Radiating composition: The whole niche occupies about 88 square meters of cliff face; the arms spread to both sides and upward, each hand holding an object.
captions: Dazu Rock Carvings · Thousand-Armed Guanyin at Baodingshan

feilaifeng.name: Feilai Feng Grottoes
feilaifeng.yearNote: 1200 is only an approximate timeline position for the traditional Southern Song dating, not the year of carving. The niche has no dated inscription, and some research proposes an early Yuan date; the year 966 is not used to impose a date.
feilaifeng.lede: Beside Lengquan Creek, the Budai Maitreya laughs openly as he leans on his cloth sack, while the arhats in the rock niche each wear their own expression. Niche 68 brings Buddhist sculpture into vivid human moods and is the most familiar face of Feilai Feng.
facts: One niche, many figures: The complete Niche 68 centers on the Budai Maitreya, with nine arhats ranged on each side; this plate shows only the principal figure and the four nearest arhats.

Sack and prayer beads: The principal figure, chest and belly bare, rests his right hand on the sack and holds prayer beads in his left, expressing devotion to Maitreya through the image of the monk Budai.

Disputed date: Popular accounts adopt a Southern Song date, while some research argues for the early Yuan; the niche bears no exact dated inscription, and no single year can stand for the carvings of the whole hill.

zijinan.name: Zijin'an Temple
zijinan.yearNote: 1200 is only an approximate timeline placement within the Song tradition of arhat art, not an exact year of sculpting; the heritage listing dates the statues to the Song–Ming, and Lei Chao and his wife are the traditionally attributed sculptors.
zijinan.lede: Tucked away in a hollow of Dongshan, sixteen arhats each have their own expression and pose. Tilted heads, lowered eyes and lightly interlaced fingers give the quiet clay figures the liveliness of everyday people.
facts: Song–Ming statues: The heritage listing dates the arhat statues of Zijin'an to the Song through Ming; they are traditionally said to be the work of Lei Chao and his wife in the Southern Song, but the authorship is unsettled.
Sixteen arhats: The arhats line both sides of the hall, differing in drapery, sitting posture and expression; this plate shows the upper body of the Venerable Panthaka.
Repairs through the ages: The statues have been repaired over time, and what is seen today includes painting and repairs from different periods; the surviving hall is dated separately.

feiying.name: Feiying Pagoda
feiying.lede: The outer pagoda of Feiying Pagoda wraps an inner stone pagoda in seven octagonal stories of timber eaves, its broad ground-floor gallery eave supporting a body that tapers story by story. Railings between the stories and a slender finial trace a landmark silhouette of the old city of Huzhou.
facts: The plate focuses on the outer pagoda, entered as a Southern Song rebuilding; sources give two dates for the rebuilding, the Jiatai era and the beginning of the Duanping era, so no single year is forced.
The outer pagoda is a seven-story octagonal pavilion-style pagoda of brick and timber that encloses a freestanding stone pagoda, forming the famous “pagoda within a pagoda.”

It has been repaired many times over the centuries; the conservation work of 1982–1987 retained its mixed brick-and-timber structure, and repair dates must not be taken as the pagoda's original construction date.
captions: Feiying Pagoda · Outer pagoda

fj_renshou.name: Renshou Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou
fj_renshou.sub: West pagoda · Octagonal five-story stone pagoda
fj_renshou.era: 1st year of Shaoding to 1st year of Jiaxi
fj_renshou.yearNote: The surviving stone pagoda was built in 1228–1237, and the completion year 1237 is used; the Five Dynasties timber pagoda was its predecessor and is not used as the date of the surviving structure.
fj_renshou.place: Fujian · Quanzhou · West Pagoda Court of Kaiyuan Temple
fj_renshou.lede: The west tower was finished more than a decade before the east tower and is slightly lower, at 45.06 m, rebuilt from brick to stone between 1228 and 1237. The two pagodas are almost identical in form and workmanship, but a closer look finds three differences: on the third, fourth and fifth storeys of the west tower there is only one intercolumnar bracket set per bay; the eighty figures on the outer walls are not ranked by stage of attainment but are Buddhist figures treated as equals; and the Sumeru base is carved with flowers and beasts rather than sutra stories. The fourth storey also carries an Indian-style male Avalokitesvara and a monkey pilgrim with the Peacock King Sutra tied at his waist.
facts: Form: a five-storey octagonal pavilion-style granite pagoda, 45.06 m high, with a ground-floor area of 270 square metres; its design and construction match the east tower, with a through core pillar, an outer shell tied storey by storey, an eaves gallery with stone balustrade on each level, and 16 carved figures per storey, 80 in all, on the outer walls.

Dating: first built in 916, under the Later Liang of the Five Dynasties, as a seven-storey timber pagoda named Wuliangshou; converted to brick and given its present name in the Chunxi era of the Southern Song; the surviving stone pagoda was built between 1228 and 1237, begun ten years and completed thirteen years before the east tower. The date used is 1237, the completion of the stone pagoda.

Differences: compared with the east tower, the west tower has only one intercolumnar bracket set on storeys three to five; its 80 figures are Buddhist personages expressing the equal Buddha-nature of all beings rather than a five-tier hierarchy; and its Sumeru base carries flower-and-beast reliefs. The Indian male Avalokitesvara and the monkey pilgrim carrying the Peacock King Sutra on the fourth storey show foreign religious imagery taking root in Quanzhou.
captions: Renshou Pagoda (west pagoda), Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou · Whole pagoda · Line drawing
Southern Song · 1228–1237

fj_zhenguo.name: Zhenguo Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou
fj_zhenguo.sub: East pagoda · Octagonal five-story stone pagoda
fj_zhenguo.era: 2nd year of Jiaxi to 10th year of Chunyou
fj_zhenguo.yearNote: The year used is 1250, the completion of the surviving granite pagoda; 865 marks the founding of the timber pagoda, and the brick pagoda of 1227 is not the surviving five-story stone pagoda.
fj_zhenguo.place: Fujian · Quanzhou · East Pagoda Court of Kaiyuan Temple
fj_zhenguo.lede: The east tower of the tallest surviving pair of Song-dynasty stone pagodas in China, 48.27 m high. Here granite imitates a timber pavilion in every detail: each wall face is carved with columns, lintels and bracket sets, every storey has an eaves gallery with a stone balustrade, and the brackets run one set over each column and two between, storey after storey. The core is an octagonal granite pillar about four metres across rising from base to top, to which the two-metre-thick outer shell is tied by beams and floors; it was this structure that kept the tower standing through the great Quanzhou earthquake of 1604.
facts: Form: a five-storey octagonal pavilion-style stone pagoda, 48.27 m high, with a ground-floor area of 255 square metres; the octagonal core pillar about 4 m in diameter runs the full height, the outer shell is about 2 m thick, and each storey is tied across by beams, brackets and floors, leaving climbable chambers; the ground storey opens doors on four sides, the doors and niches are staggered storey by storey above, and 16 Buddhist figures are carved on each storey's outer wall, 80 in all.

Dating: first built as a five-storey timber pagoda in 865, converted to a seven-storey brick pagoda in 1227, and rebuilt as the present stone pagoda between 1238 and 1250; neither the magnitude-8 Quanzhou earthquake of 1604 nor centuries of typhoons toppled it. The date used here is 1250, the completion of the surviving stone pagoda.

Comparison: with the west tower it preserves a layout of twin pagoda courts flanking the central axis, rarely seen after the 14th century; the east tower has one bracket set over each column and two between on every storey, whereas the west tower has only one intercolumnar set on storeys three to five. The 80 figures rise from heavenly generals through arhats, eminent monks and bodhisattvas to Buddhas, and 37 of the 40 reliefs on the Sumeru base tell sutra stories.

baziqiao.name: Bazi Bridge
baziqiao.sub: Three streets, three rivers · Ancient stone-beam bridge
baziqiao.yearNote: 1256 is the rebuilding year recorded in local gazetteers, and there was a further repair in 1783; what is seen today includes repairs from many periods, and not every stone member is an original of 1256.
baziqiao.lede: Stone steps rise along the riverbanks and meet above the waterway. With a single stone-beam span and flights of steps running in several directions, Bazi Bridge gathers up the crisscrossing streets and rivers of old Shaoxing.
facts: Baoyou rebuilding: The bridge was first built before the Jiatai era of the Southern Song, rebuilt in the winter of the 4th year of Baoyou (1256), and repaired again in the 48th year of Qianlong in the Qing.

Stone beams over the river: The main bridge spans the waterway with stone beams laid side by side, with a clear span of about 4.5 m at the main opening; its rectangular beam opening differs from the form of a round arch bridge.

Three streets, three rivers: The bridge stands where three streets and three rivers cross; its stone steps connect to the banks in different directions, and its name comes from a layout splayed like the Chinese character ba, “eight.”
captions: Bazi Bridge · South stone-beam span and riverside steps
Southern Song · Rebuilt in the 4th year of Baoyou (1256)

geyuan.name: Geyuan Temple, Laiyuan
geyuan.lede: A three-bay Buddha hall built to the timber grade of a seven-bay great hall: the bracket members of the Manjusri Hall (Wenshu Dian) of Geyuan Temple are the same size as those of the great hall of Shanhua Temple in Datong and the Yingxian timber pagoda, grade two in the Yingzao Fashi, which is why it has stood through a thousand years of earthquakes and has never once been dismantled for repair. Nearly square, about 15 m on a side, with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof and deep eaves, it uses column reduction and displacement to leave only two interior columns. The conventional date is 966 (Liao), making it the earliest of the eight surviving Liao timber buildings; the latticed doors and windows of the facade still contain late Liao originals.
facts: Form: three bays by three on a near-square plan about 15 m on a side, about 12.5 m high overall; single-eave hip-and-gable roof, with five-tier column-top bracket sets of two projecting arms and diagonal corner arms; inside, columns are reduced and shifted, the frame being 'a four-rafter beam in front and a two-rafter beam behind on three columns'.

Date: the temple keeps a sutra pillar of 867 (Tang), another of 966 (Liao) and an iron bell of 1114 (Liao); the hall is conventionally dated 966. Lu Sheng's survey of 1959 confirmed it as Liao work, and Feng Bingqi and Shen Tian published it in Wenwu in 1960.

Joinery and murals: the latticed doors and windows of the three front bays combine Liao, Yuan, Ming, Qing and Republican members, and some of the lozenge lattices are late Liao, among the earliest surviving timber window joinery in China; Liao murals inside, plastered over in the Ming, came to light again in the 1960s when the statues were destroyed.
captions: Line drawing of the Manjushri Hall, Geyuan Temple · Three bays wide
Single-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Liao timber structure

dule.name: Dule Temple, Tianjin
dule.lede: In the old town of Jizhou, the Guanyin Pavilion spreads its facade with two deep tiers of eaves and a balcony platform. A concealed mezzanine inside ties beams and columns together, and the space of the pavilion unfolds around a towering Guanyin statue.
facts: The surviving Guanyin Pavilion was rebuilt in the 2nd year of Tonghe in the Liao (984) and, together with the Main Gate, preserves the forms of Liao timber construction.
The Guanyin Pavilion is five bays wide and four bays deep; it appears two-storied from outside but has three levels inside, including a concealed mezzanine.
The upper level has inner and outer balcony galleries, and beams, tie-beams and bracket sets bind the two rings of columns into a single whole.
captions: Front of the Guanyin Pavilion, Dule Temple · Redrawn from photographs of the site
Rebuilt in the 2nd year of Tonghe, Liao (984) · Five bays wide; two stories outside, three levels inside

jl_nongan.name: Nong'an Liao Pagoda
jl_nongan.yearNote: 1000 is only a sorting point. Jilin local gazetteer sources give a range of 983–1030; the 1023 date, which has problems with mixed-up reign names, is not taken as the exact year of construction.
jl_nongan.place: Jilin · Nong'an · Ancient City of Huanglong Prefecture
jl_nongan.lede: In the town of Nong'an, the Liao pagoda tapers upward with a plain brick shaft and closely spaced bands of eaves. It is both a Liao survival and a present appearance left by modern repairs, and both are recorded in the source notes for the same drawing.
facts: An octagonal thirteen-story multi-eaved brick pagoda; the plate keeps its relatively plain shaft and does not transplant the wall-covering Buddha figures of the Liaoyang White Pagoda.
Local gazetteers adopt a Liao construction range; its position on the timeline is approximate, not a precise completion date.
Its present appearance has been shaped by modern repairs; full-view, eave and aerial photographs were used respectively to check proportions and details.

Liao survival · Present appearance shaped by modern repairs

kaishan.name: Kaishan Temple, Gaobeidian
kaishan.lede: The plainest of the eight surviving Liao timber buildings, yet it uses the full Liao repertoire: columns reduced and shifted so that a five-by-three-bay hall keeps only four interior columns and the worship space runs clear; huge bracket sets, deep eaves, and rear and side columns visibly leaning inward. The Mahavira Hall (Daxiong Baodian) of Kaishan Temple has a single-eave hip roof with a gently curving surface. Surveying it in 1936, Liu Dunzhen read the garbled date 'Song Chongqing 2' on a Ming stele as a corruption of the Liao era Chongxi and judged the hall Liao; the exact year is still unsettled, so this entry gives only 'Liao'.
facts: Form: five bays by three, about 30.4 by 18.5 m and about 12 m high, on a stone platform 1.11 m high with a terrace 27.6 by 11.4 m in front; single-eave hip roof, only four interior columns, and a post-and-lintel frame left exposed, with great diagonal braces at the hip ends.

Dating: in 1936 Liu Dunzhen inferred that 'Song Chongqing 2' in the 1551 Record of Repairing Kaishan Temple was a corruption of the Liao era Chongxi, and, noting construction akin to Dule Temple, judged the hall Liao; one view reads a date on an interior beam as 1033, and scholars still dispute the exact year.

Study and repair: Qi Yingtao published 'The Great Hall of Kaishan Temple, Xincheng County, Hebei' in 1957; repairs in 2001 uncovered a Liao stone Thousand-armed Guanyin inside the rear-eave cavity wall; in August 2023 floods submerged the temple, and the water in the hall drained after several days.

fengguo.name: Fengguo Temple, Yi County
fengguo.place: Liaoning · Jinzhou · Old town of Yi County
fengguo.lede: In the old town of Yi County, the Mahavira Hall of Fengguo Temple spreads its nine-bay facade beneath a single expansive hipped roof. Seven Liao painted clay Buddha statues sit side by side inside, facing the flying apsaras painted on the beam frame; timber structure, sculpture and painting together preserve the building practice of the eleventh century.
facts: Fengguo Temple was founded in the 9th year of Kaitai in the Liao (1020); its main surviving structure, the Mahavira Hall, is a Liao building.
The Mahavira Hall is nine bays wide and five bays deep, with a single-eaved hipped roof; doors open in the central seven bays of the front.

It was listed in 1961 in the first batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level; the hall preserves seven Liao painted clay Buddha statues and Liao paintings on the beam frame.

zhuozhou.name: Liao Twin Pagodas of Zhuozhou
zhuozhou.sub: Yunju Temple Pagoda · Zhidu Temple Pagoda
zhuozhou.lede: Two Liao pagodas face each other north and south, freezing the columns, windows and bracket sets of timber pavilions in brick. The north pagoda has six stories and the south five, and their differing silhouettes form the landmark of old Zhuozhou.
facts: To the north is the Yunju Temple Pagoda, of six stories; to the south the Zhidu Temple Pagoda, of five. Both are octagonal pavilion-style brick pagodas imitating timber construction.

The Zhidu Temple Pagoda was built in the 11th year of Taiping in the Liao (1031) and is 44 m tall; each cardinal face has an arched doorway, and each diagonal face a false window with vertical mullions.

Studies differ on the date of the Yunju Temple Pagoda, proposing the Chongxi era, the 8th year of Da'an and others; this entry keeps the general label of the 11th century and does not present a disputed year as settled.
captions: Yunju Temple Pagoda · Zhidu Temple Pagoda
North pagoda, six stories · South pagoda, five stories
