huayan.name: Huayan Temple
huayan.sub: Bhagavat Sutra Repository Hall · Mahavira Hall
huayan.lede: The Khitan worshipped the sun, so the whole monastery faces east. The Bhagavat Sutra Repository Hall of the lower temple is a library hall of 1038, the seventh year of Chongxi of the Liao; thirty-eight bays of two-storey pavilion-style sutra cabinets line its walls, and over the rear window an arched bridge carries the 'heavenly palace pavilions' that Liang Sicheng called unique in China. The Mahavira Hall of the upper temple burned in the Liao-Jin war of 1122 and was rebuilt in 1140, the third year of Tianjuan of the Jin, on its Liao platform, nine bays wide, the largest ancient Buddhist hall standing. The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall.
facts: Form: the Mahavira Hall stands on a platform 4 m high under a single-eave hip roof, nine bays wide and ten rafters deep, 1,559 square metres in area, with eaves projecting 3.6 m at a height of 9.5 m; the glazed owl-tail ridge ornaments are 4.5 m tall, the largest on any surviving ancient building; brackets are five-puzuo with two arms, and twelve columns are omitted inside. The Bhagavat Hall has a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, five bays wide and eight rafters deep, on a platform 3 m high.

Date: an inscription on the underside of a rafter in the Bhagavat Hall reads 'built at noon on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the seventh year of Chongxi, the wuyin year', that is 1038; the Mahavira Hall was first built in 1062, destroyed in 1122 when Jin troops took the city, rebuilt in 1140 and restored in 1997–2000. Early in the Wanli years of the Ming the monastery was divided into upper and lower temples.

Significance: the 38 bays of wall cabinets, the heavenly palace pavilions and the 29 statues in the Bhagavat Hall are all original Liao work, the cabinets being the only Liao architectural model in China, and the attendant bodhisattva 'with joined palms and bared teeth' is especially famous; the east-facing orientation is linked to the Khitan custom of 'revering spirits and worshipping the sun'; the Mahavira Hall is the largest ancient Buddhist hall surviving in China.

qingzhou.name: Qingzhou White Pagoda
qingzhou.sub: Liao city of Qingzhou · Sakyamuni Buddha Relic Pagoda
qingzhou.lede: The White Pagoda of the Liao city of Qingzhou stands on the grassland, its seven-story body imitating timber in brick. Doors and windows, reliefs of heavenly kings and tier upon tier of bracket sets interweave, preserving the refined and ornate appearance of a Khitan Buddhist pagoda.
facts: Begun in the 16th year of Chongxi (1047) and completed in the 18th year of Chongxi (1049).
An octagonal seven-story pavilion-style pagoda; carved brick bracket sets support timber eave rafters.
It stands in the northwest of the site of the Liao city of Qingzhou and is also called the Sakyamuni Buddha Relic Pagoda.

huanghuatan.name: Huanghuatan Pagoda
huanghuatan.lede: Huanghuatan Pagoda stands on Xita Hill beside the Daling River, facing the site of the Liao city of Jianzhou across the fields. Its octagonal body carries thirteen tiers of close-set eaves, and the flower baskets and flying apsaras above the arched doorways still show the delicacy of Liao brick carving.
facts: The pagoda is in Dapingfang Town, Longcheng District, Chaoyang, Liaoning; its main body is Liao, and the exact year of construction is undetermined.
The octagonal brick pagoda consists of a high platform, a double Sumeru plinth, the shaft and thirteen tiers of close-set eaves.
Repairs were completed and the finial re-erected in 2012; this plate depicts the present, post-repair appearance from 2023 photographs of the site.

yingxian.name: Yingxian Wooden Pagoda
yingxian.lede: A sixty-seven-metre tower built entirely of wood, raised in 1056, the second year of Qingning of the Liao, and still standing after nine hundred and seventy years. Five storeys and six tiers of eaves show outside, but four hidden storeys lie within, nine in all; more than fifty kinds of bracket sets carry it tier upon tier, earning it the name 'museum of dougong', and not one iron nail is used. It has ridden out repeated earthquakes, took more than two hundred shells in the warlord fighting of 1926, and in 1974 yielded Liao printed sutras and relics of the Buddha's teeth from inside its statues: the tallest and oldest wooden pagoda in the world.
facts: Form: an octagonal storeyed timber pagoda 67.31 m high, 30.27 m across at the base and weighing about 7,400 tonnes; five storeys and six eaves outside, with a hidden storey between each of the first four, nine levels in all; a secondary eave surrounds the ground storey and balconies with railings ring each level; the main timber is North China larch, the brackets elm, more than fifty bracket types in all, and an iron finial crowns the top.

Date: Ming gazetteers record construction in 1056 and repairs in the Mingchang years of the Jin; inscriptions on the plaques record further repairs in 1194, 1436 and 1471. The pagoda took more than two hundred shells in 1926; the removal of infill walls and diagonal braces in 1935 left the structure twisted; a reinforcement scheme was fixed in 2013 and work began in 2014.

Significance: the seated Shakyamuni in the ground-floor inner bay is about 10 m high; in 1966 and 1974 Liao printed and handwritten sutras and two tooth relics of the Buddha were found inside the statues. Certified by Guinness World Records in 2016 as the world's tallest wooden pagoda; the plaques 'Divine Craft Reaching the Heights' by the Yongle emperor and 'Wonder of the World' by the Zhengde emperor still hang on it.

hb_nanansi.name: Nan'an Temple Pagoda
hb_nanansi.yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau presumes a Liao date from its form; 1100 serves only as an approximate Liao value for sorting. 1706 marks the Qing encasing of the base and repairs, and in 1986 eave corners partly damaged by shelling were repaired.
hb_nanansi.lede: Nan'an Temple Pagoda rises among the rooftops of the old town of Yuzhou. A tall first story stands on an upturned-lotus base, thirteen close-set eaves taper gently, and an iron finial extends the silhouette into the sky.
facts: Dating: The surviving octagonal multi-eaved brick pagoda is dated to the Liao by its form; the exact year of founding is unknown, and this guide uses an approximate value.

Thirteen eaves: The pagoda is solid; its first story is relatively tall, with false doors on the four cardinal faces and blind windows on the four diagonal faces, and above it thirteen brick eaves are closely stacked.
Layers of repair: The present base was encased in the 45th year of Kangxi in the Qing (1706), and parts of the eave corners on the east side damaged by shelling were repaired in 1986.

tj_jizhou_baita.name: White Pagoda of Jixian, Tianjin
tj_jizhou_baita.yearNote: The national listing dates it to the Liao through Qing. 1100 is only an approximate timeline placement for the Liao form and does not represent the exact year of founding, rebuilding or making of all surviving members; the plate shows the present appearance after repairs over the centuries.
tj_jizhou_baita.lede: An octagonal lower section and three low tiers of eaves support a rounded inverted-bowl body, and a finial of tapering rings extends the silhouette above. Traces of pale plaster remain between the gray bricks, and this White Pagoda preserves a meeting of two forms, the pavilion and the stupa.
facts: The Tianjin register of national protected sites records the date of the Jixian White Pagoda as Liao to Qing; its present appearance includes later repairs, and no single early date sums up the whole pagoda.

The plate keeps the octagonal lower section, three low tiers of eaves, inverted-bowl body and ringed finial, distinguishing it from an ordinary multi-eaved pagoda or a purely Tibetan-style white stupa.
The colored plate keeps the gray brick, mottled pale-gray plaster, dark red wooden doors and darker finial, rather than repainting it as an all-white new pagoda.

ln_liaoyang.name: Liaoyang White Pagoda
ln_liaoyang.yearNote: 1100 is only a sorting position for the traditional Liao dating, not an exact construction year; neither the founding legends nor the competing Liao and Jin theories are used to force a completion year.
ln_liaoyang.lede: Thirteen tiers of close-set eaves taper step by step, and the broad first story of the shaft is filled with Buddhist niches and figures. The name White Pagoda is not an instruction to paint the masonry pure white; the colored plate keeps the gray-brown weathered surface of its present state.
facts: Octagonal with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves; the first story of the shaft has Buddhist reliefs and imitation-timber decoration.
Liaoyang Museum sources adopt a Liao date; the exact year of construction is unknown, and this entry does not use disputed precise dates.
The lower part in the reference photographs is screened by plants, so the plate gives only a conservative low platform and does not invent an unverified massive stepped terrace.

ln_chongxing.name: Twin Pagodas of Chongxing Temple
ln_chongxing.sub: West and east pagodas · Thirteen eaves each
ln_chongxing.yearNote: 1100 is an approximate sorting point for the late Liao; heritage sources conjecture the reigns of Emperors Daozong to Tianzuo, and this does not mean it was definitely built in 1100.
ln_chongxing.lede: Two octagonal brick pagodas stand side by side, each with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves, yet they are not copy-and-paste replicas of one pagoda. The west pagoda is slightly lower, and the reliefs and remaining color on each shaft follow two separate site photographs.
facts: Both pagodas are octagonal with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves; the first story of each shaft is decorated with Buddhist niches, attendant figures, flying apsaras and more.
Heritage sources conjecture construction in the late Liao; the present appearance of both the east and west pagodas also reflects later repairs.
The plate arranges photographs of the two individual pagodas as a side-by-side comparison and is not a basis for their actual spacing on site or measured proportions.

tianning.name: Tianning Temple Pagoda, Beijing
tianning.lede: Built in the 9th to 10th years of Tianqing in the Liao (1119–1120), octagonal with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves and 57.8 m tall overall, it is the oldest above-ground structure in Beijing. Above the Sumeru plinth, three tiers of upturned lotus petals support the tall shaft, and higher still thirteen eaves press one upon another, drawing ever tighter.
facts: The eight faces of the shaft: arched doorways on the four cardinal faces, flanked by brick-carved vajra guardians and bodhisattvas; windows with vertical mullions on the four diagonal faces.
All thirteen tiers of close-set eaves rest on brick bracket sets imitating timber, and the spacing between eaves shortens level by level; Liang Sicheng said it had “a rich musical rhythm.”
A solid brick pagoda that cannot be climbed; it is the only Liao building within the Liao Southern Capital to survive to the present.

huilong.name: Huilong Temple
huilong.sub: Main hall · South bank of the Zhuozhang River
huilong.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Houbi Village
huilong.lede: In Houbi Village on the south bank of the Zhuozhang River, all that remains of Huilong Temple is a three-bay main hall. Two octagonal stone columns stand in the front porch, and a low, gently pitched overhanging gable roof reaches out to either side; with no tall pagoda or multistory halls, the weight of early timber construction rests among the few bracket sets beneath the eaves.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and four rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof; two octagonal stone columns stand in the central bay of the front eave, the supports at either side are enclosed in the walls, and behind are one door and two windows.
No plate beam (pupaifang) is laid over the column heads, and the architraves do not project beyond the corner columns, preserving archaic structural features.

The national listing gives the date as Jin; other accounts, citing form and scientific dating, give the late Northern Song to early Jin. There is as yet no exact construction date, and the timeline gives only an approximate placement at the Song–Jin transition.

shanhua.name: Shanhua Temple
shanhua.sub: Mahavira Hall · Hall of the Three Sages · Puxian Pavilion
shanhua.lede: The Liao Mahavira Hall stands at the north, the Jin Three Sages Hall and gate line the axis, and the Puxian Pavilion rises on the west: the largest and most complete Liao-Jin monastery surviving. From 1128, the sixth year of Tianhui of the Jin, the monk Yuanman spent fourteen years rebuilding it, finishing in 1143. The Puxian Pavilion shown in the plate was built in 1154, the second year of Zhenyuan: two storeys outside with a hidden balcony storey between, a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, three bays square, one of the few surviving witnesses to Liao-Jin multi-storey halls.
facts: Form: the Puxian Pavilion is three bays wide and three deep under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, two storeys outside with a balcony mezzanine between the two main floors; in the side bays of the upper eave the capital, intermediate and corner sets are joined into one by shared arms, a rare device. The Mahavira Hall is seven bays and 41.8 m wide, five bays and 26.18 m deep under a single-eave hip roof; the Three Sages Hall is five bays and 32.5 m wide, its six-puzuo sets with diagonal arms stacked like opening flowers.

Date: founded in the Kaiyuan years of the Tang, destroyed by fire in 1122, the second year of Baoda of the Liao; rebuilt by the monk Yuanman from 1128 to 1143, with the Puxian Pavilion added in 1154; named Shanhua Temple by imperial decree in 1445. The Mahavira Hall is Liao, the gate, Three Sages Hall and Puxian Pavilion Jin. The Three Sages Hall underwent major repair in 2007.

Significance: the Mahavira Hall is the third-largest ancient Buddhist hall standing, with a complete set of thirty-four Jin statues, the Five Buddhas and the Twenty-four Devas; the stele of 1176 in the Three Sages Hall, with a text by Zhu Bian recording the rebuilding, is the basis of the temple's history; Liang Sicheng said of the Three Sages Hall brackets that they 'amply express the vigour of an age still on the rise'.
captions: Line drawing of the Puxian Pavilion · Three bays wide

sx_xixi_erxian.name: Erxian Temple of Xixi, Lingchuan
sx_xixi_erxian.sub: Rear hall · Cult of the Two Immortals
sx_xixi_erxian.yearNote: 1142 is the year a stele records for the start of rebuilding, not the precise completion year of the rear hall; the surviving main structure is dated by its Jin style.
sx_xixi_erxian.place: Shanxi · Lingchuan · West of Lingchang Village, Chongwen Town
sx_xixi_erxian.lede: The rear hall of the Xixi Erxian Temple carries its broad eaves on a three-bay front porch, with bracket sets running continuously beneath. The main hall and the dressing towers on either side retain Jin forms and also bear the architectural imprint of the cult of the Two Immortals in southeastern Shanxi.
facts: Jin rear hall: A stele records that rebuilding began in 1142; the surviving main hall and dressing towers retain a Jin style, while most of the temple's other buildings are Ming and Qing.
Three bays, six rafters: The rear hall sits on a stone platform, three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, and keeps a front porch before its doors.

Cult of the Two Immortals: The temple is dedicated to the Two Immortals, and two-story, triple-eaved dressing towers stand on either side of the main hall; this plate redraws only the front of the rear hall.

sx_chongfu.name: Chongfu Temple, Shuozhou
sx_chongfu.yearNote: The construction date of the surviving Amitabha Hall is used; the paintings and statues inside the hall and the later repairs belong to separate phases.
sx_chongfu.lede: A broad, gently pitched roof rests on a seven-bay grid of columns, with widely spaced yet massive bracket sets beneath the eaves. The Amitabha Hall of Chongfu Temple preserves Jin timber construction together with painted sculpture and murals in a single space.
facts: The Amitabha Hall was built in the 3rd year of Huangtong in the Jin (1143); the plate is dated by the surviving hall.
Seven bays wide and four bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; eight columns across the front define a clear column grid.
This plate shows the front of the Amitabha Hall, leaving out the offering vessels and vegetation in the courtyard; the painted sculpture and murals inside are not drawn.

sx_macun.name: Macun Brick-Carved Tombs
sx_macun.sub: Tomb No. 1 · Woman opening the door
sx_macun.yearNote: 1150 is only an approximate sorting point for the early Jin, not the exact burial year of any tomb; the cemetery as a whole spans the late Northern Song to the Jin.
sx_macun.place: Shanxi · Jishan · Macun Village, Jifeng Town
sx_macun.lede: Inside brick-built tomb chambers, bracket sets, doors, windows and balustrades form an underground mansion. In Tomb No. 1 a young maid leans out from behind a half-closed door, and the narrative reliefs beside her preserve Song–Jin life on small brick surfaces.
facts: Underground mansion: The tomb chambers imitate a timber-framed residence in carved brick, with columns, bracket sets, doors, windows and platforms together forming an architectural space.
Woman opening the door: In Tomb No. 1 the central door leaf stands half open and a maid leans out from behind it; reliefs of narrative scenes with figures survive on both sides.
Song–Jin cemetery: The cemetery as a whole dates from the late Northern Song to the Jin; this plate shows a detail of the early Jin Tomb No. 1 and does not represent all the tomb chambers.

yuanjue.name: Yuanjue Temple, Hunyuan
yuanjue.place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan · Shiqiao North Lane
yuanjue.lede: In the old town of Hunyuan, Yuanjue Temple has left a Jin brick pagoda. A tall first story carries nine tiers of close-set eaves that taper step by step; carved brick imitates timber bracket sets, and a slender iron finial traces a distinctive outline at the top.
facts: According to the Hunyuan Prefecture Gazetteer, the surviving brick pagoda was built in the 3rd year of Zhenglong in the Jin (1158) and was repaired many times in the Ming and Qing.
The pagoda is an octagonal, nine-story multi-eaved pagoda about 30 m tall; its shaft and base use carved brick to represent imitation-timber bracket sets and ornament.
The pagoda of Yuanjue Temple in Hunyuan was listed in 2013 in the seventh batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level.

chunhua.name: Chunhua Temple, Pingshun
chunhua.era: Before the 9th year of Dading, Jin
chunhua.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Yanggao Village
chunhua.lede: Of this old temple founded in the Northern Qi, only a Jin main hall remains. Before the hall stand two stone dharani pillars of the 3rd year of Kaibao in the Northern Song (970), carved with the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani Sutra and the Diamond Sutra, two hundred years older than the hall itself.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and an exposed roof frame with no ceiling.
The bracket sets are four-puzuo with a single projecting arm, and the cantilevers are cut in the split-bamboo style, a practice of the Song–Jin transition.
According to a stele, it dates from before the 9th year of Dading in the Jin (1169).

huata.name: Hua Pagoda of Guanghui Temple
huata.era: Founded in the Tang · Restored in the Dading era, Jin
huata.lede: The most ornate of China's surviving flower pagodas: the lower three stories form an octagonal pavilion, each of its four corners embracing a small hexagonal pagoda, and the top story gathers into a “bouquet,” with lions, elephants, bodhisattvas and guardian warriors clustered tier upon tier around the finial.
facts: Founded in the Tang and restored in the Dading era of the Jin; 40.5 m tall overall (another account gives 33.35 m), with four stories of brick imitating timber.

At the four corners of the first story, hexagonal annex chambers connect to the main pagoda, each with an arched doorway and an inverted-bowl top; this combination of “one main and four subsidiary” pagodas is seen nowhere else.

The bouquet-shaped body of the fourth story: its eight faces are modeled with lions, elephants, Buddhist niches and guardian warriors in staggered rows, eight tiers in all, which give the Flower Pagoda its name.
Together with the Xumi Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple, the Lingxiao Pagoda of Tianning Temple and the Chengling Pagoda of Linji Temple, it is known as one of the “Four Pagodas of Zhengding.”

sx_pingyaowenmiao.name: Pingyao Confucian Temple
sx_pingyaowenmiao.yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
sx_pingyaowenmiao.lede: Diagonal brackets spread from the column heads to either side, holding up the deep eaves of the five-bay hall. The Jin date of the Dacheng Hall of the Pingyao Confucian Temple lies hidden in an inscription on its beam frame.
facts: The Dacheng Hall is dated by a rebuilding inscription of the 3rd year of Dading in the Jin (1163); the temple's other buildings belong to separate construction phases.
Five bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; column-head bracket sets and diagonal brackets project in overlapping layers.
The plate keeps the five bays and six columns, along with the stone balustrade and side steps before the hall; later buildings in the courtyard are not counted as Jin structures.

yanshan.name: Yanshan Temple, Fanshi
yanshan.lede: In Tianyan Village, the Manjushri Hall stills the noise of its courtyard amid the mountains. Within its broad plain walls and gently sloping eaves, Jin murals set the life of the Buddha and scenes of worldly town life on the same wall.
facts: The surviving Manjushri Hall is a Jin structure; an inscription beneath a beam records a restoration in the 2nd year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1315).
The Manjushri Hall is five bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and four-puzuo bracket sets.
The Jin murals inside the hall were completed in the 7th year of Dading (1167) and are the work of the painter Wang Kui and others.

hn_baima.name: Qiyun Pagoda of White Horse Temple
hn_baima.sub: White Horse Temple · Jin brick pagoda
hn_baima.yearNote: A Jin rebuilding stele states 1175 explicitly; this is not 68, the year White Horse Temple was founded.
hn_baima.place: Henan · Luoyang · East Pagoda Court of White Horse Temple
hn_baima.lede: East of White Horse Temple, Qiyun Pagoda draws a soft curve with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves. Its square shaft steps inward level by level, preserving the form of the brick pagoda rebuilt in the Jin, with a lineage distinct from the temple's Eastern Han founding.
facts: Rebuilding date: The Jin stele beside the pagoda, the Record of the Rebuilding of the Sakyamuni Relic Pagoda of the East White Horse Temple on the Left Street of Henan Prefecture, records its rebuilding in the 15th year of Dading (1175).
Form: A square multi-eaved brick pagoda of thirteen stories, stepping inward level by level from the sixth story up, and topped by a vase-shaped finial.
Temple and pagoda: The Qiyun Pagoda Court lies southeast of White Horse Temple; the history of the present pagoda and the later, newly built halls of the pagoda court are recorded separately.

hn_baolun.name: Baolun Temple Pagoda
hn_baolun.sub: Thirteen eaves drawn into a slender silhouette
hn_baolun.yearNote: Entered according to the surviving pagoda rebuilt in the Jin; the founding date of the old Tang temple is not substituted for the date of the pagoda.
hn_baolun.lede: In the 17th year of Dading in the Jin, the monk Zhixiu rebuilt the Baolun Temple Pagoda. Its square shaft tapers level by level, and thirteen close-set eaves trace a slender outline within the old city of Shanzhou.
facts: Jin rebuilding: The surviving pagoda was built in 1177; the history of the Tang temple and pagoda is recorded separately from this Jin pagoda.
Thirteen close-set eaves: The pagoda is 26.5 m tall; its brick eaves project with saw-tooth courses and corbelling, and at the bottom there is a separate platform and base.
Interior passage: Inside are a central chamber and stairways; its echo effect has earned it the popular name Toad Pagoda.

wangbao.name: Erlang Temple of Wangbao, Gaoping
wangbao.sub: Jin opera stage · Gable facing forward
wangbao.lede: With its gable facing forward, a small one-bay stage carries a spreading hip-and-gable roof. The Erlang Temple at Wangbao preserves a Jin performance space at the south end of its courtyard, and the Dading date on its platform can still be traced.
facts: Jin stage: An inscription on the Sumeru-plinth platform records the 23rd year of Dading (1183), so the date of the surviving stage is clear; most of the temple's other buildings have been restored in the Ming and Qing.

Gable facing forward: The stage, one bay square, turns the gable of its hip-and-gable roof toward the audience; four round columns and stout bracket sets carry the roof, a form that is quite distinctive.
Surviving early stage: Official descriptions call it the earliest surviving stage in China; it sits at the south facing north and bears witness to early village temple fairs and performance spaces.

jingtusi.name: Jingtu Temple, Ying County
jingtusi.lede: In a small temple east of the Wooden Pagoda, a three-bay Jin Buddhist hall holds finely made celestial palace pavilions and caisson ceilings; widely spaced bracket sets beneath the eaves carry a gently undulating, spreading roof.
facts: The Mahavira Hall is an original Jin structure, restored in the 24th year of Dading in the Jin (1184).
The hall is three bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof.
Inside, the caisson ceilings are set within a ceiling fully covered with coffered panels, and together with the celestial palace pavilions along the walls they form rare Jin fine joinery.

hn_fengxian.name: Fengxian Temple, Jiyuan
hn_fengxian.yearNote: The Jin date of the surviving Sanqing Hall is used, not the founding of the temple in the 1st year of Chuigong in the Tang.
hn_fengxian.lede: The Sanqing Hall of Fengxian Temple holds its broad overhanging gable roof on six stone columns along the front eave. Massive bracket sets and a clear five-bay column grid make the structure of this Jin hall legible from the front.
facts: Date: The Sanqing Hall was built in the 24th year of Dading in the Jin (1184); this is recorded separately from the history of the temple's Tang founding.
Form: Five bays wide and seven rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof; the front column grid and stout bracket sets preserve Jin architectural features.
Layout: The temple also retains a Qing main gate and a Ming Jade Emperor Hall; this plate shows only the surviving Jin Sanqing Hall.

hb_linji.name: Chengling Pagoda of Linji Temple
hb_linji.yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hb_linji.lede: Close-set eaves draw inward level by level, and between the lotus base and the finial a slender, upright outline emerges. Chengling Pagoda preserves the form of the brick pagoda after its major Jin repair and also marks the ancestral temple of the Linji school.
facts: The present appearance follows the form after the major repair of the 25th year of Dading in the Jin (1185); the earlier history of a pagoda built for the founding patriarch must not stand in for the date of the present structure.
The octagonal nine-story multi-eaved body rests on a carved base and lotus petals.
The finial was reinstalled in 1985; the plate depicts the present state, and the repaired parts and the Jin main body are described separately.

bj_lugou.name: Lugou Bridge, Beijing
bj_lugou.era: Completed in the Jin · Ming–Qing repairs
bj_lugou.lede: Eleven stone arches extend beneath the low, gently sloping deck, and lion-topped balusters join into a long, slender edge. The plate views the bridge from a shallow oblique angle, keeping every arch open, and does not draw the shadows beneath the bridge as solid mass.
facts: Lugou Bridge was completed in 1192 under the Jin and later repaired in the Ming and Qing; the timeline uses the completion date and records the later repairs separately.

The bridge has eleven stone arches; this plate shows the abutments at both ends, the piers and the continuous stone-lion balustrade in full, distinguishing it from the single great arch of the Zhaozhou Bridge.

The colored plate follows the present appearance, with gray stone and lighter balustrade panels; all eleven arches are truly open, and the carved details of the stone lions are artistically simplified.

hongfu.name: Hongfu Temple, Dingxiang
hongfu.lede: On a high platform in Beishe Village, this Jin main hall, with its low, gently pitched overhanging gable roof, widely spaced five-bay doors and windows, and painted clay statues inside, keeps the atmosphere of an old temple at the southern foot of Mount Wutai.
facts: The surviving Mahavira Hall is a Jin structure; its exact year of construction has not been confirmed by any inscription.
The main hall is five bays wide, seven purlins and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof.
The hall preserves nine clay statues; Hongfu Temple was listed in 2001 as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level.

yanqing.name: Yanqing Temple, Wutai
yanqing.lede: In Shanwen Village, the Great Buddha Hall spreads its broad projecting eaves beyond a three-bay body; two beast masks beside the doors guard the central bay, and here the Jin beam frame meets later decoration.
facts: The surviving Great Buddha Hall is a Jin structure; its exact year of construction is unknown.
The hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and deep eave overhangs.
The interior column heads keep Qing beast-mask decoration; the temple also preserves a Song stone dharani pillar.
captions: Front of the Great Buddha Hall, Yanqing Temple · Shanwen Village, Wutai
Surviving Jin structure · Three-bay hip-and-gable hall, with later beast masks on the column heads retained in its present state

sx_taifu.name: Taifu Temple, Fenyang
sx_taifu.era: Jin · Hall of the Haotian Jade Emperor
sx_taifu.yearNote: 1200 is an approximate sorting point for the period indicated by the altar record of the 5th year of Cheng'an; the main hall is dated to the Jin from its architecture and heritage sources, and the altar date is not forced on the hall as a precise completion year.
sx_taifu.lede: The three-bay Haotian Hall stands on a terrace, its stout bracket sets holding up a single-eaved roof. The Jin timber structure of the main hall, the gilded melon-shaped studs on its doors and the later paintings and sculptures inside record the continuing building history of Taifu Temple.
facts: Jin main hall: The surviving Hall of the Haotian Jade Emperor is a Jin structure; a stele of the 5th year of Cheng'an records the founding of a ritual altar in the temple.
Three-bay plan: The hall is three bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the central plank door is flanked by windows with vertical mullions.

Paintings and sculptures through the ages: The statues in the hall and the other buildings in the courtyard have mostly gone through Ming and Qing construction and refurbishment; the date of the main subject drawn is judged from the timber structure of the main hall.
captions: Taifu Temple · Hall of the Haotian Jade Emperor
Jin · Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

yongle.name: Yongle Palace, Ruicheng
yongle.lede: The long eaves of the Sanqing Hall lift gently at both sides, and huge glazed dragon ridge-end ornaments guard either end of the main ridge. Inside, the mural Homage to the Primordial (Chaoyuan Tu) arrays hundreds of deities in a grand procession, so that Yuan timber architecture and murals reflect each other within a single space.
facts: Seven-bay hipped hall: The Sanqing Hall, also called the Wuji Hall, is the main hall of Yongle Palace, seven bays wide with a single-eaved hipped roof, and is dated to the 3rd year of Zhongtong (1262).
Chaoyuan Tu: The murals in the hall were completed in 1325 and are recorded separately from the construction date of the building.
Relocation for protection: For the Sanmenxia Reservoir project, the palace buildings and murals were moved to their present site in the 1960s, preserving the original halls and murals.
captions: Yongle Palace · Front of the Sanqing Hall
Seven-bay hipped hall · 3rd year of Zhongtong

hn_guanxing.name: Dengfeng Observatory
hn_guanxing.sub: Front of the platform and stone scale
hn_guanxing.yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hn_guanxing.lede: The brick-and-stone platform is divided into two chambers, with a narrow slit aligned with the stone scale that extends along the ground. The Dengfeng Observatory organizes the height, orientation and graduations needed to measure shadows into a clearly legible building.
facts: The observatory was built in the 13th year of Zhiyuan in the Yuan (1276) and is associated with the large-scale astronomical survey directed by Guo Shoujing.
A slit for measuring shadows is left between the two chambers on top of the platform, the stone scale is laid out on the north side, and twin stairways beside the platform lead to the top.
The plate shows only the observatory itself and the stone scale; the nearby Duke of Zhou's Shadow Measurement Platform is not split off as a separate entry.
captions: Dengfeng Observatory · Front of the platform and stone scale
Yuan · 1276

bj_miaoying.name: White Pagoda of Miaoying Temple, Beijing
bj_miaoying.era: Built from the 8th to the 16th year of Zhiyuan
bj_miaoying.lede: Inside Fuchengmen, the White Pagoda raises its rounded body on a broad base. The thirteen spire rings, bronze canopy and finial close the silhouette tier by tier, leaving a vivid example of the Yuan Tibetan-style stupa in the capital.
facts: The White Pagoda was built in 1271–1279 and is linked to the history of Araniko's part in Yuan construction; the temple's later halls and repairs have dates of their own.
The plate shows the whole of the surviving White Pagoda, keeping the base, inverted-bowl body, spire rings and bronze canopy, and does not merge the halls in front into the main subject.
The colored plate follows the present appearance, distinguishing the grayish-white body, gray brick base, bronze canopy and metal finial, and does not restore the whole pagoda in gold.
captions: White Pagoda of Miaoying Temple, Beijing · Inverted-bowl stupa

fenghuangsi.name: Prayer Hall of the Phoenix Mosque
fenghuangsi.sub: Hangzhou · Yuan hall of brick vaults and domes
fenghuangsi.era: Rebuilt in the Yuan · Repaired over the centuries
fenghuangsi.lede: The prayer hall of the Phoenix Mosque forms a three-part interior of brick arches and domes, covered outside by three connected pyramidal roofs. The plate takes the group of roofs visible in site photographs, the double-eaved center rising high with lower roofs on either side, presenting the distinctive silhouette of this old Hangzhou mosque.
facts: The surviving core prayer hall derives from a Yuan rebuilding funded by Ala al-Din, and was repaired many times in the Ming, the Qing and the modern period.
Inside, brick arches link three domed spaces; outside, three connected pyramidal roofs cover them, the central one higher and double-eaved, the two side ones lower.

This plate shows only the roofs and upper walls of the prayer hall that can be verified on site; it does not reconstruct the lower facade hidden by later additions, nor does it draw the modern entrance hall.
captions: Prayer Hall of the Phoenix Mosque · Roof group visible on site
Yuan core hall, repaired over the centuries · Three pyramidal roofs and upper walls

sx_jishi.name: Ji Family Residence, Gaoping
sx_jishi.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Zhongzhuang Village, Chenqu Town
sx_jishi.lede: The three-bay main house of the Ji Family Residence guards its doorway with stone columns and a shallow porch. An inscription of the 31st year of Zhiyuan on a door pier gives this Yuan dwelling a clearly legible point in time.
facts: Zhiyuan inscription: A bluestone door pier is inscribed with the 31st year of Zhiyuan of the Great Yuan, that is, 1294, providing the basis for dating the dwelling.

Three bays, shallow porch: The main house is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with an overhanging gable roof; the central entrance is set back to form a shallow porch, and the whole is low and plain.
Present doors and windows: The timber structure retains Yuan features, while the square-lattice windows are later alterations; the plate depicts the present state and distinguishes the periods.
captions: Ji Family Residence · Three-bay Yuan main house
31st year of Zhiyuan · 1294

hn_yuzhoutianning.name: Tianning Wanshou Temple, Yuzhou
hn_yuzhoutianning.sub: Three-bay Yuan Buddhist hall preserved on a school campus
hn_yuzhoutianning.yearNote: The date of the hall's rebuilding is used; it was later restored in the Ming and Qing and was dismantled and repaired in 2013. The main gate is Ming in style and is not the subject of this plate.
hn_yuzhoutianning.lede: The main hall of Tianning Wanshou Temple is tucked among old school buildings in Yuzhou. A three-bay hip-and-gable roof covers thick brick walls, and the bracket sets under the eaves and the naturally curved timbers inside bear the marks of Yuan construction.
facts: Yuan rebuilding: After the warfare at the end of the Jin, it was rebuilt in the 3rd year of Dade in the Yuan (1299) and repaired many times in the Ming and Qing.

Three-bay Buddhist hall: The hall is three bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of gray tiles; under the eaves are four-puzuo bracket sets with a single descending cantilever.
Present conservation: Two buildings survive, the main gate and the main hall, inside the grounds of the former Yuzhou No. 1 High School; the hall underwent a major dismantling repair in 2013.
captions: Main hall of Tianning Wanshou Temple, Yuzhou · Present state, near-frontal view
Rebuilt in the 3rd year of Dade, Yuan (1299) · Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

jiutian.name: Temple of the Holy Mother of the Nine Heavens
jiutian.era: Restored in the 1st year of Jianzhong Jingguo, Song · Yuan offering hall
jiutian.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Donghe Village
jiutian.lede: The temple was founded in the Tang, its Holy Mother Hall was rebuilt in the early Northern Song, and the whole temple was restored in the 1st year of Jianzhong Jingguo (1101). The Yuan offering hall before the main hall is the most unusual: it is five bays deep, longer than its three-bay width, its main ridge runs along the depth, and its roof is the highest-ranking hipped type. From the front, in the courtyard, one sees its end face, so the drawing here shows its long side, where the main ridge and both ridge-end ornaments appear.
facts: The offering hall is a Yuan structure, three bays wide and five bays deep, with sixteen chamfered square sandstone columns all around and open on all four sides; its bracket sets are four-puzuo with a single projecting arm, and it stands on a bluestone platform one meter high.
The corner eaves of the three roofs, those of the offering hall, the main hall and the dance pavilion, interlock, which locals call “hooked hearts and fighting horns” (gouxin doujiao).
The Holy Mother Hall is a Song structure, three bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; in one village temple, timber buildings of the Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing follow one after another.
captions: Line drawing of the offering hall · Side elevation · Five bays deep
Hipped roof · Main ridge along the depth · Yuan

hn_huishan.name: Huishan Temple, Dengfeng
hn_huishan.sub: Front of the Yuan main hall
hn_huishan.yearNote: The main subject drawn is dated to the Yuan; the numeric year is only an approximate sorting value.
hn_huishan.lede: At the southern foot of Mount Song, Huishan Temple has left a five-bay Yuan main hall. A broad roof, exposed bracket sets and three central doors give the temple's long history a visible form in a single timber building.
facts: The temple was founded long before the present hall; the hall drawn is entered by its surviving Yuan timber structure.
Five bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the central three bays have doors and the bays on either side have windows.
The plate shows only the front of the surviving hall; the roof and the details of doors and windows bear traces of successive repairs.
captions: Huishan Temple, Dengfeng · Front of the Yuan main hall
Yuan · Yuan period

hb_shijia.name: Sakyamuni Temple
hb_shijia.yearNote: Dated by the structure of the Yuan hall; the temple's other, Ming halls are not mixed into the main subject.
hb_shijia.lede: A low, spreading single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a wide central bay outline the Yuan layout of the middle hall of Sakyamuni Temple in Yuzhou.
facts: Main subject: The hall drawn is the temple's middle hall, usually called the Mahavira Hall, the earliest surviving and largest building here, dating from the Yuan.
Form: The hall is three bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; under the eaves are four-puzuo bracket sets with a single projecting arm.

History: The temple was enlarged in the Hongwu era of the Ming and repeatedly repaired afterward; the ridge and ridge ornaments of the middle hall include later replacements, and the ceiling inside is also a later addition.
captions: Middle hall of Sakyamuni Temple
Front of the Yuan three-bay single-eaved hip-and-gable Mahavira Hall

sx_jiangzhou_datang.name: Jiangzhou Great Hall
sx_jiangzhou_datang.sub: Main hall of the prefectural office · Seven bays, overhanging gable roof
sx_jiangzhou_datang.era: Yuan · Main hall of the prefectural office
sx_jiangzhou_datang.yearNote: 1300 is only an approximate timeline placement for a surviving Yuan structure, not an exact completion year.
sx_jiangzhou_datang.place: Shanxi · Xinjiang County · Jiangzhou Prefectural Office
sx_jiangzhou_datang.lede: The Jiangzhou Great Hall commands its seven-bay facade with a single, spreading overhanging-gable ridge. Thick timber columns, long architraves and bays of unequal width leave the plain and open space of a Yuan prefectural main hall.
facts: Yuan prefectural office: The main body of the surviving hall is a Yuan structure, a rare example of the main hall of a local government office, repaired many times in later periods.

Seven bays, overhanging gable roof: The hall is seven bays wide and eight rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof; both ends are walled, and the open center has a column grid of unequal bays.

Reduced columns, long architraves: Seventeen bracket sets along the front eave carry the overhang, and reduced columns and long architraves create a broad space; the original front porch has been destroyed.
captions: Jiangzhou Great Hall · Main hall of the prefectural office
Yuan · Seven bays, overhanging gable roof

protection.scope: Jiangzhou Great Hall · Main hall of the prefectural office · Seven bays, overhanging gable roof

sx_fusheng.name: Fusheng Temple, Xinjiang County
sx_fusheng.yearNote: 1300 serves only as an approximate sorting point for a surviving Yuan structure and does not claim completion in that year.
sx_fusheng.place: Shanxi · Xinjiang County · Guang Village, Zezhang Town
sx_fusheng.lede: Fusheng Temple in Guang Village unfolds tier upon tier with the terrain, and the Amitabha Hall organizes its inner and outer spaces with double eaves and a surrounding gallery. Its Yuan timber structure and the painted sculptures inside depend on each other, and the north elevation shows the layers of eaves, rear wall and gallery columns more clearly.
facts: Yuan hall: The Amitabha Hall preserves a Yuan timber structure and was restored in the Hongzhi era of the Ming; the temple's founding history cannot directly stand in for the date of the surviving hall.

Double eaves and gallery: The Amitabha Hall is five bays square, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a gallery all around; the ground level differs between the high platform to the south and the rear courtyard to the north.

Surviving painted sculpture: The hall preserves painted sculptures of Amitabha Buddha, attendant bodhisattvas, Guanyin Crossing the Sea and others, which have undergone various later repairs; this plate shows the north side of the hall.
captions: Fusheng Temple · North elevation of the Amitabha Hall
Surviving Yuan structure · Ming repairs

sx_zezhou_yuhuang.name: Jade Emperor Temple, Zezhou
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.sub: Fucheng · Painted sculptures of the Twenty-Eight Mansions
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.era: Yuan · Painted sculptures of the Twenty-Eight Mansions
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.yearNote: 1300 is only an approximate sorting point for the Yuan painted sculptures. Official sources give no exact date of making for the single figure selected; 1076 relates to the rebuilding of the temple and cannot substitute for the date of the sculptures.
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.place: Shanxi · Zezhou · Fucheng Village, Jincun Town
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.lede: The Jade Emperor Temple at Fucheng renders the Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions of the sky as figures with personalities. Xu Ri Shu, the Rat of the Emptiness Mansion, wears layered robes and a quiet expression, and the pairing of a small rat with a human figure gives ancient astronomical belief a visible face.
facts: Mansions in human form: The painted sculptures of the Twenty-Eight Mansions combine lunar mansions, animals and human figures, each with its own pose and expression.

Yuan painted sculpture: This plate uses the Xu Ri Shu figure dated to the Yuan in the official catalogue, and does not substitute the year of the temple's Northern Song rebuilding for the date of the sculpture.

One figure as representative: The plate redraws only Xu Ri Shu from among the Twenty-Eight Mansions, omitting the painted patterns and the hall background while keeping the hand gesture, robes and animal features.
captions: Jade Emperor Temple, Zezhou · Xu Ri Shu
Yuan · Representative painted sculpture of the Twenty-Eight Mansions

hb_ciyunge.name: Ciyun Pavilion
hb_ciyunge.yearNote: Of the original Dabei Pavilion complex only this pavilion survives; it was rebuilt in the 10th year of Dade in the Yuan.
hb_ciyunge.lede: In the old town of Dingxing, the Ciyun Pavilion raises spreading double eaves on a two-story timber frame, and inside and out it still keeps the features of Yuan framing. Most of the original temple buildings have vanished, and this small pavilion alone records the old name of the Dabei Pavilion.
facts: Date: The present pavilion was rebuilt in the 10th year of Dade in the Yuan (1306) and is a surviving Yuan timber structure.
Layout: Three bays wide and three bays deep, nearly square in plan, in the form of a two-story pavilion.
Frame: The beam frame combines hanging columns, diagonal corner beams and other devices, preserving Yuan structural and workmanship methods.
captions: Dingxing · Ciyun Pavilion
Two stories, three bays · Rebuilt in the 10th year of Dade, Yuan

yongan.name: Yong'an Chan Temple, Hunyuan
yongan.sub: Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma
yongan.place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan
yongan.lede: The Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma at Yong'an Chan Temple holds down its five-bay facade with a broad hipped roof, its ridge ornaments answering the deep eaves. Inside this hall built in the 2nd year of Yanyou in the Yuan, water-and-land ritual murals gather Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist figures; timber structure and painting together form a precious survival in the old town of Hunyuan.
facts: Yong'an Temple was founded in the Jin; the surviving Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma was built with funds donated by Gao Pu in the 2nd year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1315).
The main hall is five bays wide, with a single-eaved hipped roof; the central three bays have doors, and the solid walls at both ends retain large calligraphic inscriptions.

Yong'an Temple was listed in 2001 in the fifth batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level; the Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma preserves water-and-land ritual murals.
captions: Line drawing of the Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma · Five bays wide
Single-eaved hipped roof · 2nd year of Yanyou, Yuan

protection.scope: Yong'an Chan Temple, Hunyuan · Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma

yanfu.name: Yanfu Temple, Wuyi
yanfu.sub: Main hall · Yuan structure in Jiangnan
yanfu.era: Yuan · Rebuilt in the 4th year of Yanyou
yanfu.lede: Upper and lower tiers of flying eaves spread out the body of the hall, and a broad central bay flanked by lattice windows resolves into a clean, simple front. The Yuan main hall of Yanfu Temple in Wuyi still preserves memories of earlier timber construction.
facts: Yuan rebuilding: The rebuilding of the surviving main hall began in the 4th year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1317), with funds raised by the monks Huaifa and Dehuan.
Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof: Timber bracket sets show between the two tiers of eaves, and a broad central bay with narrower side bays sets the rhythm of the facade.
Song and Yuan joined: The hall retains Song members, and together with the Yuan rebuilding its visible forms leave construction traces that span periods.
captions: Yanfu Temple · Main hall
4th year of Yanyou, Yuan · Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof

jinhuatianning.name: Tianning Temple, Jinhua
jinhuatianning.lede: A single tier of long eaves lifts high, with light, upturned corners drawn in at either side. Using a scale of only three bays, the main hall of Tianning Temple in Jinhua arranges its wide central bay, lattice windows and the bracket sets beneath its eaves into a front both upright and expansive.
facts: Ink-written date: An ink inscription on a beam records a rebuilding in the 5th year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1318), the direct clue for dating the surviving hall.
Three bays, single eaves: The hall is three bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the wide central bay and the window lattices of the side bays form clear layers.

Yuan structure under national protection: The main hall of Tianning Temple was listed in 1988 in the third batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level and is an important Yuan survival in the old city of Jinhua.
captions: Tianning Temple, Jinhua · Main hall
5th year of Yanyou, Yuan · Single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

sh_zhenru.name: Main Hall of Zhenru Temple
sh_zhenru.sub: Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Yuan timber structure
sh_zhenru.yearNote: 1320 corresponds to the construction inscription on the hall's timber frame; the present appearance was restored through repairs including those of 1963, which removed a later lower eave. The temple's other buildings and the new pagoda behind the hall are not included in this plate of the Yuan structure.
sh_zhenru.lede: A broad gray-tiled roof rests on the three-bay timber hall, with ridge-end ornaments curling skyward at both ends. The main hall of Zhenru Temple preserves Yuan Jiangnan timber construction within today's city, and an inscription among its beams still records its construction in the 7th year of Yanyou.
facts: An inscription on an interior architrave records that the hall was erected in the 7th year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1320); the hall retains Yuan timber members and is an important Yuan architectural survival in Shanghai.
Three bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; four columns across the front frame central lattice doors with windows at the sides, and ridge-end ornaments stand at both ends of the roof.

Repairs in 1963 removed a lower eave added later, restoring its single-eaved appearance. The plate shows only the main hall; the new pagoda behind it and the later buildings on either side have dates of their own.
captions: Front elevation of the main hall · Three bays wide
Yuan · 7th year of Yanyou (1320)

xiayu.name: Xia Yu Shrine
xiayu.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Houbi Village
xiayu.lede: On the Yuwang Hillock, the highest point of Houbi Village in the Zhuozhang River valley, a temple of a single courtyard packs Yuan, Ming and Qing timber buildings into 877 square metres: the gate is Ming, with a rear-facing stage on its upper floor looking straight at the Yuan main hall, while the side halls and wing rooms were added in the Qing. The plate shows the main hall, a surviving structure of 1336 (2nd year of Zhiyuan, Yuan), three bays wide under a gable roof with a two-rafter-deep front porch; its framing of four-rafter beam against front ru-beam on four columns is a ready textbook for Yuan village temples of southeastern Shanxi.
facts: Main hall: three bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, with a two-rafter-deep front porch; column-top bracket sets are four-puzuo with one downward ang, the three intercolumnar sets were added in the Qing; framing is a four-rafter beam against a front ru-beam, with four columns across the depth.

Dating: the shrine was founded in 1336 (2nd year of Zhiyuan, Yuan) and repaired repeatedly in the Ming and Qing; the hall keeps one Ming and two Qing inscribed wall stones and three stone offering tables of the Wanli reign; the gate is Ming, the side halls and wings Qing.

Layout: a single courtyard of only 877 square metres; the three-bay, four-rafter gate carries a rear-facing stage on its upper floor facing the main hall, and the convex altar terrace before the hall is carved in relief on three sides; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers the site as "Yuan to Qing", three dynasties of timber work in one yard.
captions: Line drawing of the main hall · Three bays wide
Single-eaved overhanging gable roof · Yuan

protection.scope: Xia Yu Shrine · Houbi Village

duanliang.name: Second Gate of Tiger Hill
duanliang.sub: Suzhou · Duanliang Hall of Tiger Hill
duanliang.era: Yuan · Rebuilt in the 4th year of Zhiyuan
duanliang.lede: The Second Gate of Tiger Hill covers its three-bay body with a broad, horizontal hip-and-gable roof, and a central round arch with round windows on either side forms a spare front. The name “Duanliang,” or “broken beam,” comes from the ridge purlin, which is joined from separate sections.
facts: According to the Suzhou Municipal Administration of Landscaping and Greening, the surviving Second Gate was rebuilt in the 4th year of Zhiyuan in the Yuan (1338).
The gate is three bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; a central round-arched doorway and round windows to left and right form the openings of the front.
“Broken beam” refers to the ridge purlin made of two round logs joined end to end; it does not mean that the hall has no beams, nor that a beam has broken and hangs in midair.
captions: Second Gate of Tiger Hill · Front of the Duanliang Hall
Rebuilt in the 4th year of Zhiyuan, Yuan (1338) · Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

protection.note: The first-batch listing of the Yunyan Temple Pagoda in Suzhou notes that it includes other buildings of Yunyan Temple; this entry depicts the Second Gate of Tiger Hill.

sx_doudafu.name: Shrine of Grand Master Dou, Taiyuan
sx_doudafu.sub: Offering pavilion and main hall · Shanglan Village
sx_doudafu.era: Rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng
sx_doudafu.yearNote: Placed by the Yuan rebuilding date, the 3rd year of Zhizheng, of the surviving offering pavilion and main hall; neither the Spring and Autumn date of the person venerated nor the earlier history of the shrine is used as the date of the timber structures.
sx_doudafu.lede: Stout timber columns hold up deep eaves, and the offering pavilion joins the main hall behind it. Among the gray-brown old timbers, dark green glazed tiles outline the ridges and eave-tile ends; the Shrine of Grand Master Dou gathers its ritual space into a tight group of timber buildings.
facts: The shrine is dedicated to Dou Chou, a grand master of the state of Jin, and is also called the Lieshi Shrine and the Yingji Shrine; the early history of the shrine and the dates of the surviving buildings are described separately.

The surviving gate, offering pavilion and main hall were rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng in the Yuan (1343). The plate selects the offering pavilion and main hall and does not count the Qing side buildings as Yuan structures.

The hip-and-gable roof of the offering pavilion links with the overhanging gable roof of the main hall behind, and thick columns and massive bracket sets create a striking contrast of scale; the colored plate follows the surviving old timber, gray tiles and glazed tiles, and is not a reconstruction of historical painted decoration.
captions: Shrine of Grand Master Dou, Taiyuan · Front of the offering pavilion and main hall
Yuan · Rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng (1343)

bj_juyong_yuntai.name: Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass, Beijing
bj_juyong_yuntai.sub: Yuan base of a street-spanning stupa · Half-hexagonal arched passage
bj_juyong_yuntai.era: Built from the 2nd to the 5th year of Zhizheng
bj_juyong_yuntai.lede: A high white stone platform straddles the old passage, its body tapering upward and its top rail running flat. The half-hexagonal arched passage and the reliefs on its door frame remain from the stone base of a Yuan street-spanning stupa; the vanished stupa halls on the platform are not reconstructed.
facts: The Cloud Platform is the base of a Yuan street-spanning stupa, built in 1342–1345; the original stupa halls no longer stand on the platform today.

The inner opening of the central passage is half-hexagonal, and the door frame and passage walls bear reliefs and sutras carved in several scripts; the plate only suggests the carving with sparse lines.
The present-state drawing keeps the empty platform, stone balustrade, tapering body and arched passage, removes modern barriers and surroundings, and does not add the three historical stupas.
captions: Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass · Surviving base of the street-spanning stupa
Yuan · Built 1342–1345

hb_beiyue.name: Beiyue Temple
hb_beiyue.sub: Front elevation of the Dening Hall (with gallery and platform)
hb_beiyue.yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau lists the present hall under the 7th year of Zhizheng (1347); the county gazetteer records completion in the 7th year of Zhiyuan (1270), so both construction phases need to be recorded.
hb_beiyue.lede: The Dening Hall of Beiyue Temple sits on a high platform, its two tiers of hipped eaves stretching horizontally. Once the place where the court made sacrifices from afar to the Northern Peak, Mount Heng, it preserves the memory of this ancient peak temple through its Yuan timber structure, murals and the steles of sacrifices from many dynasties.
facts: Date: The present hall is Yuan; sources record completion in 1270 and rebuilding in 1347 respectively, and the timeline enters it with an approximate Yuan value.
Hall: A double-eaved hipped roof with a surrounding gallery, nine bays wide and six bays deep overall; a central stairway climbs the high platform.
Sacrifices: Beiyue Temple was originally a temple for sacrifices to Mount Heng from afar; the hall preserves Yuan murals, and steles of many dynasties are gathered in the courtyard.
captions: Quyang · Dening Hall of Beiyue Temple
Yuan timber structure · Double-eaved hipped roof

xuanyuan.name: Main Hall of Xuanyuan Palace
xuanyuan.lede: The main hall of Xuanyuan Palace at Yangwan on Dongshan covers its three-bay body with deep hip-and-gable eaves, its window lattices set within undulating cusped (kunmen) outlines on either side. Yuan framing features and traces of Ming and Qing building remain together on this small hall.
facts: The national listing dates it to the Yuan; the surviving main hall has undergone Ming and Qing rebuilding and repair, and its overall present appearance must not be taken as an unaltered Yuan original.
The hall is three bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; four central columns help form a grid-shaped beam frame.
This was originally the Xuwang Temple, dedicated to Wu Zixu; in the Republican period it was rededicated to the Yellow Emperor and called Xuanyuan Palace.
captions: Yangwan, Dongshan · Main hall of Xuanyuan Palace
Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Yuan features alongside Ming–Qing building

shisi.name: Shisi Temple, Jingning
shisi.sub: Main hall · Yuan structure in a mountain village
shisi.lede: Between two tiers of flying eaves, deep bracket sets line up against white walls. With its light timber frame and low stone steps, the main hall of Shisi Temple lies hidden in an old temple in the mountain village of Daji.
facts: Yuan main hall: The hall was built in the 16th year of Zhizheng in the Yuan (1356) and still retains many Yuan members.

Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof: The upper and lower eaves spread wide, the bracket sets of the upper eave show their full layering, and a central doorway with windows on either side forms a simple facade.
Several periods side by side: The temple's bell tower, Sanqing Hall and Mei clan ancestral hall form a complex spanning the Yuan, Ming and Qing; the plate takes only the Yuan main hall.
captions: Shisi Temple · Main hall
16th year of Zhizheng, Yuan · Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof

protection.scope: Shisi Temple, Jingning · Main hall · Yuan structure in a mountain village

jijian.name: Stone Halls of Jijian Temple
jijian.lede: The Xitian Temple stone hall of Jijian Temple stands hard against the mountain rock, imitating a timber hall with stone columns, stone tie-beams and large stone slabs. A shallow, gently sloping roof and three-bay openings make this Yuan stone hall look low and compact.
facts: The Xitian Temple stone hall was built in the 17th year of Zhizheng in the Yuan (1357); it stands as a separate structure from the small stone houses of Doushuai Palace and Jile Garden beside it.
The main hall is three bays wide (about 7.64 m) and two bays deep (about 5.52 m), with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a plan with a projecting central section.
Apart from the lattice doors used for entry, the main members are carved from stone in imitation of timber, and the rear abuts the natural rock of the mountain.
captions: Jijian Temple · Front of the Xitian Temple stone hall
17th year of Zhizheng, Yuan (1357) · Three-bay stone structure imitating timber

protection.scope: Stone Halls of Jijian Temple · Suzhou · Xitian Temple, Mount Tianchi

sx_jishan_qinglong.name: Qinglong Temple, Jishan
sx_jishan_qinglong.era: Late Yuan–early Ming · Middle hall murals
sx_jishan_qinglong.yearNote: The subject drawn is the middle hall murals, using the dating range of Sun Bo cited by the Yuncheng Museum; 1360 is only a sorting coordinate. It is not 1289, the completion year of the timber structure, and scholarly opinions on the dating of the murals still differ.
sx_jishan_qinglong.place: Shanxi · Jishan · Macun Village, Jifeng Town
sx_jishan_qinglong.lede: The earliest surviving wall painting of a Water-and-Land ritual in China is in the Middle Hall (yaodian) of Qinglong Temple at Macun: deities of Buddhism, Daoism and Confucianism parade in tiers, the Buddhas of the Three Ages enthroned at the top, drawn from the same southern Shanxi pattern books as the Yongle Palace one ridge away, yet in a manner of its own. An ink inscription of 1289 (26th year of Zhiyuan) under the hall's beams names the master carpenters; for the murals themselves there are two views, contemporary with the timber frame or repainted in the late Yuan to early Ming, and the timeline follows the latter. The plate redraws the Buddhas of the Three Ages in the upper part of the west wall and does not stand for all the murals and sculpture of the hall.
facts: Panels: each "Deities of the Three Realms" panel in the Middle Hall measures 223 cm high by 773 cm wide, principal Buddhas in the top register and lesser deities ranked below, linked by clouds; the line work is mainly iron-wire and nail-head-rat-tail strokes, the colouring based on azurite and malachite with vermilion, yellow, white and red.

Dating: the temple was founded in 662 (2nd year of Longshuo, Tang) and repaired repeatedly in the Yuan and Ming; an ink inscription under the ridge-brick tie beam of the Middle Hall reads "Great Yuan, 26th year of Zhiyuan, mid-autumn ... master carpenters ... respectfully recorded", i.e. the timber frame was completed in 1289; since Sun Bo's 2010 thesis the murals are dated to the Yuan, with a late-Yuan-to-early-Ming view as well.

Significance: the temple holds 196.38 square metres of Yuan and Ming murals; the Middle Hall cycle is regarded as the earliest extant Water-and-Land painting, its three-teachings pantheon leading on to Ming examples such as Pilu Temple; with the Sanqing Hall of Yongle Palace and the Mingying Wang Hall of the Water God Temple it belongs to the group of Yuan murals of southern Shanxi.
captions: Qinglong Temple · Buddhas of the Three Ages on the west wall of the middle hall (detail)
Late Yuan–early Ming · Mural redrawn in line

protection.scope: Qinglong Temple, Jishan · Middle hall · Water-and-land murals

sx_pingyaowall.name: Pingyao City Wall
sx_pingyaowall.sub: Yingxun Gate and adjoining wall sections
sx_pingyaowall.yearNote: 1370 is used for sorting by the phase of the wall's expansion; the gate tower and surviving wall faces include later repairs.
sx_pingyaowall.lede: After the enlargement and brick facing of 1370 (3rd year of Hongwu, Ming), this circuit of wall at Pingyao, over six thousand metres round and about twelve metres high, was never pulled down: six gates, four corner towers, seventy-two bastions and more than three thousand merlons can still be counted. It is the most complete county-town wall in China and the core of the "one city, two temples" World Heritage property of 1997. The plate takes the south gate, Yingxun Gate, where the arched passage, gate platform and double-eave gate tower stack into one group and the battlemented wall runs off east and west; both tower and wall surfaces include later repairs.
facts: Wall: about 6.4 km in circuit and about 12 m high, rammed earth faced with grey brick, paved on top with a horse ramp inside; a bastion with an enemy tower projects roughly every 50 m, 72 in all, with over three thousand merlons; the moat outside is about 4 m wide and 4 m deep.

History: tradition dates the first wall to King Xuan of Zhou; the present wall was enlarged and brick-cased in 1370 (3rd year of Hongwu, Ming) on the old town, and dozens of later repairs kept the early-Ming scheme; part of the south wall collapsed in 2004 and was rebuilt in 2005.

Heritage: in 1997 the Ancient City of Pingyao, with Shuanglin and Zhenguo temples, was inscribed as World Heritage, the wall enclosing a 225-hectare property; nearly four thousand Ming and Qing shops and dwellings inside bear witness to the town's years as China's financial centre from the 19th to the early 20th century.
captions: Pingyao City Wall · Yingxun Gate and adjoining wall sections
Ming–Qing · Ming–Qing

sn_hancheng.name: Dacheng Hall of Hancheng Confucian Temple
sn_hancheng.era: Rebuilt in the Hongwu era, maintained over the centuries
sn_hancheng.yearNote: 1371 is the recorded rebuilding of the Confucian Temple on its Yuan site; the Dacheng Hall retains Yuan building methods and has been maintained over the centuries, so not every surviving member can be assigned to 1371.
sn_hancheng.place: Shaanxi · Weinan · Old town of Hancheng
sn_hancheng.lede: Beneath a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, a broad front porch fronts the five-bay hall. The Hancheng Confucian Temple was rebuilt on its Yuan site, and between columns and architraves the continuation of earlier timber methods can still be seen.
facts: Rebuilding: The local gazetteer records rebuilding on the Yuan site in 1371, followed by repeated maintenance.
Main structure: The Dacheng Hall is five bays wide, its front porch spans three large bays, and it has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof.
Dating: It retains Yuan building methods; neither the whole temple nor all of its members are equated with a single year.
captions: Dacheng Hall of Hancheng Confucian Temple, whole hall · Line drawing
Ming · Rebuilt 1371 · Later maintenance

protection.scope: Dacheng Hall of Hancheng Confucian Temple · Five-bay hall · Timber front porch

yuhuang.name: Jade Emperor Pavilion of Yuzhou
yuhuang.era: Founded in the 10th year of Hongwu
yuhuang.place: Hebei · Yu County · North city wall
yuhuang.lede: On the north wall of the old city of Yuzhou, Jingbian Tower spreads three tiers of eaves yet has only two stories. A gallery runs around the upper story, and here a defensive tower and the cult of the Jade Emperor overlap.
facts: Built in the 10th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1377) and also called Jingbian Tower, it is the landmark pavilion on the northern rampart of the old city of Yuzhou.
The main hall is five bays wide, with three tiers of eaves on two stories and a glazed-tile hip-and-gable roof; a waist eave gives the two-story pavilion the appearance of three eaves.
The upper story has a timber gallery around the building, and the lower story a surrounding colonnade; the surviving building preserves the historical layers of many Ming and Qing repairs.
captions: Jade Emperor Pavilion of Yuzhou · Front
Three eaves, two stories · Five bays wide

xianwall.name: Xi'an City Wall
xianwall.sub: Arrow tower of Anding Gate · Ming rampart
xianwall.lede: A massive wall platform carries a broad arrow tower, four rows of arrow windows stretch across it, and a single gate passage pierces the defenses. The layout of the west gate preserved at Anding Gate makes the scale and defensive purpose of the Xi'an City Wall clearly legible.
facts: Ming rampart: The main body of the surviving wall was built in the 7th to 11th years of Hongwu (1374–1378), extended from an earlier city site, and later gradually faced with brick and reinforced.

Anding Gate section: The plate takes the arrow tower of the main west gate and its single central arched passage; the broad tower has four rows of arrow windows, and the thick walls and gate tower together form a defensive space.

Repairs through the ages: Anding Gate has been repaired many times in the Ming, the Qing and the modern period and still preserves a defensive layout in which arrow tower, gate tower and barbican are linked.
captions: Xi'an City Wall · Arrow tower and central arched passage of Anding Gate
Ming rampart · Ming, Qing and modern repairs

xianzhonggu.name: Bell Tower and Drum Tower of Xi'an
xianzhonggu.era: Founded in the Hongwu era · Moved in the Wanli era
xianzhonggu.place: Shaanxi · Xi'an · Center of the prefectural city
xianzhonggu.lede: The Bell Tower stands with its pyramidal roof where streets meet, and the long ridge of the Drum Tower stretches across the south end of Beiyuanmen. These two Ming towers once announced the hours of the city with the sound of bell and drum.
facts: The Drum Tower was founded in 1380 and the Bell Tower in 1384; the Bell Tower was moved to its present site in 1582 on a newly built base, so the platform at the present site cannot be equated with the original founding date.

The Bell Tower is a triple-eaved pavilion with a four-sided pyramidal roof on a square platform; the Drum Tower stands on a rectangular platform, its body seven bays wide with a surrounding gallery and a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof on the upper story.

The plate sets near-frontal views of the Bell Tower and the Drum Tower side by side, keeping each one's complete outline; this is a composite of two subjects, not a view of the two towers actually standing next to each other.
captions: Xi'an Bell Tower · Drum Tower
Composite of two subjects, not adjacent in reality

linggu.name: Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple
linggu.lede: The Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple carries its roof on massive brick walls and continuous vaults, and three arched doorways pierce the broad wall of its front. Above two shallow tiers of eaves, three pagoda-shaped ridge ornaments mark the outline of this Ming brick hall.
facts: The surviving Beamless Hall is a Ming building; Linggu Temple was moved here in the 14th year of Hongwu (1381).

The hall uses no timber beams, and masonry vaults bear the structure; two homophonous names are used side by side, Wuliang Hall meaning “Hall of the Immeasurable” and Wuliang Hall meaning “Beamless Hall.”
According to the scenic area, the hall is about 50 m wide and about 34 m deep, and three pagoda-shaped ridge ornaments stand on its double-eaved hip-and-gable roof.
captions: Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple · Front of the brick-vaulted hall
Surviving Ming structure · Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof with three pagoda-shaped ridge ornaments

protection.unitName: Cemetery of the Fallen Soldiers of the National Revolutionary Army
protection.scope: Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple · Nanjing · Brick-vaulted hall
protection.note: In 1933 the Beamless Hall was converted into the memorial hall of the Cemetery of the Fallen Soldiers of the National Revolutionary Army; in the fifth batch the cemetery was incorporated into the first-batch listing of the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum. It is not a separately listed national protected site under the name “Linggu Temple.”

sx_chongshan.name: Chongshan Temple, Taiyuan
sx_chongshan.sub: Hall of Great Compassion · Early Ming official-style timber structure
sx_chongshan.era: Hongwu era, Ming · Hall of Great Compassion
sx_chongshan.yearNote: 1385 is only an approximate timeline placement within the Hongwu reign, not a precise completion year. Neither the temple's history nor its Qing main gate replaces the date of the Ming main subject drawn.
sx_chongshan.lede: In 1381 (14th year of Hongwu, Ming) Zhu Gang, Prince Gong of Jin, enlarged this temple for his late mother Empress Ma; at 140,000 square metres with six great halls on the axis it was once the largest in Shanxi. After a fire in 1864 (3rd year of Tongzhi, Qing) only the fifth hall on the axis, the Dabei Hall, was left. Seven bays wide under double eaves and nearly twenty metres high, together with its three Hongwu-era painted statues over eight metres tall, it is the most dependable specimen of an early-Ming official-style Buddhist hall in Taiyuan. The plate shows the front of the Dabei Hall.
facts: Dabei Hall: seven bays wide and four bays deep, double-eave hip-and-gable (xieshan) roof, nearly 20 m high overall; in the centre stands the Thousand-armed, Thousand-eyed, Eleven-headed Guanyin, flanked by the Thousand-bowl Manjusri and Samantabhadra, all three original Hongwu-period statues over 8 m tall.

History: according to the Daoguang-era Yangqu County Gazetteer the site was a travel palace of Emperor Yang of Sui and was called Baima Temple in the early Tang; the enlargement ran from 1381 to 1391 (14th to 24th years of Hongwu), and the present name dates from the Jiajing reign; after the fire of 1864, Zhang Zhidong in 1882 (8th year of Guangxu) turned the ruined front part into the Taiyuan Prefectural Confucian Temple.

Scale: in the Ming the temple had nearly a thousand bays of halls, the axis running through the Vajra, Heavenly Kings, Mahavira, Vairocana, Dabei and Jinling halls, the Dabei Hall second only to the nine-bay Mahavira Hall; today the temple measures 119.2 m east-west by 71.7 m north-south, covering 8,547 square metres.
captions: Chongshan Temple · Hall of Great Compassion
Hongwu era, Ming · Seven bays, double-eaved hipped roof
