protection.scope: Chongshan Temple, Taiyuan · Hall of Great Compassion · Early Ming official-style timber structure

fj_chongwu.name: South Gate of Chongwu Ancient City
fj_chongwu.sub: Granite gate platform · South gate wall section
fj_chongwu.era: City built in the 20th year of Hongwu, later repaired
fj_chongwu.yearNote: 1387 is the founding date of the Chongwu stone city and an approximate timeline placement; the surviving south gate section has undergone later repairs, and the upper gate tower seen in photographs is not labeled as original 1387 fabric.
fj_chongwu.lede: China's most complete surviving granite coastal fortress town. In 1387 Zhou Dexing, Marquis of Jiangxia, was ordered to build the Chongwu Battalion (qianhusuo) city on the Hui'an headland against pirate raids: a wall of some 2,500 metres, seven metres high, with gates on four sides and barbicans added to the east and west gates. The plate shows a section at the South Gate, a low, massive granite platform with the arched gateway in the middle; the gatehouse above is as it appeared after the comprehensive 1980s restoration 'to the original appearance', and should not be taken as early Ming fabric.
facts: Scale: the walls are built entirely of granite blocks, 2,567 m in circuit, about 500 m north-south and 300 m east-west, 5 m thick at the base and 7 m high; there were originally 26 guard huts, 1,304 crenels and 1,300 arrow slits, with a two- to three-tier rampart walk. The South Gate platform and its arch are one section of this.

History: begun in 1387 and completed in 1394; in 1558 pirates besieged the city for six days and nights and took it; in 1567 Qi Jiguang garrisoned troops here and reorganised the defences. Five major repairs followed between the Yongle and Daoguang reigns, and in 1983-1987 the State Administration of Cultural Heritage funded three phases of restoration, rebuilding 2,517 m of wall to the original appearance.

Comparison: Chongwu was a battalion city in the early Ming coastal garrison (weisuo) system of Fujian, and survives whole because its stone was quarried from local Hui'an granite; within half a square kilometre the town still keeps over twenty temples and nunneries, dozens of ancestral halls and more than two hundred old houses, a live example of the social structure of a southern Fujian military town.
captions: South Gate of Chongwu Ancient City and a short adjoining stretch of wall · Line drawing
Ming · Founded 1387 · Repaired over the centuries

protection.scope: South Gate of Chongwu Ancient City · Granite gate platform · South gate wall section

sx_jiulongbi.name: Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong
sx_jiulongbi.sub: Glazed spirit screen of the Prince of Dai's mansion · Nine-dragon relief
sx_jiulongbi.yearNote: The date given by the Palace Museum, the 25th year of Hongwu (1392), is used; the plate depicts only the surviving Nine-Dragon Screen and not the present-day reconstruction of the Prince of Dai's mansion.
sx_jiulongbi.place: Shanxi · Datong · Heyang Street, Old city
sx_jiulongbi.lede: Nine dragons twist among blue-green glazed tiles, with clouds and waves spreading along the long screen. The Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong contains its dense relief between a low coping and a layered Sumeru plinth, leaving behind the screen of an early Ming princely mansion.
facts: The Nine-Dragon Screen was originally the glazed spirit screen in front of the mansion of Zhu Gui, Prince of Dai. The Palace Museum records it as built in the 25th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1392), and it is assigned to the Ming according to the main body of the screen drawn.
The screen is about 45.5 m long and about 8 m high, with nine principal dragons arrayed along its continuous body; the hipped coping and the glazed Sumeru plinth form its upper and lower borders.

A spirit screen serves as a barrier and decoration in front of a building and is not a city wall or fortification. The plate removes the railings, trees and reflecting pool and simplifies the details of the cloud-and-dragon relief, while keeping the multicolored distribution of the actual glazes.
captions: Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong · Front of the glazed nine-dragon spirit screen
Ming · 25th year of Hongwu (1392)

shuanglin.name: Shuanglin Temple, Pingyao
shuanglin.sub: Hall of Heavenly Kings · Painted sculpture
shuanglin.era: Restored in the 2nd year of Wuping, Northern Qi · Rebuilt in the early Ming
shuanglin.lede: It is the first thing you see inside the fortified gate: the five-bay, gable-roofed Hall of the Heavenly Kings, with four guardian Vajra figures three metres tall lined up in its front porch, the opening statement of Shuanglin Temple's more than two thousand Ming painted sculptures. The temple began as Zhongdu Temple; a Northern Song stele in the compound records a rebuilding as early as 571 (2nd year of Wuping, Northern Qi), while today's halls and statues mostly come from a Ming rebuilding, repainted in the Qing. In 1997 it was inscribed as World Heritage with Zhenguo Temple as part of the Ancient City of Pingyao. The plate shows the front of the hall and the porch guardians; the Maitreya, Indra, Brahma and Four Heavenly Kings inside are not in the picture.
facts: Hall of the Heavenly Kings: five bays wide and three deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof; four guardian Vajra figures about 3 m tall stand in the front porch; inside, the crowned Maitreya is 2.2 m high, the attendant Indra and Brahma about 1.75 m, the Four Heavenly Kings face inward from the south wall and the Eight Bodhisattvas line the sides.

Dating: the Gugu Stele of 1011 (4th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Northern Song) in the temple records that "Zhongdu Temple was rebuilt in the 2nd year of Wuping of Northern Qi (571)"; the Song renamed it after the Buddha's passing between twin sal trees; the existing halls and sculptures come mainly from a Ming rebuilding, repainted in the Qing, and the Ming rammed-earth enclosure with its battlements gives the temple the look of a fort.

Sculpture: ten halls hold 2,052 painted clay figures, 1,566 of them intact, the largest over 3 m and the smallest 30 cm, about three quarters modelled in suspended relief leaning forward 10 to 20 degrees; the clay is local red clay and the eyes are inlaid black glass.
captions: Line drawing of the Hall of Heavenly Kings · Five bays wide
Single-eaved overhanging gable roof · Four vajra guardians in the front porch

hb_zixiao.name: Zixiao Palace
hb_zixiao.era: Built in the Yongle era, Ming
hb_zixiao.yearNote: The Zixiao Hall is placed by its construction in the Yongle era of the Ming; 1413 is a sorting reference for this phase of the palace's construction and is not presented as the hall's exact completion year. It was later repaired, and the drawing shows the present state seen in research photographs. The Song founding history is kept separate from the Ming hall drawn.
hb_zixiao.lede: Green double eaves cover a red hall, and tiers of stone terraces raise the main hall high. Keeping only the hall and its steps is enough to show how Wudang architecture unfolds with the mountain terrain.
facts: Main subject: The Zixiao Hall of Zixiao Palace and its front platform.

Date: The Zixiao Hall is placed by its construction in the Yongle era of the Ming; 1413 is a sorting reference for this phase of the palace's construction and is not presented as the hall's exact completion year. It was later repaired, and the drawing shows the present state seen in research photographs. The Song founding history is kept separate from the Ming hall drawn.

Scope of the plate: The five-bay Zixiao Hall, its double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, the three-tiered stone terrace in front and the central stairway; the side halls to left and right and the distant mountains are not drawn, and steles, incense burners and visitors are removed.

hb_jindian.name: Golden Hall of Wudang Mountains
hb_jindian.sub: Cast bronze, gilded · Double-eaved hipped roof
hb_jindian.yearNote: The drawing shows the surviving Ming Golden Hall on Tianzhu Peak, placed at the 14th year of Yongle (1416); it is not to be confused with the ancient Yuan bronze hall moved into the Zhuanyun Hall. The formal national listing includes both the Yuan and Ming bronze halls; this plate shows only the Ming hall.
hb_jindian.lede: The tile ridges, beams, columns and bracket sets are not wood but cast bronze members. Its double roof still looks like that of a small timber hall, and its quiet gold rests on the highest point of Wudang.
facts: Main subject: The Ming Golden Hall on Tianzhu Peak, Wudang Mountains.

Date: The drawing shows the surviving Ming Golden Hall on Tianzhu Peak, placed at the 14th year of Yongle (1416); it is not to be confused with the ancient Yuan bronze hall moved into the Zhuanyun Hall. The formal national listing includes both the Yuan and Ming bronze halls; this plate shows only the Ming hall.

Scope of the plate: The complete Ming Golden Hall, with its two tiers of eaves, three-bay facade, and cast-bronze imitation-timber bracket sets and door leaves; the bronze cranes to either side, incense burner, prayer cushions and surrounding temple buildings are not drawn, and it is not the single-eaved ancient Yuan bronze hall.

tiantan.name: Temple of Heaven, Beijing
tiantan.sub: Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests
tiantan.era: Founded in the 18th year of Yongle · Rebuilt in the 22nd year of Guangxu
tiantan.lede: The Hall of Great Sacrifice was built in the 18th year of Yongle in the Ming (1420); in the Jiajing era it became a round, triple-eaved hall, and under Qianlong it received blue tiles and was renamed the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests. Struck by lightning and burned in the 15th year of Guangxu (1889), it was rebuilt to the original design six years later — what we see today is timber of 1896.
facts: Round, triple-eaved and conical, with blue glazed tiles and a gilded finial; 32.72 m in diameter and 38 m tall overall, it stands on a three-tiered round terrace of white marble.
Twenty-eight columns stand inside: four Dragon Well Columns represent the four seasons, twelve golden columns the twelve months, and twelve eave columns the twelve two-hour periods of the day.
The hall has no great beams; columns, tie-beams and bracket sets support the conical roof layer by layer, the pinnacle of Ming–Qing official-style timber construction.

Conical roof · Three-tiered round terrace

hb_jimingyi.name: Jimingyi Post Town
hb_jimingyi.sub: East gate platform and flanking old city walls
hb_jimingyi.yearNote: 1420 is the founding year of the Ming post town recognized by the provincial cultural heritage bureau, with further construction in the Ming and Qing; this plate includes a gate tower restored in modern times, and its timber roof is not claimed as Ming original.
hb_jimingyi.lede: The brick platform of Jimingyi's east gate and the walls on either side preserve the depth of the post town's entrance. What it connects is not just a town but a whole Ming–Qing system of postal relay and military courier roads.
facts: Town site: The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau records that Jimingyi Post Town was built in the 18th year of Yongle in the Ming (1420), with further construction in both the Ming and Qing.
Walls: Brick-faced with rammed-earth cores, with one gate each on the east and west; this plate selects the east gate platform and the adjoining wall sections.
Distinguishing restorations: The gate tower in the drawing is based on present-day site photographs, and the dates of the modern restored timber roof and the Ming walls are given separately.

bj_changling.name: Ling'en Hall of Changling, Beijing
bj_changling.sub: Nine-bay nanmu hall · Double-eaved hipped roof
bj_changling.era: Built from Yongle to Xuande · Repaired over the centuries
bj_changling.yearNote: Palace Museum sources record that the sacrificial hall was completed in 1416 and the halls of the mausoleum precinct finished in 1427, while other accounts adopt 1427 as the completion of the hall. 1420 is only an approximate sorting point within the early Ming construction history of the hall drawn; the initial construction of the mausoleum in 1409 is not used as the hall's completion year.
bj_changling.lede: The nine-bay hall spreads beneath a long, broad double-eaved hipped roof, its grid of nanmu columns carrying the roof, while the stone terrace and imperial steps join tier upon tier in front. This plate depicts the Ling'en Hall and does not substitute the initial construction date of the whole Changling precinct for the date of the hall.
facts: The Ling'en Hall is nine bays wide and five bays deep, the core building of Changling's ritual space; the plate selects the surviving hall and its platform.

The Palace Museum's account records that the sacrificial hall was completed in 1416 and the halls of the mausoleum precinct finished in 1427; the construction history and later repairs are marked separately.

Yellow glazed tiles, dark red timberwork, blue-green painted decoration under the eaves and a pale stone platform are zoned according to the present appearance; the nanmu inside the hall is not uniformly drawn as gold.

baoen.name: Pagoda of Great Bao'en Temple, Nanjing
baoen.era: Begun in the 10th year of Yongle · Completed in the 3rd year of Xuande
baoen.lede: Begun in the 10th year of Yongle in the Ming (1412) and completed in the 3rd year of Xuande (1428), it was octagonal with nine stories and 78.2 m tall, clad entirely in white porcelain bricks and five-colored glazed tiles, and more than a hundred lamps on the pagoda burned every night — Europeans called it the “Porcelain Tower of Nanjing” and counted it among the Seven Wonders of the medieval world. It was destroyed in 1856 in the Taiping war, and a glass reconstruction now stands on the original site.
facts: The glazed pagoda had nine stories and eight faces, with a balcony platform and balustrade on every story and bells hanging from the eave corners; 78.2 m tall overall, it was the tallest building in Ming Nanjing.
The body was faced with white porcelain bricks, and the arched doorways were pieced together in five-colored glaze with lions, elephants, flying goats and garudas.

After its destruction, an underground crypt and a Seven-Treasure Ashoka Stupa were excavated at the original site; the reconstruction completed in 2015 uses light steel and glass, taking only the outline and not recreating the brick body.
captions: Nine stories, eight faces · Drawn from the Tushanwan model of the old pagoda
Original pagoda destroyed · Not the modern glass tower

bj_zhihua.name: Zhihua Temple, Beijing
bj_zhihua.sub: Tathagata Hall · Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion
bj_zhihua.era: Founded in the Zhengtong era · Surviving Ming halls
bj_zhihua.yearNote: Official descriptions give 1443 and 1444 respectively as the founding year of Zhihua Temple. 1444 is used for approximate sorting; the temple's founding year cannot be taken directly as the precise date of making of every surviving member.
bj_zhihua.lede: Black-gray glazed tiles cover the upper and lower roofs, and dark red colonnades and blue-green painted decoration are tucked beneath deep eaves. The five-bay Tathagata Hall below and the three-bay Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion above form a compact and clear layering of hall and pavilion.
facts: This plate shows only the south side of the Tathagata Hall and the Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion above it, and does not fold other buildings such as the Zhihua Hall in under the temple's general name.
The lower story is five bays wide and the upper story three; the black glazed tile roofs and the painted decoration under the eaves each keep the colors of their surviving materials.
Zhihua Temple was founded in the Zhengtong era of the Ming; official sources give two founding dates, 1443 and 1444, and the timeline keeps this explanation rather than inventing a precise date.
captions: Zhihua Temple, Beijing · Tathagata Hall and Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion
Ming · Founded 1443–1444

hunyuanwenmiao.name: Hunyuan Confucian Temple
hunyuanwenmiao.place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan · Yong'an West Street
hunyuanwenmiao.lede: At the prefectural school of Hunyuan below the Northern Sacred Peak, the Dacheng Hall is the one building in the compound with real presence: five bays wide and three deep, roofed in yellow and green glazed tile, its central and second bays fully fitted with six-rail lattice doors while the end bays are solid brick, and the brick rear wall carries the four large characters "loyalty, filial piety, chastity, righteousness". The gazetteer records a large-scale rebuilding in 1472 (8th year of Chenghua, Ming), and the surviving hall is generally taken as a Ming structure; the omission of the front interior columns and the plain four-puzuo bracket sets under the eaves keep an older feel. The plate shows the front of the Dacheng Hall.
facts: Dacheng Hall: five bays and 27.6 m wide, three bays and 14.6 m deep, single-eave hip-and-gable roof in yellow and green glazed tile; four-puzuo bracket sets with two intercolumnar sets each in the central and second bays, the front row of interior columns omitted; the terrace in front is about 13 m long, 6 m wide and 1.5 m high, with a two-dragons-and-pearl imperial ramp in the middle.

Dating: the Qianlong-era Hunyuan Prefecture Gazetteer says the temple predates the Liao and Jin, was enlarged in the early Yuan, rebuilt on a large scale in 1472 (8th year of Chenghua, Ming) and completed in the Wanli reign; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Ming to Qing, and the hall itself has no firm completion date.

Layout: along the axis only the Ji Gate, Dacheng Hall, Zunjing Pavilion and Chongsheng Shrine survive, the pavilion a brick vault below and a timber loft above; the "loyalty, filial piety, chastity, righteousness" brickwork resembles the carved brick inscriptions of nearby Yong'an Temple, whose glazed roof fittings also match those of this hall.
captions: Line drawing of the Dacheng Hall of the Confucian Temple · Five bays wide
Single-eaved hipped roof · Surviving Ming structure

bj_zhenjue.name: Diamond Throne Pagoda of Zhenjue Temple, Beijing
bj_zhenjue.era: Completed in the 9th year of Chenghua
bj_zhenjue.lede: Five small multi-eaved pagodas stand on a stone throne. Five rows of Buddha figures on the front, animal and floral patterns at the base and an arched entrance are layered one upon another, forming the most striking carved stone silhouette of Beijing's Five Pagoda Temple.
facts: The diamond throne was completed in the 9th year of Chenghua in the Ming (1473); the five pagodas and the throne form a single stone structure, not five separate brick pagodas.

The facade of the throne has five tiers of Buddhist niches, with additional bands of animals and floral patterns at the bottom. In the frontal view the two rear pagodas are hidden, and the five pagodas are not forcibly spread out in a row.

The pagoda eaves and niche figures are carved stone, and the present appearance is mainly gray-beige stone; the glazed members of the small pavilion over the stair to the top are colored separately from the stone pagoda eaves.
captions: Diamond Throne Pagoda of Zhenjue Temple, Beijing · South side
Ming · 1473

hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.name: Qingyuan Tower, Xuanhua
hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.sub: Triple-eaved bell tower with cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, and brick platform
hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.yearNote: Only one Xuanhua city tower is selected as representative; Zhenshuo Tower and the Five-Dragon Screen are not added.
hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.lede: Cross-shaped hip-and-gable roofs overlap tier upon tier, and the bell tower stands on a tall brick platform at the heart of old Xuanhua's streets, its north and south arched passages letting the street run through the tower.
facts: Date: Qingyuan Tower was built in the 18th year of Chenghua in the Ming (1482) and has been repaired through the ages; the surviving main body follows the Ming form.
Structure: The tower has three stories and a triple-eaved cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, with the central and wing roofs interpenetrating front and back to form a complex yet clear outline.
City tower: An arched passage runs through the center of the huge brick platform; this entry uses Qingyuan Tower to represent the towers of Xuanhua and does not split off neighboring buildings.

Triple-eaved cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof and arched passage through the brick platform

yn_jianshui.name: Jianshui Confucian Temple
yn_jianshui.sub: Hall of the First Teacher · Dacheng Hall
yn_jianshui.yearNote: 1495 is only an approximate sorting point within the Hongzhi era (1488–1505); dating follows the Hall of the First Teacher drawn, and the temple's founding date of 1285 is not substituted for it.
yn_jianshui.place: Yunnan · Jianshui · Old city of Lin'an
yn_jianshui.lede: Beyond the Sea of Learning pond and the successive courtyards, the Hall of the First Teacher faces the old city with a single, spreading roof. The Confucian Temple dates back to the Yuan, while this single-eaved hip-and-gable main hall belongs to the Hongzhi era of the Ming; its stone columns and lattice doors preserve Yunnan craft details in Confucian architecture.
facts: Main subject drawn: The Hall of the First Teacher, that is, the Dacheng Hall, five bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof.
Date: The hall was built in the Hongzhi era of the Ming (1488–1505); 1285 is the date of the Confucian Temple's original founding.

Stonework: Bluestone columns along the outer eave and carved lattice doors are its distinctive features; the plate shows only the Hall of the First Teacher itself and does not stand for the whole Confucian Temple.
captions: Hall of the First Teacher, Jianshui Confucian Temple · Line drawing · Pending user review
Ming · Hongzhi era

sx_yuci_chenghuang.name: City God Temple of Yuci
sx_yuci_chenghuang.sub: Xuanjian Tower · Music tower and stage
sx_yuci_chenghuang.era: Ming · Xuanjian Tower and music tower
sx_yuci_chenghuang.yearNote: Xuanjian Tower (1497) and the music tower (1511) are supported by stele records; the date of about 1523 for the stage in front is an inference by the cultural relics survey from a date on the screen wall.
sx_yuci_chenghuang.lede: Xuanjian Tower is not one building but a group stacked up by three generations: in 1497 (10th year of Hongzhi, Ming) the five-bay, two-storey, triple-eaved tower, seventeen metres high, went up south of the main hall; later a music hall was fitted against its north eave, less than a metre between the two roofs, and a one-bay, round-ridged, hip-and-gable street stage pushed further north, flanked by Ming glazed-tile splayed screen walls. The peacock-blue glazed roofs rise and fall, and from the courtyard they read as a single whole. The plate shows this northern group; the main hall, Xianyou Hall, and the gate are not in the picture.
facts: Xuanjian Tower: five bays wide and four rafters deep, two storeys under three tiers of hip-and-gable eaves, 17 m high overall, peacock-blue glazed roof, three hollow caisson ceilings inside; to the north adjoins the two-rafter-deep music hall, and beyond it a one-bay street stage with a single round-ridged hip-and-gable roof, flanked by glazed splayed screen walls under hip-and-gable roofs.

Dating: the temple was founded in 1362 (22nd year of Zhizheng, Yuan), moved to the present site in 1431 (6th year of Xuande, Ming) and enlarged in the Chenghua and Hongzhi reigns; the tower was built in 1497 (10th year of Hongzhi), the gate in 1509 (4th year of Zhengde), and the music hall and stage were completed by the early Jiajing reign (around 1523), giving the present scale.

Significance: roofs of three periods interlock, and the screen walls and music hall enclose an acoustic space, a model of the Ming city-god-temple composite of tower, music hall and stage; it became a national key protected site in 1996 and was placed on the World Monuments Fund Watch list in 2000.
captions: City God Temple of Yuci · North side of Xuanjian Tower
Ming · Music tower and pass-through stage

zhaoling.name: Zhaoling Palace, Xianyou
zhaoling.era: Ming · Exact date to be determined
zhaoling.place: Fujian · Putian · Dingdonghu Village, Xiyuan Township, Xianyou
zhaoling.lede: The hip-and-gable roof spreads low, and slanting wooden rain boards run along the gallery beneath the eaves. Wooden railings and curved-back railing seats enclose the light hall, and a stone platform holds this small temple on the hillside of Dingdonghu Village.
facts: Old temple of Donghu: Located in Dingdonghu Village, Xiyuan Township, Xianyou County, Fujian, and also called Donghu Zhaoling Palace.
Gallery under the eaves: The single hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; on three sides beneath the eaves are a gallery and curved-back railing seats, covered by slanting wooden rain boards.
Date to be determined: Based on existing field accounts, the date is provisionally listed as Ming; the years of construction and repair remain to be determined.

sn_yanan.name: Yan'an Pagoda (Lingshan Temple Pagoda)
sn_yanan.sub: Octagonal nine-story brick pagoda · Surviving Ming form
sn_yanan.era: Tang–Song history, restored in the Ming
sn_yanan.yearNote: The combined national listing marks it as Song; educational sources describe the surviving pagoda as a Ming building. The plate and timeline list it as Ming according to its surviving restored form; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point, not a confirmed rebuilding year.
sn_yanan.lede: The octagonal nine-story brick pagoda stands on Baota Hill, its outline now the emblem of Yan'an. The pagoda's Tang–Song history and its layers of Ming restoration coexist, and the plate is drawn according to the form seen today.
facts: Form: An octagonal nine-story pavilion-style brick pagoda with a tall lower story and corbelled eaves that taper gradually with the body.

Layers of date: The national listing marks it as Song, while sources on the surviving pagoda form record it as Ming; this entry enters the timeline by its present Ming-restored appearance, leaving the exact year open to further research.
Scope of the plate: Only the pagoda itself is drawn, without other historic sites on the hill or modern lighting installations.

Ming · Ming restoration · Exact year undetermined

gx_dashi.name: Dashi Pavilion of Yong'an, Hepu
gx_dashi.sub: Low front, high rear · Linked timber pavilions
gx_dashi.yearNote: Listed as Ming in the third batch of national protected sites; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point within the Ming, not an established construction year. The plate shows the linked front and rear pavilions; the incense-burner pavilions around them are not part of the subject drawn.
gx_dashi.lede: The front pavilion is low and the rear one high, the roofs rising step by step, and between the open timber columns the beam frame inside can be seen. This small pavilion at Yong'an in Hepu leaves a distinct silhouette through its linked volumes and timber structure.
facts: Subject: the front pavilion of the Dashi Pavilion at Yong'an, Hepu, and the rear pavilion joined to it.

Dating: listed as Ming in the third batch of national protected sites; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point within the Ming, not an established construction year. The plate shows the linked front and rear pavilions; the incense-burner pavilions around them are not part of the subject drawn.

Plate scope: the linked pavilions, low in front and high behind, with open timber columns on the lower level, gray tiles and blue-green painted eaves; the incense-burner pavilions on the left and right are not included.

gs_jiayuguan.name: Jiayu Pass
gs_jiayuguan.era: Built in the Hongzhi to Zhengde reigns, Ming
gs_jiayuguan.yearNote: The drawing shows the Jiayuguan Tower on the west side and its gate platform. The tower was built during the Hongzhi to Zhengde reigns of the Ming and repaired continuously in later periods; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point and does not equal a completion year, nor is the establishment of the pass in 1372 used in place of the tower's date.
gs_jiayuguan.lede: A three-story gate tower stands on a massive gate platform, with an arched passage cutting through the loess-colored wall. Only the west tower is shown; the Guanghua and Rouyuan towers are not combined into the same drawing.
facts: Subject: the Jiayuguan Tower on the west side and its gate platform.

Dating: the drawing shows the Jiayuguan Tower on the west side and its gate platform. The tower was built during the Hongzhi to Zhengde reigns of the Ming and repaired continuously in later periods; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point and does not equal a completion year, nor is the establishment of the pass in 1372 used in place of the tower's date.

Plate scope: a three-story, triple-eaved tower; the thick gate platform, a single arch directly below it, and short crenellated wall sections to the left and right; complete roof corners and base. The other two towers are not drawn.

gs_dafo_tuta.name: Earthen Stupa of the Great Buddha Temple, Zhangye
gs_dafo_tuta.era: Built in the Ming · Later restored
gs_dafo_tuta.yearNote: The earthen stupa was built in about the Ming dynasty; 1500 is only an approximate Ming sorting point. An earthquake in 1927 damaged the top, which was restored in 1986. The drawing takes the upper stupa body and finial visible in photographs and does not invent the lower base hidden by the front hall and courtyard walls.
gs_dafo_tuta.lede: A massive inverted-bowl dome carries a slender stack of spire rings, with small stupas clustered around it. The drawing keeps the clearly visible upper part of the earthen stupa and leaves out the front hall and courtyard walls; this is neither the Great Buddha Hall nor the wooden pagoda.
facts: Subject: the exposed body and finial of the Amitabha Thousand-Buddha Stupa.

Dating: the earthen stupa was built in about the Ming dynasty; 1500 is only an approximate Ming sorting point. An earthquake in 1927 damaged the top, which was restored in 1986. The drawing takes the upper stupa body and finial visible in photographs and does not invent the lower base hidden by the front hall and courtyard walls.

Plate scope: only the upper part of the earthen stupa exposed in photographs — part of the square Sumeru plinth, the small stupas visible at the four corners, the massive inverted-bowl dome, the niche section, the slender spire rings, and the canopy and crowning jewel. The hidden two-tier gallery and the full large base are not added.

gongzhu.name: Gongzhu Temple, Fanshi
gongzhu.lede: This small temple in Princess Village, named for a Northern Wei princess, keeps its interest indoors: the Mahavira Hall is only three bays wide under a gable roof, with not even bracket sets under the eaves, yet its four walls are covered with Ming Water-and-Land murals in which Buddhas, bodhisattvas, devas and Daoist gods assemble in tiers, a complete Ming mural cycle of this genre. Tradition credits the founding to Princess Chengxin, fourth daughter of Emperor Wencheng of Northern Wei; the surviving halls are dated by a restoration of 1503 (16th year of Hongzhi, Ming), and the Mahavira Hall and the passage hall before it are the temple's only Ming structures. The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall; the murals are inside.
facts: Mahavira Hall: three bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, no bracket sets under the eaves; the passage hall in front is three bays square under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with five-puzuo bracket sets, and these two are the only Ming buildings left in the temple.

Dating: tradition attributes the temple to Princess Chengxin, fourth daughter of Emperor Wencheng of Northern Wei; it was restored in 1503 (16th year of Hongzhi, Ming) and is registered by the National Cultural Heritage Administration as Ming to Qing; facing south with three courtyards, it covers 4,347 square metres with 1,116 square metres of buildings.

Murals: the Mahavira Hall preserves Ming Water-and-Land murals with Buddhist and Daoist deities painted in one assembly; the Qielan, Horse King, God of Wealth and Erlang halls on either side were all built in the Qing and belong to a different period from the murals inside.
captions: Front of the Mahavira Hall, Gongzhu Temple · Redrawn from photographs
Restored in the 16th year of Hongzhi, Ming (1503) · Three bays, single-eaved overhanging gable roof, no bracket sets under the eaves

hb_xtkaiyuan.name: Kaiyuan Temple, Xingtai
hb_xtkaiyuan.sub: Bodhisattva Hall of the old Kaiyuan Temple (third hall / Sakyamuni Hall), full facade and four coiling-dragon stone columns
hb_xtkaiyuan.yearNote: The Vairocana Hall burned in 1988 and was rebuilt in 1997, so it was not chosen. Instead the plate uses the Bodhisattva Hall, restored in the 13th year of Zhengde in the Ming, and its four coiling-dragon stone columns inscribed 1518. It must be distinguished from the new temple of 2013 on the east side.
hb_xtkaiyuan.lede: The Bodhisattva Hall of the old Kaiyuan Temple carries its front eaves on four coiling-dragon stone columns; beneath the broad flush gable roof, the layers of the Ming restoration can still be read.
facts: Surviving subject: the drawing shows the Bodhisattva Hall, the third hall of the old temple, also called the Sakyamuni Hall; it was restored in the 13th year of Zhengde in the Ming (1518).
Four columns: the hall is five bays wide; the four coiling-dragon stone columns of the front eaves carry inscriptions dated 1518 and are the key identifying feature of this drawing.
Old and new: neither the Vairocana Hall, rebuilt after the 1988 fire, nor the buildings of the new temple on the east side are taken to represent original Ming fabric.

sx_jiexiu_houtu.name: Houtu Temple, Jiexiu
sx_jiexiu_houtu.sub: Sanqing Tower · Hall and stage combined
sx_jiexiu_houtu.yearNote: The construction of the Sanqing Tower and the Offering Tower in about the Zhengde period is used as the sorting point; the dates 1516 and 1519 in stele records and sources each refer to different things, and 1519 is not forced to stand as the completion year of every component drawn.
sx_jiexiu_houtu.lede: Jiexiu's Houtu Temple stacks hall, stage and tower into one building: the lower floor of the Sanqing Tower is the Sanqing Hall, the upper floor is wrapped by a gallery on three sides, and the back is a stage facing the Houtu Great Hall, thirteen metres high, the tallest surviving Ming theatre stage; the double-eaved splayed screen walls on either side were forced up to match, with a brick eave below and a timber eave above. The Jiexiu heritage office records its founding in 1519 (14th year of Zhengde, Ming), and every roof in the temple is glazed, five-coloured except for the yellow of the Houtu Hall group; here glazed tile is not trim but the main event. The plate shows the stage on the north face of the Sanqing Tower with its splayed screen walls.
facts: Sanqing Tower: two storeys under three tiers of hip-and-gable eaves, 15.2 m high overall, with a two-storey, triple-eaved cross-ridged porch projecting in front to join the offering hall; the stage at the back is 13 m high, its lower level barely tall enough to stand in; the splayed screen walls on either side have double gable eaves, carved brick below and timber above, their bargeboards decorated with purple-and-white glazed "mice stealing grapes".

Dating: the Jiexiu heritage office dates the founding of the Sanqing Tower to 1519 (14th year of Zhengde, Ming); the restoration of 1516 (11th year of Zhengde) absorbed the Zhenwu Hall and Sanguan Shrine, the Earth God Temple of 1730 (8th year of Yongzheng, Qing) completed the layout of eight linked temples, and repairs followed in 1835 (15th year of Daoguang).

Glazed tile: all 29 buildings are roofed in glazed tile, the Houtu Hall group in yellow and the rest in yellow, green, blue, white and ochre, mostly replaced in Qing repairs, while a few Song tiles survive on the Sanqing Tower; the more than a thousand Ming Daoist painted statues inside are equally rare.
captions: Houtu Temple, Jiexiu · North stage of the Sanqing Tower
Ming–Qing · Stage and splayed screen walls

tiefo.name: Iron Buddha Temple, Gaoping
tiefo.era: Restored in the 1st year of Jiajing
tiefo.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Mishan Town · Mixi Village
tiefo.lede: In the lanes of Mixi Village, the three-bay main hall of the Iron Buddha Temple is finished with an overhanging gable roof and glazed ridge ornaments. Step inside and the Twenty-Four Devas unfold along the walls — glaring, smiling, eyes lowered — their beards, hair and streamers held out on iron wire, giving the clay figures expressions on the verge of movement.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof. The front-eave bracket sets are five-tiered (wucai) with double cantilevers (ang), and a glazed ornament of a lion bearing a treasure vase stands at the center of the ridge.

The Ming painted clay figures of the Twenty-Four Devas inside the hall are modeled in clay over wooden armatures; their beards, hair, headdresses and streamers are shaped with iron wire, making the details light yet full of tension.

The founding date is unknown. In the 7th year of Dading in the Jin (1167) an iron Buddha was cast and the temple restored; it was repaired again in the 1st year of Jiajing (1522) and the 3rd year of Wanli (1575) in the Ming, and in the Qing. The surviving buildings show a Ming–Qing style.
captions: Main hall line drawing · Three bays wide
Single-eaved overhanging gable roof · Ming

feihong.name: Feihong Pagoda of Guangsheng Temple
feihong.era: Begun in the 10th year of Zhengde · Completed in the 6th year of Jiajing
feihong.lede: Between 1515 and 1527 (10th year of Zhengde to 6th year of Jiajing, Ming) the monk Dalian raised funds for over a decade and set this brick pagoda, octagonal, thirteen storeys and over forty-seven metres high, at the very front of the axis of the Upper Temple on Mount Huo. Its outer skin, from eaves and bracket sets to Buddhas, guardians and coiling dragons, is entirely fired glaze in red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet, making it the largest and most complete glazed pagoda surviving in China. It stands on the site of a Yuan predecessor and later rode out the great earthquakes of 1556 in Guanzhong and 1695 in Pingyang. The plate shows the whole Feihong Pagoda.
facts: Body: octagonal in plan, thirteen storeys, 47.31 m high overall (47.6 m in another source), tapering sharply into a cone; the core is brick and stone, and on every storey the eaves, bracket sets, niches, figures and coiling dragons are glazed components in red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

Dating: rebuilt on the Yuan site from 1515 (10th year of Zhengde, Ming) with funds raised by the eminent monk Dalian and completed in 1527 (6th year of Jiajing); it then survived unharmed the Guanzhong earthquake of 1556 (35th year of Jiajing) and the Pingyang earthquake of 1695 (34th year of Kangxi).

Connections: Guangsheng Temple was listed among the first batch of national key protected sites in 1961; the Yuan murals of the Lower Temple were sold in 1928 and are now divided among three American museums; the "Tang monk sweeps the pagoda" episode of the 1986 television series Journey to the West was filmed here.
captions: Line drawing · Octagonal, thirteen stories
Glazed tile · First-story gallery

hb_xianling.name: Ming Xianling Mausoleum
hb_xianling.sub: Lingxing Gate · Dragon and Phoenix Gate
hb_xianling.yearNote: The surviving Lingxing Gate belongs to the Ming stone remains of the Xianling; 1540 is only a broad sorting point within the Jiajing period, not the exact completion year of this stone archway. Only the stone archway and its linked glazed screen walls are drawn; the stele tower (minglou) restored in 1990 is not drawn, and the founding year of the imperial tomb is not applied to all of its buildings.
hb_xianling.lede: Stone columns raise three gateways, with yellow-glazed screen walls filling the spaces between them. The roof-like stone tops step back to either side, and the central gate opens onto the spirit way, leaving the clearest outline of the mausoleum.
facts: Subject: the stone archway of the Lingxing Gate of the Ming Xianling Mausoleum and its linked glazed screen walls.

Dating: the surviving Lingxing Gate belongs to the Ming stone remains of the Xianling; 1540 is only a broad sorting point within the Jiajing period, not the exact completion year of this stone archway. Only the stone archway and its linked glazed screen walls are drawn; the stele tower (minglou) restored in 1990 is not drawn, and the founding year of the imperial tomb is not applied to all of its buildings.

Plate scope: the Lingxing Gate with three openings, six columns and four roofed tops; the stone columns rising above the gate at the center and sides, with hou beasts and jewels; and the linked yellow-glazed screen walls. The stone civil-official statues in front, the full spirit way and the restored stele tower are not included.

taimiao.name: Imperial Ancestral Temple, Beijing
taimiao.lede: The Sacrificial Hall of the Imperial Ancestral Temple spreads its eleven-bay eaves over a three-tier white stone base. Here the emperors once performed rites to their ancestors; massive nanmu columns and a double-eaved hipped roof together hold up this solemn ancestral space.
facts: The Imperial Ancestral Temple was first built in the 18th year of Yongle (1420); this entry follows the date of the Sacrificial Hall's rebuilding in the 24th year of Jiajing (1545).
The Sacrificial Hall is eleven bays wide and six bays deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof of yellow glazed tiles.
The hall stands on a three-tier white marble Sumeru plinth, and its interior preserves sixty-eight columns, each made from a single nanmu trunk.

fuzhoubaita.name: White Pagoda, Fuzhou
fuzhoubaita.lede: The Black Pagoda is stone; the White Pagoda is brick. In 904 Wang Shenzhi built the Bao'en Dingguang Duobao Pagoda at the western foot of Yushan to earn merit for his parents, originally a seven-storey tower with a brick core and timber galleries. Struck by lightning and burnt in 1534, it was rebuilt in 1548, when the brick core was simply made the body of the pagoda itself, coated in white lime, octagonal and seven storeys high with a gourd-shaped finial. The clean, plain silhouette seen today is the Ming rebuilding.
facts: Form: an octagonal seven-storey pavilion-style brick pagoda, 41 m high, with plain white-limed walls and a gourd finial; the brick core contains a hanging-post spiral stair to the top. In 1963, while the surroundings were cleared, fifteen Tang-dynasty carved bluestone panels from a Sumeru-base waist were unearthed, with sea legends, lions and peonies, and are now set up on the spot.

History: the Shiguo Chunqiu records that in 904 Wang Shenzhi built the pagoda for his late parents; the original had a brick core with timber work outside. It was destroyed by lightning fire in 1534 and rebuilt as the present pagoda in 1548; the stair was replaced in a 1958 repair, and in 1991 it was listed as a Fujian provincial protected site.

Counterpart: it faces the Five Dynasties Black Pagoda at the eastern foot of Wushan across the old city; together they are the 'Three Hills and Two Pagodas' that have marked Fuzhou for a millennium, and the pairing of stone with brick, black with white, shows the different materials and methods of Five Dynasties and Ming pagoda building.
captions: White Pagoda, Fuzhou · Dingguang Pagoda
Seven stories, octagonal · Ming rebuilding

sx_haihui.name: Twin Pagodas of Haihui Temple, Yangcheng
sx_haihui.sub: Hexagonal brick pagoda · Octagonal glazed pagoda
sx_haihui.yearNote: 1565 is only a sorting point for the construction period of the large Ming pagoda; sources give either 1561 or 1565–1568. The small pagoda was founded in the Five Dynasties and altered in the Song; the two pagodas were not built in the same year.
sx_haihui.place: Shanxi · Yangcheng · Pagoda courtyard of Haihui Temple, Daqiao Village
sx_haihui.lede: Two pagodas stand one behind the other, six centuries apart: the small one in front, hexagonal and ten storeys, is the relic pagoda built for the Chan master Shunmin in 922 (2nd year of Longde, Later Liang), studded with little niches and leaning slightly west; the great one behind, octagonal, thirteen storeys and about fifty-seven metres high, was built between 1565 and 1568 (Jiajing to Longqing reigns, Ming) with over two thousand taels of silver donated by the merchant Li Sixiao, its lowest three storeys wrapped in a battlemented wall like a castle while the tenth storey throws out a ring of glazed hanging galleries. Among the storeyed pagodas of north China there is no second example. The plate shows both pagodas together.
facts: Two pagodas: the small pagoda is grey brick, hexagonal, ten storeys with corbelled eaves, about 20 m high, its outer walls covered with Buddha niches; the great pagoda is octagonal, thirteen storeys and about 57 m high, its bottom three storeys enclosed by a battlemented masonry wall, and at the tenth storey a glazed balcony gallery projects, three bays to a side, twenty-four in all, with glazed columns, balustrades and brackets.

Dating: the stele "Later Record of Longquan Chan Cloister" of 956 (3rd year of Xiande, Later Zhou) in the temple dates the small pagoda to 922 (2nd year of Longde, Later Liang); the stele by Wang Guoguang, Ming Minister of Rites, "Record of Rebuilding the Precious Pagoda and Buddha Hall of Longquan Temple", dates the great pagoda to the Jiajing-Longqing years 1565 to 1568, with another view favouring 1561 (40th year of Jiajing).

Assessment: the great pagoda is also called the Glazed Pagoda for its glazed eave edges and galleries, and Zhang Yuhuan ranked it "the crown of the famous pagodas of Shangdang"; the temple housed the Haihui Academy in the Ming and Qing, was among the first provincial protected sites of Shanxi in 1965, and became a national key protected site together with the pagodas in 2006.
captions: Haihui Temple · Small brick pagoda and large glazed pagoda

gx_zhenwu.name: Zhenwu Pavilion on the Jinglue Terrace
gx_zhenwu.sub: Timber pavilion of Rong County · Triple eaves
gx_zhenwu.yearNote: 1573 is taken as the construction date of the Zhenwu Pavilion; the earlier history of the Jinglue Terrace is listed separately from the surviving pavilion, and later repairs do not amount to rebuilding the whole pavilion.
gx_zhenwu.lede: Three tiers of eaves reach outward, the timber columns of the lower level stand open, and the pavilion sits firmly on the Jinglue Terrace. The way its timber members carry one another is more intriguing than the height of its stories.
facts: Subject: the complete Zhenwu Pavilion on the Jinglue Terrace.

guanyintang.name: Guanyin Hall, Changzhi
guanyintang.lede: A small hall of three bays whose walls, roof frame and the spaces above doors and windows are entirely taken over by sculpture: Guanyin sits in the centre with Manjusri and Samantabhadra at her sides, celestial palaces rise tier upon tier behind her, the Eighteen Arhats, Twenty-four Devas and Twelve Bodhisattvas of Perfect Enlightenment ring the room in layers, and on the top tier the south wall carries Daoist immortals, the north wall Confucian worthies, so that Sakyamuni, Laozi and Confucius share one hall. Over five hundred suspended clay figures of around 1582 (10th year of Wanli, Ming) turn the belief in the unity of the three teachings into a visible world. The plate takes the central Guanyin and part of the celestial palaces and does not stand for the whole hall.
facts: Main hall: three bays wide and four rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof covered in yellow and green glazed tile with coiling-dragon and passion-flower patterns; inside are more than five hundred Ming suspended clay figures, gilded and painted, arranged in tiers on the walls, roof frame and upper parts of doors and windows.

Dating: the Guanyin Hall was built in 1582 (10th year of Wanli, Ming) and repaired in the Qing; the name board was written in 1583 (11th year of Wanli) by Gao Qin, Vice Minister of War; the temple faces west with two courtyards over 7,400 square metres, the main hall Ming and the rest Qing.

Subjects: the altar holds Guanyin, Manjusri and Samantabhadra, the rear wall shows the life of the Buddha, the sides carry the Eighteen Arhats, Twenty-four Devas and Twelve Bodhisattvas of Perfect Enlightenment, and the fourth tier has Daoist figures on the south wall and Confucian ones on the north, with Sakyamuni in the middle and Laozi and Confucius to either side, a physical record of the merging of the three teachings in a village temple.
captions: Guanyin Hall, Changzhi · Detail of Guanyin and the suspended heavenly-palace sculpture
Wanli reign, Ming · Painted and suspended sculpture

xuankong.name: Hanging Temple, Hunyuan
xuankong.sub: Pavilions on a sheer cliff · Unity of the Three Teachings
xuankong.place: Shanxi · Hunyuan · Jinlong Gorge, Mount Heng
xuankong.lede: The whole temple hangs in a recess halfway up Cuiping Mountain, its highest point more than ninety metres above the valley floor. It looks as if dozens of slender timber posts hold it up, but the real load is carried by twenty-seven beams driven into the rock; most of the posts are little more than reassurance. The north and south flying pavilions, three storeys and over ten metres high, float free on three sides and are linked by two plank walks wide enough for one person; the Three Teachings Hall on the top floor of the north pavilion seats Sakyamuni, Confucius and Laozi together. A Northern Wei founding has long been claimed, yet the surviving forty bays of timber work are all products of Ming and Qing rebuilding. The plate shows the two pavilions and the walkways between them.
facts: Structure: 27 timber beams about 50 cm in diameter, soaked in tung oil, are bedded under the temple, one end tenoned into the rock and the other carrying the buildings and projecting about 1 m to support the walkways; the temple has 40 bays and 152.5 square metres of timber building, the two flying pavilions each three storeys with nine-ridged roofs and posts more than ten metres long on the outer side.

History: one account has Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei found it in 491 (15th year of Taihe) to relocate the Celestial Masters' Daoist seat, another gives 398 (1st year of Tianxing); it was repaired in the Jin, Ming and the Tongzhi reign of the Qing, and most existing buildings are Ming and Qing rebuildings; the 1978 overhaul that replaced load-bearing beams reconfirmed the cantilevered-beam system.

Three teachings: the upper floor of the main hall holds the Three Buddhas Hall, Taiyi Hall and Guandi Temple; the south pavilion rises through the Chunyang Palace, Sanguan Hall and Leiyin Hall, the north pavilion through the Four Buddhas Hall, Three Sages Hall and Three Teachings Hall, where Sakyamuni, Confucius and Laozi share one shrine; the temple became a national key protected site in 1982.
captions: Hanging Temple · Cliffside building group
Ming–Qing structures · North and south towers and suspended walkway

hn_bigan.name: Temple of Bi Gan
hn_bigan.sub: Memorial to loyal remonstrance, with temple and tomb joined
hn_bigan.yearNote: 1600 is only an approximate sorting point for the Ming–Qing structures. The expansion in the 7th year of Hongzhi in the Ming (1494) belongs to the history of the temple complex and is not taken directly as the construction year of every component of the front of the Sacrificial Hall drawn here.
hn_bigan.lede: The Temple of Bi Gan commemorates the loyal Shang-dynasty minister Bi Gan in a layout that joins temple and tomb. The surviving buildings took shape mainly in the Ming and Qing, and the front of the Sacrificial Hall spreads its five-bay facade among ancient cypresses.
facts: Surviving Ming–Qing fabric: the history of the temple complex can be traced to the Northern Wei; the surviving buildings were rebuilt and repaired in the Ming and Qing, and the period of the person commemorated cannot be taken as the date of the buildings.
Temple in front, tomb behind: the central axis runs from the gate through the stele gallery and the Sacrificial Hall to the burial mound at the rear, forming a layout that combines temple and tomb.
Detail of the Sacrificial Hall: the hall is five bays wide and three bays deep; the plate draws the front facade identifiable in photographs and does not invent the roof hidden behind the trees.

hb_wahuang.name: Wahuang Palace and Stone Carvings
hb_wahuang.sub: Front of the cliff-hugging Wahuang Pavilion
hb_wahuang.yearNote: The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau lists the Wahuang Pavilion and other buildings on the mountain as Ming–Qing remains; Handan cultural tourism sources record that a three-story timber pavilion was added on the stone vault in the Ming. 1600 is used only as an approximate sorting value for the Ming–Qing pavilion, and the pavilion is not dated by the year of the Northern Qi carved sutras.
hb_wahuang.lede: The Wahuang Pavilion stands against the cliff of Mount Fenghuang in She County. A three-story timber pavilion is stacked on a grotto and stone vault, its tiers of eaves hugging the slope of the mountain; Northern Qi carved sutras and Ming–Qing architecture lie side by side here.
facts: Surviving date: the pavilion in the drawing is recorded as a Ming–Qing structure; the Northern Qi cliff-carved sutras around it are earlier, and the two are not merged into a single construction date.

Four levels: at the bottom a stone vault fronts a natural cave, with a three-story timber pavilion set above, forming a four-level main structure; the plate shows the visible pavilion facade and the front gallery of the lower level.

Composition: based on 2025 photographs, the drawing shows the cliff-hugging front and the terrace just before it, omits the neighboring pavilions that block the view, and does not reconstruct the unseen rear or a section through the high platform.

im_dazhao.era: Founded in the Ming · Altered in the Qing
im_dazhao.yearNote: 1600 is only an approximate sorting point for the Ming–Qing main structure and does not claim an exact completion year for the Mahavira Hall; the temple was completed in 1580, and the Qing expansion and the relaying of yellow glazed tiles are recorded separately.
im_dazhao.lede: In the old city of Hohhot, Da Zhao joins a Tibetan Buddhist assembly hall and Chinese-style halls into a single whole. The temple is named for its silver Buddha, and its surviving buildings also bear the layers of Qing alterations. The plate draws only the Mahavira Hall and does not compress the whole monastery into a single gate.
facts: Temple history: built under the direction of Altan Khan in the Ming and completed in 1580; it was altered repeatedly in the Qing.

sn_chongwen.name: Chongwen Pagoda, Jingyang
sn_chongwen.yearNote: According to the Record of the Permanent Fields Endowed for the Community of the Iron Buddha Chongwen Pagoda Temple, as cited in published reports, construction began in 1591 and was completed in 1608; other accounts give different dates. This drawing follows present-day photographs and does not add the earlier finial.
sn_chongwen.lede: The octagonal brick body is stacked high, its eaves stepping inward as they rise. Chongwen Pagoda stands in Jingyang, where the Ming construction records meet the brick pagoda as it appears today.
facts: Construction: the dates 1591–1608 given in the stele record are adopted; accounts over the years give different dates, and the source records keep these differences.
Form: an octagonal, thirteen-story, pavilion-style brick pagoda, with arched doorways and niche openings arranged story by story.

sx_yongzuo.name: Twin Pagodas of Yongzuo Temple, Taiyuan
sx_yongzuo.yearNote: 1612 is only an approximate sorting point for the period in which the twin pagodas took shape; the two were built one after the other, and this year is not given as the founding year of both.
sx_yongzuo.lede: On the high ground southeast of Taiyuan two thirteen-storey brick pagodas stand shoulder to shoulder, forty-six metres apart and both around fifty-four metres tall, the tallest pair of twin pagodas surviving in China. The east pagoda, Wenfeng Pagoda, came first, built in 1599 (27th year of Wanli, Ming) under Fu Lin and his son Fu Zhimo as a geomantic tower to mend the city's literary fortunes; the west pagoda, Xuanwen Pagoda, followed more than a decade later, completed in 1612 (40th year of Wanli) for the Prince of Jin by the eminent Wutai monk Miaofeng, its eaves edged entirely in peacock-blue glaze and named for the honorific title of the Wanli emperor's mother. The plate shows both pagodas, each with its own finial and taper.
facts: Twin pagodas: both are octagonal thirteen-storey brick pagodas of storeyed type, hollow double-shell structures with spiral stairs inside; the west Xuanwen Pagoda is 54.78 m high and the east Wenfeng Pagoda 53.3 m, 46 m apart, and all thirteen eaves of the Xuanwen Pagoda are edged with peacock-blue glazed tile.

Dating: Yongming Temple was founded in 1597 (25th year of Wanli, Ming) and the east pagoda finished in 1599; in 1608 (36th year of Wanli) Zhu Minchun, Prince of Jin, invited the Chan master Miaofeng to enlarge it, and in 1612 (40th year) the west pagoda and the beamless brick hall were completed and the temple renamed Yongzuo; additions in the Shunzhi and Kangxi reigns of the Qing gave it its present form.

Conservation: the east pagoda once leaned 2.87 m and was righted and strengthened in 1995 to 1996, the west pagoda was strengthened in 1981 to 1984, and only the west pagoda is now open to climb; the pair has been the emblem of Taiyuan since 1985, and the temple also keeps a Ming beamless brick hall and more than 260 stone steles.

hn_luwang.short: Tomb of the Prince of Lu
hn_luwang.yearNote: 1615 is only an approximate sorting point for the tomb's construction phase in the late Wanli reign; the conversion error found online, “the 40th year of Wanli (1615),” is not carried over as the exact construction year of the stone archway.

Fine dragon patterns are carved into the heavy stone, preserving at the foot of the mountain the ceremonial order of a Ming princely tomb.

rulong.name: Rulong Bridge
rulong.yearNote: According to the county gazetteer it was built in 1625; later repairs do not mean that every component of the bridge is original Ming fabric.
rulong.lede: A long gallery spans the stream, a tall tower lifts its ridge at the bridgehead, and the timber arch traces a broad angular line beneath the board siding. Rulong Bridge joins the road across the stream with a gallery where people can linger; it is the Ming timber-arch covered bridge of Yueshan Village.
facts: Built in the Tianqi reign: the county gazetteer records that Rulong Bridge was built in the 5th year of Tianqi in the Ming (1625); it is one of the surviving Ming timber-arch covered bridges in Qingyuan.

Timber arch structure: the bridge spans the stream on a timber arch frame, its ends resting on masonry abutments; protective boards shield the arch frame, and the gallery shelters travelers from wind and rain.

Staggered heights: the bell tower at the north end, with a triple-eaved hip-and-gable roof, rises high and, together with the central roof and the south entrance, forms a layered outline along the long bridge.

ln_dazheng.sub: Octagonal hall with double-eaved pyramidal roof
ln_dazheng.yearNote: 1625 is an approximate sorting point for the early Qing construction; the construction span of the whole palace complex is not taken as the exact completion year of this single hall.
ln_dazheng.lede: An octagonal hall body and a two-tier pyramidal roof gather an early Qing court space for deliberating state affairs beneath yellow tiles. The coiling-dragon columns and red doors and windows on the front are drawn as they look today, without shrinking the whole palace into a single-hall drawing.

quanzhoukaiyuan.name: Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou
quanzhoukaiyuan.sub: Mahavira Hall · Hall of a Hundred Columns
quanzhoukaiyuan.era: Ming · Restored in the 10th year of Chongzhen
quanzhoukaiyuan.lede: Nine bays across the front under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof: the highest grade of Buddhist hall in China. The hall should hold a hundred stone columns, but to make room for the huge Five Buddhas and the worship space two rows of fourteen were omitted, leaving eighty-six, and the name 'Hall of a Hundred Columns' stuck anyway. More remarkable still are the twenty-four bracket sets carved as celestial musicians, kalavinka with human bodies, feathered wings and bird legs, holding instruments or scholars' implements: structural members that carry the beams and at the same time a scene of music before the Buddha. The present form dates from the rebuilding of 1637 by the general Zheng Zhilong and others.
facts: Form: nine bays wide and six deep, about 1,388 square metres in area, with a double-eave hip-and-gable roof about 20 m high; a palatial-type frame with two rows of 14 columns omitted in the middle, leaving 86 stone columns and 76 bracket sets; where the two central rows of stone columns meet the beams, the brackets are carved as 24 flying musicians.

History: founded in 686 (second year of Chuigong, Tang); the present plan and frame proportions largely follow the rebuilding of 1155 in the Southern Song, the outer eaves were extended in 1389, and the hall was rebuilt to its present state in 1637 by the general Zheng Zhilong and others. The Sumeru base of the terrace in front carries 73 panels of lions and sphinx-like figures, moved here during the Ming rebuilding from a Hindu temple abandoned at the end of the Yuan.

Plurality: the hall enshrines the Five Buddhas of esoteric Buddhism, each 6 m high; two Hindu stone columns under the rear gallery eaves were also reused in the 1637 rebuilding, nine of their 24 medallions showing Vishnu, Krishna and other myths. That a Buddhist hall was rebuilt with Hindu members is the most tangible evidence of the port's mixed cultures.
captions: Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou · Mahavira Hall
Restored in the 10th year of Chongzhen, Ming · Nine-bay Hall of a Hundred Columns

xiaoxitian.name: Xiaoxitian, Xi County
xiaoxitian.sub: Hall filled with suspended sculpture · Thousand Buddha Hermitage
xiaoxitian.lede: The Mahavira Hall is under one hundred and seventy square metres, yet nearly two thousand painted figures are packed into it: celestial palaces rise tier upon tier above the main Buddha, twelve musician bodhisattvas dance on the balustraded platform in front, human-faced apsaras and divine birds perch on clouds, the largest over three metres, the smallest no bigger than a thumb. All are clay, gilded and painted, suspended between roof frame and walls, begun in the Chongzhen reign at the end of the Ming and finished under Shunzhi in the early Qing. Qianfo Nunnery itself covers barely eleven hundred square metres, two thirds of its halls built in two storeys with cave-like openings for doors. The plate takes the central shrine and part of the celestial palaces and does not stand for the whole hall.
facts: Mahavira Hall: five bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, interior under 170 square metres; nearly two thousand suspended figures are arranged in tiers on the roof frame, walls and shrines, the largest over 3 m high and the smallest able to sit in a palm.

Dating: Qianfo Nunnery was founded at the end of the Ming by the Chan master Dongming; the suspended sculpture of the Mahavira Hall was begun in the Chongzhen reign and completed in the Shunzhi reign of the Qing, about thirty years in all; the temple faces east on the hillside in an upper and a lower court, and became a national key protected site in 1996.

Layout: the whole temple has little over 1,100 square metres of building, two thirds of its halls in two storeys, with cave-like doorways dividing the upper, middle and front courts; the upper court holds the Mahavira, Manjusri and Samantabhadra halls, the lower court the Wuliang Hall, Weituo Hall, Moyun Pavilion and the bell and drum towers.

tj_wenmiao.lede: Beneath orange-yellow glazed tiles, blue-green painted decoration and dark red doors and windows frame the entrance to the Dacheng Hall. The plate focuses on the central facade, the incense burner and the stone ceremonial stair; it is explicitly a detail and does not use close-up photographs to invent the unseen full hall.
facts: The Tianjin Confucian Temple was founded in 1436 and preserves a layout in which the prefectural temple, the county temple and the school stand side by side; this drawing takes the central part of the prefectural temple's Dacheng Hall.

The plate shows the three central bays of the facade beneath the eaves, the incense burner and the ceremonial stair; it does not represent the hall's full number of bays or the layout of the whole temple.

The colors of the present yellow glazed tiles, blue-green painted decoration, dark red timberwork and light gray stone terrace are taken from photographs; modern repairs and the original founding are described separately.

xianshen.name: Xianshen Tower, Jiexiu
xianshen.sub: Street-spanning tower and music tower · Composite pavilion
xianshen.era: Qing · Late Shunzhi to early Kangxi
xianshen.lede: One building does three jobs: the street runs beneath it, making it the over-street tower of Shuncheng Gate Street; one floor up it is the gate of the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers; above that a five-bay theatre stage faces back to the north, the whole stacking into a four-storey silhouette. It is also the only surviving building in China linked to Zoroastrianism, the carved bull-headed and camel-headed beasts under its eaves read by Jiang Boqin as incarnations of Zoroastrian deities. Tradition credits the temple to Wen Yanbo of the Northern Song; it burned in the early Qing, and the present tower is a rebuilding of 1660 to 1668 (late Shunzhi to early Kangxi), with an inscription of 1667 (6th year of Kangxi) under the finial of the music hall ridge. The plate shows the over-street tower and the music hall.
facts: Form: the plan is T-shaped, about 20 m deep in all; the over-street tower at the front and the porch before the stage are each three bays square, the stage block behind is five bays wide and four deep with a surrounding gallery; the lower floor is the gate, the upper floor the stage, and with the music hall and double eaves it rises four storeys.

Dating: the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers burned in the early Qing and was rebuilt from 1660 (17th year of Shunzhi) to 1668 (7th year of Kangxi), with an inscription of 1667 (6th year of Kangxi) under the vase finial of the music hall ridge and an offering pavilion added in 1786 (51st year of Qianlong); in 1985 the over-street tower was jacked up 1.5 m as a whole and the restoration was completed in 1987.

Zoroastrian link: the stele record says Duke Wen Lu (Wen Yanbo) of the Song built the temple for the Xian god, and a Jiajing-era magistrate of the Ming turned it into the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers; Jiang Boqin judged from the bull- and camel-headed carvings under the eaves that it is the remnant of a Zoroastrian shrine, and Chen Mingda's 1951 survey already called its artistry outstanding and warned against dismissing it for its late date.
captions: Xianshen Tower, Jiexiu · Street-spanning tower and music tower

gz_wenchang.name: Wenchang Pavilion, Guiyang
gz_wenchang.sub: East of the old city · Three stories, three eaves
gz_wenchang.era: Rebuilt in the 8th year of Kangxi
gz_wenchang.yearNote: First built in 1609; the entry is placed according to the surviving pavilion formed by the 1669 rebuilding and later repairs, as given in official Guiyang municipal sources, and the founding year is not substituted for the surviving main structure.
gz_wenchang.lede: The Wenchang Pavilion rises from the eastern part of Guiyang's old city, yet its three-story, triple-eaved roof is neither the usual four-cornered nor eight-cornered form. Its nine-cornered outline is its identifying feature; the Ming founding, the Qing rebuilding and repeated repairs together shaped the pavilion seen today.
facts: Dates: first built in the 37th year of Wanli in the Ming (1609), rebuilt in the 8th year of Kangxi in the Qing (1669), and repaired many times since.
Form: three stories, triple eaves and a nine-cornered roof; the plate does not mix the adjacent city gate tower into the Wenchang Pavilion.
Dating: this guide places it by the surviving rebuilding phase, with the founding date explained separately.

yn_jindian.name: Golden Hall, Kunming
yn_jindian.era: Recast in the 10th year of Kangxi
yn_jindian.yearNote: The surviving bronze hall drawn here was rebuilt by Wu Sangui in 1671; the bronze hall first built in 1602 and its relocation are recorded separately, and the Golden Hall of the Wudang Mountains is not mistakenly used as a reference.
yn_jindian.lede: From afar it looks like a timber hall; only up close does one find that the roof, columns, beams, doors and windows are all cast in bronze. The surviving Golden Hall on Mount Mingfeng was built in the 10th year of Kangxi; the bronze has darkened through wind and rain, yet the metal structure still keeps the details of a traditional hall.
facts: Surviving subject: the bronze hall rebuilt by Wu Sangui in the 10th year of Kangxi in the Qing (1671).

Distinguishing its history: the bronze hall first built in the 30th year of Wanli in the Ming (1602) was later moved away, and its date is not taken as the construction year of the bronze hall seen today.

hb_qingdongling.name: Eastern Qing Tombs
hb_qingdongling.sub: Stone memorial archway on the Xiaoling spirit way
hb_qingdongling.yearNote: The date 1672 is adopted for the stone archway drawn here: Wang Qiheng, on the basis of the Xiaoling drawings and the archives on the transport of stone, established that the components were transported at the end of 1671 and the archway completed in early 1672. The early main works of the Xiaoling in 1663–1664 and the traditionally recorded ancillary works of 1668 are not used as the date of this stone archway.
hb_qingdongling.lede: The five-bay, six-column, eleven-roof stone memorial archway stands at the southern end of the Xiaoling spirit way, opening the ceremonial sequence of the Eastern Qing Tombs with a run of stone roofs at staggered heights.
facts: Construction: the architectural historian Wang Qiheng established from archival records that the stone archway was completed early in the 11th year of Kangxi (1672).
Form: five bays, six stone columns and eleven roofed tops at staggered heights make up a complete stone archway imitating timber construction.

Scope of the entry: the whole Eastern Qing Tombs area forms a single record; this drawing takes the stone archway on the Xiaoling spirit way as representative and does not split the entry into the individual imperial tombs.

sd_mengmiao.name: Yasheng Hall of the Mencius Temple, Zoucheng
sd_mengmiao.sub: Seven bays, double-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Green glazed tiles
sd_mengmiao.era: Rebuilt in the 12th year of Kangxi, later repaired
sd_mengmiao.yearNote: The surviving hall is placed at 1673, when it was rebuilt five years after the earthquake damage of 1668; the comprehensive repair of 1736 and modern renovations are described separately. It is not the original fabric of the hall first built in the Northern Song.
sd_mengmiao.lede: Double green eaves spread over the seven-bay hall, and stone columns alternate with vermilion doors beneath them. Rebuilt in the Qing after an earthquake, the Yasheng Hall of the Mencius Temple remains the center of the worship of Mencius in Zoucheng.
facts: History: an earthquake in 1668 damaged the main hall, which was rebuilt five years later; it underwent a comprehensive repair in 1736, and its present state also reflects modern renovation.
Form: seven bays wide, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof covered in green glazed tiles; stone columns on the outer eaves and timberwork on the inner eaves together support the hall.

Identifying the subject: the drawing shows the Yasheng Hall of the Mencius Temple, not the main hall of the adjoining Mencius Family Mansion, and it is not to be confused with the Dacheng Hall of the Temple of Confucius in Qufu.

daimiao.name: Tiankuang Hall of the Dai Temple
daimiao.lede: At the foot of Mount Tai, the Tiankuang Hall spreads two broad tiers of eaves to the scale of the rites to the sacred mountain. From its founding in the Song to its Qing restoration, its beam frame, doors, windows and murals layer the memories of different periods.
facts: The Tiankuang Hall is the main hall of the Dai Temple, dedicated to the god of Mount Tai; founded in the Song, it has been repaired many times since.
The hall is nine bays wide and five bays deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof covered in yellow glazed tiles.
The proportions and construction methods of the surviving timber frame show Qing characteristics, and the murals inside the hall were repainted in the early Qing.

A Kangxi-era stele records that the restoration was completed in 1677, keeping the usable beams and columns of the hall and replacing damaged members; the timeline places it approximately on this basis, with later repairs counted separately.

gugong.name: Forbidden City, Beijing
gugong.lede: The Hall of Supreme Harmony stands on a three-tier white marble base, commanding the Outer Court with its eleven-bay width and double-eaved hipped roof. Broad ceremonial stairs lift the hall on high; its present form comes from the rebuilding of the Kangxi reign.
facts: Work on the surviving Hall of Supreme Harmony began in the 34th year of Kangxi (1695) and was completed in the 36th year (1697).
Eleven bays wide and five bays deep, it is the foremost of the three great halls of the Outer Court of the Forbidden City.

The roof is a double-eaved hipped roof, with the number of ridge beasts on the eave corners increased to ten; important ceremonies such as enthronements and imperial weddings were once held in the hall.

mimi.name: Mimi Temple, Fanshi
mimi.place: Shanxi · Fanshi · Yantou Township · Mimo Cliff
mimi.lede: Thirty-eight kilometres southwest of Taihuai on Mount Wutai, this temple below Mimo Cliff on Mount Weiping was once the place of the saying that to visit Wutai without the Dragon Cave was to see only half the mountain. Tradition takes it back to the Northern Qi; the Tang monk Mucha retreated and built here, and it flourished in the Tang and Song, leaving outside the walls the Tang-founded, Ming-repaired pagoda of Patriarch Mucha and the pagoda of Master Xuanjue of 963 (7th year of Tianhui, Northern Han). The halls themselves are Qing rebuildings, the main halls of the front and middle courts both five bays wide. The plate shows the front of the Manjusri Hall: five bays with a front porch, a central stair climbing to the raised platform, and Qing paintings surviving on the porch panels and inside.
facts: Manjusri Hall: as drawn, five bays wide with a front porch under a flush-gable (yingshan) roof, standing on a raised platform reached by a central stone stair; in the temple the main halls of the front and middle courts are both five bays, the north and south sutra lofts five bays each, and only a five-bay north pavilion survives in the rear court.

Dating: the Qingliang Shan Gazetteer records that the Tang monk Mucha founded the temple while in retreat at Mimi Cliff, and another account has a Northern Qi nun's hermitage before it; of thirty-two hermitages once here the front, middle and rear courts and the West and Middle hermitages remain; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Qing, and it became a national key protected site in 2006.

Stonework: before the temple stand a Jin-dynasty stone pillar and two brick pagodas, the pagoda of Patriarch Mucha, Tang-founded and Ming-repaired, hexagonal, four storeys and about 10 m high, and the pagoda of Master Xuanjue of 963 (7th year of Tianhui, Northern Han), hexagonal and two storeys; the Golden Buddha Loft in the Middle Hermitage holds a stone Amitabha about 7 m high carved in 1535 (14th year of Jiajing, Ming).
captions: Mimi Temple · Front of the Manjushri Hall

hn_kangbaiwan.name: Kang Baiwan Manor
hn_kangbaiwan.era: Late Ming–early Qing · Extended over generations
hn_kangbaiwan.yearNote: The Zhengzhou Municipal Bureau of Cultural Heritage dates the manor as a whole to the late Ming–early Qing, with continued construction in later periods. 1700 is only an approximate sorting point for the manor's Ming–Qing structures; the storied cave dwelling shown in the photographs has as yet no exact construction date of its own, and neither the Kang family's move here nor any individual's life dates are used as the date of the building.
hn_kangbaiwan.lede: The facade of a storied cave dwelling and the buildings on either side enclose a long, deep inner courtyard. Kang Baiwan Manor combines caves dug into the cliff with siheyuan courtyard houses, preserving the living spaces of a merchant family of the Heluo region.
facts: Date of the manor: the Zhengzhou Municipal Bureau of Cultural Heritage dates the manor to the late Ming–early Qing; it was built up over many generations of the Kang family, and the surviving courtyards were not completed in the same year.
Local form: the manor has cave dwellings dug against the cliff and storied buildings along the street, with residential courtyards laid out as siheyuan, combining timber, brick and stone elements.

Plate scope: based on photographs of the inner courtyard, it shows the front of the storied cave dwelling with arched openings above and below and the inward-facing houses on either side; the incomplete surrounding walls are left blank at the edges, and hidden exterior views are not added.

hu_zhanggu.era: Built over generations in the Ming–Qing

facts: Subject: part of the roofscape of the Ming–Qing dwellings of Zhangguying Village.

yn_jingzhen.sub: Dai Theravada Buddhist temple · Ordination hall
yn_jingzhen.yearNote: 1701 is the year the Octagonal Pavilion was founded; later repairs, such as those of 1978 and 1993, are recorded separately, and the other, now destroyed buildings of Jingzhen Temple are not invented in the drawing.
yn_jingzhen.lede: The Octagonal Pavilion is not a small garden pavilion for enjoying the view but the ordination hall of a Dai Theravada Buddhist temple. Tiered roofs spread out in eight directions and close lightly into a spire; most of the original Jingzhen Temple no longer survives, and the ordination hall built in 1701 has lasted to the present through repeated repairs.
facts: Use: the ordination hall of a Theravada Buddhist temple, and also an important surviving historic building of Jingzhen Temple.
Date: founded in the 40th year of Kangxi in the Qing (1701) and repaired many times in modern times; the traces of repair are not hidden.
Form: tiered roofs spreading in eight directions, decorated eaves and a brick pavilion body; the plate follows present-day photographs.
