cq_huguang.era: Qing guild hall · Enlarged in the Daoguang reign
cq_huguang.yearNote: The guild hall complex took shape in the Qing and was enlarged in the Daoguang reign; about 1846 places the surviving Qing structure, and the plate shows the opera stage as repaired in 2003–2005, without asserting that every beam and column is original 1846 work.
cq_huguang.lede: Carved wooden balustrade panels run across the front of the raised stage, and beneath the flying eaves a three-bay stage opens. The opera stage of the Huguang Guild Hall in Chongqing hosted the public life of migrant gatherings, rituals and theatergoing.
facts: The Huguang Guild Hall of Chongqing, in the Dongshuimen area of Yuzhong District, is a Qing complex of migrant guild halls and is now in the sixth batch of national protected sites.

The guild hall was enlarged in the Daoguang reign, and its present state has also undergone modern conservation repairs; the plate takes the front of one opera stage and does not draw the whole group of courtyards.

The balustrade panels, beams and backstage decoration come from photographs; the colored plate keeps the dark brown carved wood, red backstage and bluish-gray tiles, rather than tinting the Qing building uniformly in a dynasty color.

cq_diaoyu.name: Diaoyu Fortress Site
cq_diaoyu.era: Fortifications expanded 1243 · Gate tower built later
cq_diaoyu.yearNote: 1243 is a key milestone in the building of the Southern Song defensive system at Diaoyu Fortress, and the timeline is placed by the site. The upper timber gate tower of Huguo Gate was built later, and not all the structure in the photographs is taken as original Song work.
cq_diaoyu.lede: A thick stone wall is pierced by a single arched opening, and stone steps up to the walls cling to the cliff. Huguo Gate condenses the strategic terrain and mountain-fortress defenses of Diaoyu Fortress into a narrow entrance.
facts: Diaoyu Fortress is the site of a Southern Song mountain fortress, expanded in 1243, that endured a long war of siege defense.
The plate takes the stone gateway of Huguo Gate, the later gate tower and the stone steps in front, keeping the passage along the cliff; it does not reconstruct the whole fortress.
The original fourth-batch national protected site list registered it under "Hechuan City, Sichuan Province"; it now lies within Chongqing, and the page uses Chongqing as its region.

cq_tongnan.name: Cliff Carvings of the Great Buddha Temple, Tongnan
cq_tongnan.era: Head carved in the Tang · Whole statue completed 1151
cq_tongnan.yearNote: The Buddha's head was carved in the Tang and the body continued in the Northern Song, with the whole statue completed in 1151; the surviving gold leaf includes the results of conservation and restoration in the 2010s, and the timeline is not placed by the temple's founding year.
cq_tongnan.lede: Gold leaf covers the broad face and flowing robe folds, and dark snail-shell curls set off the Great Buddha's calm. The head and body of the Tongnan Great Buddha were carved in turn, and the seated figure was completed only after spanning the Tang and Song.
facts: The head was carved first, the body was continued in the Northern Song, and the whole statue was completed in 1151; the plate takes this Great Buddha and does not represent all the cliff niches and figures of the temple.

The surviving seated figure rests its right hand flat before the abdomen and its left hand on the knee, with snail-shell curls on the head and a kasaya draped over the body; the feet hidden by the offering table are not conjecturally completed.

The gilding has been renewed over the centuries and has undergone modern conservation and restoration. The colored plate follows photographs of the gold leaf and dark snail-shell curls, and this artistic rendering is not a reconstruction of the original Song finish.

hn_yanqing.yearNote: Surviving Yuan Jade Emperor Pavilion; approximate timeline placement.
hn_yanqing.lede: A square brick pavilion narrows upward into an octagonal kiosk, with glazed components lifting the roof tier by tier. The Jade Emperor Pavilion preserves the distinctive outline of the Yuan architecture of Yanqing Daoist Temple.
facts: The Jade Emperor Pavilion is the main surviving historic building of Yanqing Daoist Temple, a brick pavilion imitating timber construction and three stories in outward appearance.
Its lower story is square and its upper part octagonal; the plate takes the Jade Emperor Pavilion and its platform, excluding the halls added in modern times.
The building has been jacked up as a whole for protection. The timeline uses an approximate Yuan placement and does not take the date of the conservation work as the construction date.

hn_yuefei.era: Ming–Qing buildings and later repairs; exact construction year of the Second Hall unknown

facts: The Yue Fei Temple of Tangyin is in the fifth batch of national protected sites; its surviving buildings went through construction and repair in the Ming and Qing.

hn_songyang.name: Songyang Academy
hn_songyang.sub: Front of the Qing main gate
hn_songyang.era: Surviving gate is Qing, with later repairs; approximately placed in the Kangxi period
hn_songyang.yearNote: The surviving gate is Qing and has been repaired; it is placed approximately in the Kangxi period.
hn_songyang.lede: A round-ridged roof sits low over the three-bay main gate, and stone columns and gray brick keep the entrance plain. The academy's fame comes from teaching in the Song, while the buildings seen today continue a Qing layout.
facts: The central axis of Songyang Academy runs, in order, through the main gate, the Hall of the Former Sages, the Lecture Hall, the Daotong Shrine and the Library Tower.

The surviving buildings and layout are mainly Qing; the plate shows only the main gate and does not use the Northern Wei founding of the temple or the Northern Song year of the conferred name as the construction date of this gate.

hn_xiangguo.name: Daxiangguo Temple
hn_xiangguo.era: Qianlong rebuilding phase (Qing), not the Northern Qi founding year
hn_xiangguo.yearNote: The Qianlong rebuilding phase of the Qing, not the Northern Qi founding year of the temple.
hn_xiangguo.lede: In 1642 a breach of the Yellow River buried Kaifeng, and Daxiangguo Temple with it, under silt; the halls seen today follow the layout fixed by a rebuilding in 1661 (Shunzhi 18) and a renovation in 1766 (Qianlong 31). The Daxiong Baodian (Mahavira Hall) shown here stands at the centre of the second courtyard: seven bays wide, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, set on a Sumeru-base terrace ringed by stone balustrades whose posts are carved with small lions. The Northern Song complex of sixty-four cloisters is long gone, but the scale of a Qing state-sponsored monastery remains.
facts: Form: the Daxiong Baodian is seven bays wide and five deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of yellow and green glazed tile and a total height of about 13 m. In front lies a Sumeru-base terrace; white stone balustrades surround hall and terrace, their post-heads carved with more than fifty small lions, no two alike.

History: in 712 (Yanhe 1) Emperor Ruizong of Tang bestowed the name Xiangguo Si. After the flood of 1642, the gate, Hall of Heavenly Kings and Daxiong Baodian were rebuilt in 1661 (Shunzhi 18) and renovated again in 1766 (Qianlong 31); the existing halls took their present form then, and Qianlong wrote the plaque 'Imperially Built Xiangguo Si'.

Fortunes: in 1927 troops of Feng Yuxiang destroyed every Buddhist image in the temple except the Thousand-Armed Guanyin and turned the temple into the Zhongshan Market; the main hall long stood empty and was used for exhibitions. In Northern Song the temple governed sixty-four cloisters on 540 mu of land; what stands today is only a corner of that core.

hn_zzchenghuang.name: Zhengzhou City God Temple
hn_zzchenghuang.sub: Front of the three-bay main hall
hn_zzchenghuang.era: Surviving Ming–Qing historic buildings; exact construction year of the individual building unknown
hn_zzchenghuang.yearNote: Surviving Ming–Qing historic buildings; the exact construction year of the individual building is unknown.
hn_zzchenghuang.lede: The best-preserved group of Ming-Qing buildings in old Zhengzhou is not a government office but this City God Temple. The Republican-era Zhengxian Gazetteer records renovations led by seven prefectural magistrates between 1501 (Hongzhi 14) and 1890 (Guangxu 16), and the gate, passage hall, stage, main hall and rear chambers still line up on one axis. The three-bay front shown here, with its green glazed-tile overhanging-gable roof, four small-octagonal stone columns in the central bay and three pairs of red plank doors, corresponds in the gazetteer's description to the temple's front gate hall; the main hall proper, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, stands north of the stage.
facts: Form: the front shown is three bays wide and two deep, with a green glazed-tile overhanging-gable roof and seven-tier bracket sets with three ang under the eaves, the ang-tips shaped as triple clouds and the beam-ends as elephant trunks. Four small-octagonal stone columns stand front and back in the central bay; three pairs of solid plank doors hang on the through-columns, with a fan-shaped flight of six steps and a pair of stone lions before them.

History: originally named the Temple of the City God, Marquis Lingyou, it enshrines Ji Xin, a general of Liu Bang of Han, and was founded in the early Ming. According to the Republican-era Zhengxian Gazetteer it was repeatedly renovated by magistrates: Shi Chuncui in 1501 (Hongzhi 14), Liu Ru in Jiajing 6, Li Shixuan in Longqing 4, and others in the Kangxi, Qianlong and Guangxu reigns. A stele with the cursive 'Eulogy of Fortune' by the early-Ming deputy magistrate Zhang Dayou survives in the temple.

Comparison: on the axis, the stage is a two-storey hip-and-gable pavilion whose nineteen roof ridges cross and overlap; the main hall is three bays square under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with gilt-style bracket sets in the central bay; the five-bay rear chamber has an overhanging-gable roof fronted by a rolled-ridge worship porch. With gate, tower, hall and chamber roof types all present, it is one of the larger and more complete surviving City God temples in Henan.

hn_jiawenmiao.name: Jia County Confucian Temple
hn_jiawenmiao.era: Surviving Dacheng Hall with Ming–Qing repairs; Five Dynasties founding year not used
hn_jiawenmiao.yearNote: Surviving Dacheng Hall with Ming–Qing repairs; the Five Dynasties founding year of the temple is not used.
hn_jiawenmiao.lede: The four front-eave columns of the Dacheng Hall are carved through their whole length with coiling dragons, their capitals cut as tiger heads, and the dragon columns are of wood: Qing wooden dragon columns of this kind survive nowhere else in Henan. The hall is five bays wide under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of green glazed tile, and the dragon slab before its terrace shows two dragons playing with a 'spider' rather than a flaming pearl. The temple began as a Kong family shrine completed in 954 (Xiande 1 of Later Zhou) and became the official Confucian temple in 1206 (Taihe 6 of Jin); the Dacheng Hall shown here is the Qing timber structure left by repeated Ming and Qing renovations.
facts: Form: the Dacheng Hall is five bays wide and three deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of green glazed tile, 15.5 m high and 19.7 m across the front. The four wooden eave columns are carved through with coiling dragons, their capitals cut as fanged tiger faces looking down on the dragons; the column bases are covered with auspicious scenes, and the architraves, bracket sets and sparrow braces are also pierced with figures, carts, birds, flowers and clouds.

History: descendants of Confucius built a family shrine here in 954 (Xiande 1 of Later Zhou); in 1206 (Taihe 6 of Jin) the magistrate Zhang Zhixing enlarged it on the same site into the official Confucian temple. The Dacheng Hall was restored and its dragon slab carved under the Yingzong emperor of Ming (1459); the temple was rebuilt eleven times, and the surviving Dacheng Hall, Ji Gate and side halls are all Qing timber structures.

Comparison: the wooden dragon columns are later than the Song dragon columns of the Sage Mother Hall at Jinci, yet they are the only surviving example in Henan. The outer bracket sets and purlins keep original painted decoration that is neither the Beijing 'palace style' nor the Suzhou-Hangzhou 'Su style' but a Central Plains local manner. The temple retains 22 buildings with 71 bays, laid out with the school on the left and the shrine on the right, serving as both Kong family shrine and county school.

hn_jiahuiguan.name: Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall, Jia County
hn_jiahuiguan.sub: Gate tower with bell and drum towers
hn_jiahuiguan.era: Qing buildings; exact dates of the individual buildings in the surviving group unknown
hn_jiahuiguan.yearNote: Qing buildings; the exact dates of the individual buildings in the surviving group are unknown.
hn_jiahuiguan.lede: Seen from the street, the three-bay gatehouse is flanked by the bell and drum towers; its upper storey is the theatre stage, which faces north into the courtyard where the audience filled the open ground. The Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall of Jiaxian was founded in 1693 (Kangxi 32) by merchants from Shanxi and Shaanxi as a way-station and guild house where the old Nanyang-Luoyang and Xuchang-Luoyang roads crossed. Shown here are the gatehouse and the two towers: each tower stands on a 4 m base, with twelve round timber columns carrying a cross-beamed roof under two tiers of flaring eaves, rising above the ridge of the gatehouse.
facts: Form: the gatehouse is three bays wide, the central bay for passage and the side bays for gatekeepers and reception; the open three-bay upper storey faces north as the stage, its brick-carved ridge crowned at the centre by a qilin bearing a treasure vase. The bell and drum towers on either side stand on bases 4 m high, each with twelve round timber columns supporting cross beams, double tiers of flaring eaves and solid bracket sets.

History: the guild hall was founded in 1693 (Kangxi 32) with funds from Shanxi and Shaanxi merchants and is also called the Shan-Shaan Temple or Guandi Temple. It faces south over a watercourse on a site of 6,300 square metres; the river-guarding screen wall before the gate is 8 m wide, 7 m high and 1 m thick, with a brick-carved coiled dragon on a red-sandstone base.

Comparison: the east and west galleries have eleven bays each, the courtyard could hold a thousand spectators, and to the north stand the five-bay Guan Gong Hall and, behind it, the Spring-and-Autumn Pavilion. Jiaxian lay where the Nanyang-Luoyang and Xuchang-Luoyang roads met; the tea route north from Nanyang branched here toward Shanxi, and the hall is regarded as a surviving relic of the Qing 'Ten-Thousand-Li Tea Road' in Henan.

hn_linfeng.name: Linfeng Fortified Village
hn_linfeng.sub: West Gate and connected red-stone wall
hn_linfeng.era: Red-stone walls rebuilt in the 1st year of Tongzhi
hn_linfeng.yearNote: Red-stone walls rebuilt in the 1st year of Tongzhi.
hn_linfeng.lede: The red-stone plaque above the gate is cut with the two characters 'Linfeng', and the iron sheathing of the doors is chiselled 'first year of Tongzhi, the year renxu': this wall wears its own birthday on its face. Linfeng Fort was originally a late-Ming earthen stockade; in 1862 (Tongzhi 1) the villager Zhu Zifeng led its rebuilding in purplish-red ashlar, an oval ring 1,100 m around and 6.6 m high, with five watch-towers and eight hundred merlons, and three gates set by the trigram directions to the north-west, south-west and south-east. Shown here are the west-facing Linfeng Gate and the wall joined to it.
facts: Form: the wall is stone outside and earth within, built of purplish-red ashlar on an oval plan 1,100 m around and 6.6 m high, with five watch-towers and 800 merlons. Each gate is a barrel-vaulted opening fitted with a pair of elm doors sheathed in 10 cm iron plate, with flood gates and drainage culverts outside; a moat 13 m wide circles the fort.

History: the Zhu clan is said to have moved here from Hongtong, Shanxi, in the Wanli reign of Ming and first raised an earthen stockade. In 1862 (Tongzhi 1) Zhu Zifeng, a native holding a purchased magistrate's rank, led the building of the red-stone fort; the words 'first year of Tongzhi, the year renxu' chiselled on the iron of the north-west gate are still legible. Inside survive one Ming courtyard house and more than a hundred Qing buildings with over four hundred bays.

Comparison: after 1949 village walls were pulled down across the region, but Linfeng's low-lying site and the need for flood defence saved it; Luo Zhewen called it 'the first red-stone fort of the Central Plains'. It was listed as a Chinese Historic and Cultural Village in 2005, among the first batch of Traditional Chinese Villages in 2012, and from 2014 the National Cultural Heritage Administration funded its overall restoration.

hn_gaoge.name: Gaoge Temple
hn_gaoge.sub: Pavilion and upper part of the high platform
hn_gaoge.era: Ming building with later repairs; approximate timeline placement
hn_gaoge.yearNote: Ming building with later repairs; approximate timeline placement.
hn_gaoge.lede: The one pavilion-hall left from a Ming princely palace. In 1404 (Yongle 2) the Yongle emperor enfeoffed his third son Zhu Gaosui as Prince of Zhao; the prince took up residence at Zhangde (Anyang) in 1425 (Hongxi 1) and turned the prefectural offices into his palace. The palace was abolished with the fall of the Ming in 1644, and by the Republican era only this Dashi Pavilion remained; because it stands on a brick platform about 8 m high it is known as Gaoge Si, the 'High Pavilion Temple'. The existing pavilion was rebuilt in 1470 (Chenghua 6), with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of glazed tile; shown here are the pavilion body and its two tiers of eaves above the stone balustrade of the platform.
facts: Form: a pavilion on a high platform, more than 20 m in total height. The square brick platform is about 8 m high and 13 m on a side, with a flight of 32 stone steps on the south; white marble balustrades with carved lions line the steps and the platform top. The pavilion is three bays square, about 9 m each way, under a double-eaved nine-ridge hip-and-gable roof of glazed tile, with four round timber through-columns rising inside to the top beams.

History: Zhu Gaosui was made Prince of Zhao in 1404 (Yongle 2), took up residence at Zhangde in 1425 (Hongxi 1) and converted the prefectural offices into the Prince of Zhao's palace, of which the Dashi Pavilion was one hall; the existing building was rebuilt in 1470 (Chenghua 6). The Zhao line passed through eleven generations until the palace was abolished in 1644 (Chongzhen 17); by the Republican era its buildings had collapsed, leaving only this pavilion.

Comparison: most Ming princely palaces were demolished after the dynasty fell, and what survives elsewhere, such as the gate of the Jingjiang palace in Guilin, the Longting of the Zhou palace in Kaifeng or the Wangjing Tower of the Lu palace in Xinxiang, are fragments; Gaoge Si is the only building left of the Zhao palace. Twenty-five dragons carved in stone, interspersed with Sanskrit script, run around the outer walls of the pavilion, a rare decoration for a princely hall.

hn_wenzhige.name: Wenzhi Pavilion, Xun County
hn_wenzhige.sub: Surviving crossroads bell and drum tower
hn_wenzhige.era: Surviving pavilion rebuilt in the Kangxi period according to research, approximately placed on the timeline; the Ming date in the national list is for the city wall and Wenzhi Pavilion as a whole
hn_wenzhige.yearNote: According to research, the surviving pavilion was rebuilt in the Kangxi period, and its timeline placement is approximate; the Ming date in the national protected site list refers to the city wall and Wenzhi Pavilion as a whole.
hn_wenzhige.lede: The east-west and north-south main streets of old Junxian cross here; the base is pierced by vaulted openings on all four sides, and carts and pedestrians pass beneath the pavilion. It is at once the bell-and-drum tower at the heart of the town and a gate-tower over the street. Originally called the Central Pavilion, of unknown founding date, it received the town bell after 1615 (Wanli 43) and has been known as the Bell-and-Drum Tower ever since; it burned in 1649 (Shunzhi 6) and was rebuilt in 1709 (Kangxi 48) by magistrate Liang Tongluo, who renamed it Wenzhi Ge, 'Pavilion of Civil Rule'. Shown here are the brick base and the two-storey, double-eaved pyramidal-roofed pavilion that make up the surviving structure.
facts: Form: about 20 m high in all, in two parts, base and pavilion. The square brick base is about 12 m on a side, with an arched vault through the middle of each face so that the four openings align east-west and north-south. On top stands a two-storey square pavilion about 10 m high, with a double-eaved four-sided pyramidal roof, upturned corners and ornamental ridges trimmed with glazed tile; the lower storey opens on all four sides, and the platform is ringed by a gallery and a 1 m parapet with square openings.

History: the Jiaqing-era Junxian Gazetteer records that 'after the yimao year of Wanli (1615) the bell was moved to the Central Pavilion'. It was destroyed by fire in 1649 (Shunzhi 6) and rebuilt in 1709 (Kangxi 48) by magistrate Liang Tongluo, who renamed it Wenzhi Ge after the idea of 'ruling by civil virtue'; Zhang Xi wrote a 'Record of the Rebuilding of Wenzhi Ge'. The present pavilion is the structure left by that rebuilding, with later repairs.

Comparison: above the four vaults are Qing bluestone horizontal tablets, 'Red glow streams from the eastern wall' and 'Jade pours from the western hills' by Zhao Sulu on the east and west, 'Clear waters ring the Li' and 'Dark mist guards the Pi' by Zhang Zhe on the south and north. The pavilion is listed together with the surviving stretch of city wall on the Wei River, first built in 1370 (Hongwu 3), and is one of the heritage points of the Junxian section of the Grand Canal.

mm_ananda.sub: Whole temple body, central spire and projecting entrances
mm_ananda.yearNote: The Indian government's conservation project description gives the early 12th century; 1110 is only an approximate placement within that period, and none of the unverified exact years 1090, 1091 or 1105 is chosen. The surviving form includes later restoration.
mm_ananda.lede: Tiers of terraces stack up on the broad temple body, the golden central spire points to the sky, and the entrances project beyond the square main mass. The Ananda Temple shows the outline of a large Bagan Buddhist temple with interior chambers.
facts: The plate includes the whole temple body, the central spire and the projecting entrances, and does not substitute a detail of the central spire for the whole temple; the outer enclosure wall and freestanding gateways are excluded.

The Indian government's description records construction in the early 12th century and notes that after the 2016 earthquake the Archaeological Survey of India took part in its conservation and restoration.

The Indian government's conservation project description gives the early 12th century; 1110 is only an approximate placement within that period, and none of the unverified exact years 1090, 1091 or 1105 is chosen. The surviving form includes later restoration.

la_xieng_thong_sim.name: Sim of Wat Xieng Thong
la_xieng_thong_sim.sub: The sim (main hall) and its supporting platform
la_xieng_thong_sim.yearNote: Official sources record its founding in about 1560; the main hall was repaired in 1928, in 1952–1960 and at other times, so not all the surviving decoration can be regarded as original 16th-century work.
la_xieng_thong_sim.lede: Low-sweeping roofs spread to either side, and the layered gables and fine gold ornament reflect the lightness of the timber structure. The sim of Wat Xieng Thong rests quietly on its platform beneath the traditional roof curves of Luang Prabang.
facts: The depicted subject is the sim and its supporting platform, excluding the later Royal Funerary Carriage House; the tiles, timberwork and gold ornament are colored from photographs of their present state.
Official tourism sources record the founding of the temple in about 1560 and repeated repairs to the main hall; the founding phase and later decoration are described separately.

Official sources record its founding in about 1560; the main hall was repaired in 1928, in 1952–1960 and at other times, so not all the surviving decoration can be regarded as original 16th-century work.

About 1560

vn_po_klong_garai.name: Main Tower of Po Klong Garai
vn_po_klong_garai.sub: Surviving main shrine tower with entrance and base
vn_po_klong_garai.yearNote: Official Khánh Hòa Province sources give the late 13th–early 14th century; 1300 is only for approximate ordering, and the construction date of the tower is not inferred from the life dates of the king worshipped there.
vn_po_klong_garai.place: Khánh Hòa Province · Phan Rang–Tháp Chàm
vn_po_klong_garai.lede: The red-brick tower body is divided by pilasters and false doors, and the layered brick ornament of the upper tiers tapers steadily. The main tower of Po Klong Garai preserves the outline of a Cham temple tower and also carries on local ritual traditions.
facts: The plate shows only the main shrine tower of the three towers, excluding the gate tower and the long-ridged fire tower; the main tower's entrance has an inset stone door frame and a relief of the dancing Shiva.

Official Khánh Hòa Province sources record that the tower group was built in the late 13th–early 14th century. The location is registered under the current Khánh Hòa Province, and the former name, Ninh Thuận Province, is kept for search.

Official Khánh Hòa Province sources give the late 13th–early 14th century; 1300 is only for approximate ordering, and the construction date of the tower is not inferred from the life dates of the king worshipped there.
captions: Main Tower of Po Klong Garai · Surviving main shrine tower with entrance and base
Late 13th–early 14th century

vn_hue_ngo_mon.name: Meridian Gate (Ngọ Môn) of the Huế Imperial City
vn_hue_ngo_mon.sub: Complete gate platform and Five Phoenix Pavilion
vn_hue_ngo_mon.yearNote: 1833 is the construction date of the Meridian Gate; the surviving timber pavilion, roofs and platform have undergone later repairs, and there are also records of modern repairs.
vn_hue_ngo_mon.lede: The broad gate platform folds forward into wings at both sides, and above it the Five Phoenix Pavilion spreads out under roofs of differing heights. The Meridian Gate combines a masonry palace gate with a timber pavilion to form the front outline of the Huế Imperial City.
facts: The platform is U-shaped, with five passages in all: three on the front and two in the side wings; the five passages must not be drawn as five openings on the front.

Official tourism sources record its construction in 1833, with yellow tiles on the central roof and blue-green tiles on either side; the plate includes the complete platform and the Five Phoenix Pavilion.
1833 is the construction date of the Meridian Gate; the surviving timber pavilion, roofs and platform have undergone later repairs, and there are also records of modern repairs.
captions: Meridian Gate of the Huế Imperial City · Complete gate platform and Five Phoenix Pavilion
1833 · Reign of Emperor Minh Mạng

ph_manila_san_agustin.name: San Agustin Church, Manila
ph_manila_san_agustin.sub: Surviving church facade and bell tower
ph_manila_san_agustin.yearNote: 1607 is the completion date of the surviving stone church, as distinct from the earlier wooden churches. The bell tower and later repairs have their own histories, and the present building as a whole is not dated as original fabric of a single year.
ph_manila_san_agustin.lede: Tiered orders of columns divide the doors and windows of the stone facade, a round window and a cross mark the triangular pediment, and the surviving bell tower adjoins it on the right. San Agustin Church preserves another architectural tradition of old Manila.
facts: The plate shows the surviving main facade and the single bell tower on the right; the low remnant of the lost left tower is kept and not reconstructed as symmetrical twin towers.

The National Museum of the Philippines records that the surviving stone church was completed in 1607; the original wooden church and later repairs are described separately, and the monastery as a whole is not drawn.

1607 is the completion date of the surviving stone church, as distinct from the earlier wooden churches. The bell tower and later repairs have their own histories, and the present building as a whole is not dated as original fabric of a single year.
captions: San Agustin Church, Manila · Surviving church facade and bell tower
Stone church completed 1607

kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.name: Sudeoksa Daeungjeon
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.sub: Single Daeungjeon hall and stone platform
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.era: Hall built 1308; the temple's founding is dated separately.
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.yearNote: Hall built in 1308; the temple's founding is dated separately.
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.lede: A gently sloping overhanging gable roof of tiles rests on the three-bay timber hall, with beam ends projecting tier by tier from the gable side. With its gray-brown timber and simple lattice doors, Sudeoksa Daeungjeon preserves the airy form of a Buddhist hall of the late Goryeo.
facts: The surviving Daeungjeon was built in 1308; the temple's founding and the hall's construction date are recorded separately.
Three bays wide and four bays deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof; the columns carry the eaves, and the beam frame on the gable side is an important part of identifying the structure.
The plate shows only the Daeungjeon and its stone platform, excluding the stone lantern in front and the temple's other buildings.
captions: Sudeoksa Daeungjeon · Single Daeungjeon hall and stone platform
Goryeo · 1308

kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.name: Buseoksa Muryangsujeon
kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.era: Surviving Muryangsujeon rebuilt in 1376; the temple was founded in 676.
kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.yearNote: The surviving Muryangsujeon was rebuilt in 1376; the temple was founded in 676.
kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.lede: Long eaves extend along the five-bay hall, its timber columns slightly curved, and pale lattice doors line up beneath the deep eaves. Set high within Buseoksa, the Muryangsujeon is an important surviving timber Buddhist hall of the Goryeo period.
facts: The temple was founded in 676, and the surviving Muryangsujeon shown here is assigned to the Goryeo by its 1376 rebuilding date.
Five bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the columns swell at mid-height, and the lattice doors and stone platform are preserved in their present state.
The hall enshrines Amitabha Buddha; the plate takes the exterior of the hall, and the stone lantern in front is not included in this subject.
captions: Buseoksa Muryangsujeon · Single Muryangsujeon hall and steps
Goryeo · 1376

kr_bulguksa_dabotap.name: Dabotap of Bulguksa
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.sub: Complete Dabotap stone pagoda with stairways on four sides
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.era: Officially dated to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, and the pagoda's ordering year is approximately taken as 751.
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.yearNote: Officially dated to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, and the pagoda's ordering year is approximately taken as 751.
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.lede: Square stone pillars support a pagoda body whose tiers keep changing form, while balustrades and an octagonal canopy shift its scale in the upper part. Carved from granite into a complex outline close to timber construction, Dabotap is entirely different from the common multi-roofed stone pagodas.
facts: Korean authorities officially date Dabotap to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, the ordering uses an approximate value, and no precise completion year is claimed for the pagoda.

Square stone pillars and stairways on four sides below combine with octagonal elements above, and official sources explain that its number of stories is hard to count in the way used for an ordinary pavilion-style pagoda.
Following its present state, the single surviving stone lion is kept, the lost lions are not added back, and the neighboring Seokgatap is not drawn.
captions: Dabotap of Bulguksa · Complete stone pagoda with stairways on four sides
Unified Silla · Approximate placement

kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.name: Changdeokgung Injeongjeon
kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.era: The surviving Injeongjeon shown here was rebuilt in 1804; the palace's founding and successive fires are dated separately.
kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.yearNote: The surviving Injeongjeon shown here was rebuilt in 1804; the palace's founding and successive fires are dated separately.
kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.lede: Double flying eaves support a broad gray-tiled roof, and red columns and blue-green dancheong painting surround the five-bay hall. With its terrace, central stairway and tall, open interior, Injeongjeon forms the main hall of Changdeokgung where state ceremonies were held.
facts: The National Heritage Portal gives the date of the surviving building as the 4th year of King Sunjo of Joseon (1804), and the palace's founding year is not substituted for it.
Five bays wide and four bays deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the double eaves outside do not mean there are two separate floors inside.
The plate shows only Injeongjeon and its terrace; the side corridors, the rank stones in the courtyard and other palace buildings are not included.
captions: Changdeokgung Injeongjeon · Injeongjeon hall and terrace
Joseon · 1804

kp_kaesong_namdaemun.name: Namdaemun of Kaesong
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.sub: Stone gate platform and postwar rebuilt gate tower
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.era: Inner-city gate first built 1391–1393; the gate tower was destroyed in war in 1950 and rebuilt from 1954, a caption in the World Heritage nomination file records its restoration in 1955, and the timeline is placed by the surviving gate tower.
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.yearNote: The inner-city gate was first built in 1391–1393; the gate tower was destroyed in war in 1950 and rebuilt from 1954, a caption in the World Heritage nomination file records its restoration in 1955, and the timeline is placed by the surviving gate tower.
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.lede: A single stone arch pierces the gate platform, and the open three-bay gate tower is covered by a broad tiled roof. Namdaemun of Kaesong layers the gate site of the Goryeo capital, the old stone platform and the timber gate tower restored after the war in a single place.
facts: The gate was built together with the inner city wall in 1391–1393; the surviving gate tower is a postwar reconstruction, and the timeline uses 1955.

The ICOMOS evaluation records that the gate tower was destroyed in 1950 and restored from 1954; the caption in the nomination file and the repair notes give 1955, and the dating note keeps both records.
The gate platform has a single arch, and the gate tower is three bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a great bell hanging inside; this entry does not include the small shrine nearby.
captions: Namdaemun of Kaesong · Stone gate platform and postwar rebuilt gate tower
Postwar reconstruction · 1955

kp_pothong_gate.name: Pyongyang Pothong Gate
kp_pothong_gate.sub: Gate platform and double-eaved gate tower of Pothong Gate
kp_pothong_gate.era: According to Kim Il Sung University sources, the surviving Pothong Gate was extensively repaired in 1473, with further repairs and extensions later; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not used as the date of the surviving gate tower.
kp_pothong_gate.yearNote: According to Kim Il Sung University sources, the surviving Pothong Gate was extensively repaired in 1473, with further repairs and extensions later; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not used as the date of the surviving gate tower.
kp_pothong_gate.lede: A massive stone platform is pierced by a single arched gateway, and the double-eaved gate tower rises from its top. Pothong Gate preserves the form of the western city gate of old Pyongyang, its masonry platform and painted timber tower forming two clearly distinct upper and lower parts.
facts: Kim Il Sung University sources record that the surviving gate underwent major repairs in 1473, followed by further extensions; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not the exact date of the surviving timberwork.
The gate tower is three bays wide and three bays deep, with two tiers of eaves; the platform is built of granite, with a single semicircular arched gateway at the center.
The depicted subject is the surviving platform and gate tower; the extending city walls are not reconstructed, and the modern streetscape is not included.
captions: Pyongyang Pothong Gate · Gate platform and double-eaved gate tower
Joseon · 1473

kp_sungyang_hall.name: Lecture Hall of Sungyang Academy
kp_sungyang_hall.sub: Five-bay lecture hall of the academy
kp_sungyang_hall.era: The academy was established in 1573, and the lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the exact construction year of the surviving timberwork is undetermined, and about 1600 is only a timeline position within the Joseon period.
kp_sungyang_hall.yearNote: The academy was established in 1573, and the lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the exact construction year of the surviving timberwork is undetermined, and about 1600 is only a timeline position within the Joseon period.
kp_sungyang_hall.lede: The five-bay lecture hall stands across the academy terrace, its open central wooden floor and end rooms forming a simple hall. Sungyang Academy places teaching and rites at the front and back, and the lecture hall is its space for study.
facts: The academy was established in 1573 and received a royal name in 1575, and the surviving lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the specific construction year of the timberwork is unclear, and about 1600 serves only for timeline placement.

The World Heritage nomination file records the lecture hall as five bays wide and three bays deep; the plan has an open three-bay central hall with rooms on either side, under a single-eaved overhanging gable roof.
The plate shows only the lecture hall, referring to nomination photographs, old photographs and plans; neither the three-door gate in front nor the shrine above is mistaken for the lecture hall.
captions: Lecture Hall of Sungyang Academy · Five-bay lecture hall of the academy
Joseon · Approximate placement

kp_sonjuk_bridge.name: Sonjuk Bridge, Kaesong
kp_sonjuk_bridge.sub: Old stone beam bridge and 1780 stone balustrades
kp_sonjuk_bridge.era: The nomination file says the bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, exact year unknown; about 1100 is an ordering position, 1392 is the year Jeong Mong-ju was killed, and the stone balustrades were added in 1780.
kp_sonjuk_bridge.yearNote: The nomination file says the bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, exact year unknown; about 1100 is an ordering position, 1392 is the year Jeong Mong-ju was killed, and the stone balustrades were added in 1780.
kp_sonjuk_bridge.lede: A short granite beam bridge spans a shallow stream, its deck enclosed by round-topped stone posts and rails. Sonjuk Bridge became a memorial site because Jeong Mong-ju was killed there, and the later balustrades also record its withdrawal from everyday traffic.
facts: The nomination file says the stone bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, and its exact construction year has not been confirmed; about 1100 is an ordering position, and 1392 is the year of the killing.
The bridge is 8.35 m long and 3.36 m wide, with stone piers carrying stone beams topped by stone slabs; it is not an arch bridge. The surviving stone balustrades on both sides were added in 1780.
Only the old Sonjuk Bridge and its later balustrades are drawn; the separate bridge built alongside for traffic, the stele pavilion and the inscribed steles are not part of the subject.
captions: Sonjuk Bridge, Kaesong · Old stone beam bridge and 1780 stone balustrades
Goryeo · Approximate placement

jp_ueno_toshogu_karamon.name: Karamon of Ueno Tōshō-gū
jp_ueno_toshogu_karamon.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1651 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
jp_ueno_toshogu_karamon.lede: An undulating karahafu gable spreads above the doors, and gilded carving is concentrated on the small, intricate entrance. The plate takes the Karamon of Ueno Tōshō-gū, built in 1651.
facts: Cultural Heritage Online dates the Karamon to 1651 and records it as a mukaikaramon gate one bay wide and one bay deep, with copper-tile roofing.
The plate shows only the Karamon; the shrine buildings behind it, the openwork fences on either side and the lanterns along the approach are outside its scope.
The gold leaf and painted color are taken from photographs of the present state, and the surface colors after restoration cannot be directly equated with the original state of 1651.
captions: Karamon of Ueno Tōshō-gū · The Karamon alone
Edo period · 1651

jp_nezu_romon.name: Rōmon of Nezu Shrine
jp_nezu_romon.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1706 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
jp_nezu_romon.lede: Vermilion columns support the upper story and a broad tiled roof, and the central passage is flanked by two niches for guardian figures. The Rōmon of Nezu Shrine covers its two-story gate with a single large roof, in compact proportions.
facts: The Rōmon belongs to the building of Nezu Shrine completed in 1706; Cultural Heritage Online records it as a three-bay, single-passage two-story gate with an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof and pantile roofing.
The lower story has only a single central passage, with niches for zuishin guardian figures on either side; a balustrade runs around the outer edge of the upper story.
The plate takes the front of the Rōmon and does not merge in the shrine's Karamon, main sanctuary or Senbon Torii.
captions: Rōmon of Nezu Shrine · Three-bay, single-passage two-story gate
Edo period · 1706

jp_asakusa_jinja.name: Asakusa Shrine
jp_asakusa_jinja.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1649 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
jp_asakusa_jinja.lede: On the east side of Sensō-ji, this shrine preserves early Edo shrine buildings. The low, broad worship hall spreads out in vermilion columns and gold ornament, on a scale quite different from the nearby main hall of Sensō-ji.
facts: The surviving shrine buildings were built and donated by Tokugawa Iemitsu in 1649 and have come through disasters and war.

The main sanctuary (honden), offering hall (heiden) and worship hall (haiden) form the core of the shrine, with the main sanctuary linked to the offering hall and worship hall by a connecting passage.
This plate shows only the front of the worship hall. Asakusa Shrine and Sensō-ji are separate entries, and their dates and personal records are kept separately.
captions: Asakusa Shrine · Front of the worship hall
Edo period · 1649

jp_zojoji_sangedatsumon.name: Sangedatsumon of Zōjō-ji
jp_zojoji_sangedatsumon.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1622 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_zojoji_sangedatsumon.lede: Two tiers of deep eaves and a horizontal balustrade weigh down on the broad gate front, and three passages run through the lower story. The Sangedatsumon of Zōjō-ji preserves the grand scale of an early Edo temple entrance.
facts: The temple officially records the construction date of the surviving Sangedatsumon as 1622.
The gate is a five-bay, three-passage nijūmon (two-story gate); the plate keeps the upper and lower roofs and the three central passages.

The plate is drawn from photographs taken before the conservation repairs and omits the temporary curtains; the temple has announced conservation repairs from 2025, and the illustration does not represent what is currently visible on site.
captions: Sangedatsumon of Zōjō-ji · Five-bay, three-passage two-story gate
Edo period · 1622

jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.name: Kiyomizu Kannon-dō of Kan'ei-ji
jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.sub: Kannon Hall and the stage in front
jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1631 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding. It was moved to its present site in 1694, and conservation repairs were completed in 1996.
jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.lede: The vermilion Kannon Hall overlooks the slopes of Ueno, its wooden stage projecting toward Shinobazu Pond. It borrows the concept of Kiyomizu-dera in Kyoto, yet has survived through Tokyo's own history of construction and relocation.
facts: The Kannon Hall was built by Tenkai in 1631 and moved to its present site in 1694 for the construction of Kan'ei-ji's Konponchūdō.
The temple officially records conservation repairs to the cultural property from 1990 to 1996, restoring its appearance at the time of the Genroku-era relocation.
The plate shows the Kannon Hall and the stage in front, omitting the Moon Pine (Tsuki no Matsu) and the hillside scenery; the raised stage of Kiyomizu-dera in Kyoto is not applied to this hall.
captions: Kiyomizu Kannon-dō of Kan'ei-ji · Kannon Hall and the stage in front
Edo period · 1631

jp_gokokuji_hondo.name: Main Hall of Gokoku-ji
jp_gokokuji_hondo.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1697 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_gokokuji_hondo.lede: The copper-plate roof has oxidized to blue-green, and the broad curved roof covers a solid timber structure. The main hall of Gokoku-ji carries on the scale and craftsmanship of an Edo prayer temple of the Genroku period.
facts: Gokoku-ji was founded in 1681; the surviving Kannon Hall shown was completed in 1697, and the founding year of the temple cannot be substituted for the building's date.
Cultural Heritage Online records the main hall as seven bays wide and seven bays deep, with an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof, a three-bay kōhai (front canopy) and batten-seam copper-plate roofing.
The plate includes only the main hall, its veranda and steps, and does not merge in the later tahōtō pagoda or the relocated Gekkō-den.
captions: Main Hall of Gokoku-ji · Main hall · Kannon Hall
Edo period · 1697

jp_ikegami_pagoda.name: Five-Story Pagoda of Ikegami Honmon-ji
jp_ikegami_pagoda.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1608 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_ikegami_pagoda.lede: The five-story wooden pagoda rises from the Ikegami cemetery grounds, its dark tiled eaves tapering tier by tier. The old vermilion of the body and the bronze sōrin finial give its early Edo outline a clear, quiet presence.
facts: The official cultural property list of Ikegami Honmon-ji records the five-story pagoda as dating to the 13th year of Keichō, that is, 1608.
The pagoda has five tiers of eaves topped by a sōrin finial; the plate keeps the complete body, finial and base.
This plate does not include gravestones, the surrounding temple buildings or modern facilities; the present colors of the materials are rendered from daytime photographs.
captions: Five-Story Pagoda of Ikegami Honmon-ji · Surviving five-story wooden pagoda
Edo period · 1608

jp_shofukuji_jizodo.name: Jizō Hall of Shōfuku-ji
jp_shofukuji_jizodo.sub: Single-story Zen Buddhist hall with mokoshi
jp_shofukuji_jizodo.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1407 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_shofukuji_jizodo.lede: The great eaves of the main roof are raised high, with a low mokoshi skirt roof encircling the building below. With its compact square mass, the Jizō Hall of Shōfuku-ji preserves the form of a Muromachi-period Zen Buddhist hall in the Kantō region.
facts: Based on an ink inscription dated the 14th year of Ōei found during repairs, Cultural Heritage Online records the Jizō Hall's construction date as 1407.

The building is a Buddhist hall three bays square, single-story with a mokoshi, under an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof; the upper roof is covered with wood shingles and the mokoshi with copper plate. The two tiers of eaves do not mean two stories.
It stands in Higashimurayama, Tokyo; the plate shows only the Jizō Hall, not the other buildings of Shōfuku-ji.
captions: Jizō Hall of Shōfuku-ji · Single-story Zen Buddhist hall with mokoshi
Muromachi period · 1407

tang_timber.name: Three and a Half Tang Timber Halls
tang_timber.lede: The only Tang-dynasty timber buildings that can still be confirmed in China are three halls in Shanxi. The Amitabha Hall of Tiantai Hermitage in Pingshun was long regarded as Tang, but recent research mostly dates it to the Five Dynasties, so enthusiasts speak of “three and a half.”
tang_timber.note: Four entries correspond to the “three and a half.” Following current research, this catalog places Tiantai Hermitage in the Five Dynasties, but it stays on this list to record the traditional view.

liao_eight.name: Eight Great Liao Timber Structures
liao_eight.eyebrow: Liao timber · North and Northeast China
liao_eight.lede: Few Liao-dynasty timber buildings survive, and enthusiasts call them the “Eight Great Liao Timber Structures”: the Guanyin Pavilion and Main Gate of Dule Temple, the Mahavira Hall of Fengguo Temple, the Mahavira Hall of Kaishan Temple, the Manjushri Hall of Geyuan Temple, the Bhagavat Sutra Repository Hall of Huayan Temple, the Mahavira Hall of Shanhua Temple and the Yingxian Wooden Pagoda.
liao_eight.note: The Guanyin Pavilion and Main Gate of Dule Temple are one entry in this catalog, so seven entries stand for the eight structures. Another version of the list includes the lost Hall of the Three Great Bodhisattvas of Guangji Temple in Baodi; this list does not count it.

zhuozhang_valley.name: Zhuozhang River Valley
zhuozhang_valley.lede: The Zhuozhang River runs through the valleys around Pingshun and Lucheng. Villages along its banks preserve a dense cluster of small temples and shrines from the Five Dynasties to the Yuan, making it the classic heritage route of southeast Shanxi.
zhuozhang_valley.note: Only valley monuments already in this catalog are listed, in chronological order; a trip can follow the valley from west to east or the reverse.
